title: Race cars speed through D.C. in finale of Trump-backed Freedom 250 series
text:
WASHINGTON — IndyCar took over the streets of the nation’s capital for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the last in a series of events coordinated and promoted by President Donald Trump to mark the 250th anniversary of the United States.Just over two dozen racers zipped through a 1.66-mile course, reaching speeds up to 190 miles per hour as they traced a course down Pennsylvania and Independence avenues, crossing the National Mall twice, for the first-ever IndyCar series event in Washington, D.C.Trump’s motorcade traveled on the course down Pennsylvania Avenue ahead of the race, and the president waved the green flag at 1:10 p.m Eastern to start the 147 laps.Several military aircraft crossed the sky shortly before the race, including flyovers featuring a B-2 bomber and Air Force One.

 







Air Force One and fighter jets flew over Pennsylvania Avenue ahead of the NTT IndyCar Series Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, Aug. 23, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

Thousands gathered along the course fencing with close-up views. Many won free tickets via drawing earlier in the summer. Scott and Jackie Cunningham paid for a VIP Champions package and traveled from Salt Lake City for the experience.“I love this street, the venue. This is phenomenal,” said Jackie, 62. “We’re so thrilled to be here, and so thankful to President Trump for getting this organized.” 

 







Team Penske mechanics worked before the Freedom 250 Grand Prix. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

The couple was rooting for star driver and “soon-to-be champion” Alex Palou, Scott, 67, said as they walked around the paddock area where team crews work on the cars ahead of the race.“We are excited for him and his success, and also excited to see some of the other teams out here, like the McLaren team. One of my favorites because I'm also a big Formula One fan,” Scott said.Bryan Bystol, 25, the strength and conditioning coach for team Rahal Letterman Lanigan, sat for a quick lunch with fellow crew members outside the team tent in the paddock. The team is based in Zionsville, Indiana.An IndyCar race through Washington, D.C., was the final event in President Trump's Freedom 250 series to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. (Video by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)  “My responsibility when we're in the shop is to train the drivers, the pit crew guys, everybody in the shop to improve their performance,” Bystol told States Newsroom.The team trainer takes the drivers and crew through Pilates courses and other conditioning, with a main focus on core muscles.“These street races are pretty physical. Even though there is power steering, for them to be able to keep turning their car back and forth on its tight turns. It's really physically demanding,” Bystol said.

 







An IndyCar races along Pennsylvania Avenue. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix was the last among a series of events organized by the Trump administration for the nation’s semiquincentennial. Freedom 250 is distinct from the bipartisan America250 commission created by Congress in 2016 to plan programming around the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The Trump-backed Freedom 250 received some federal money through the Republican “big, beautiful” law in 2025, but is mostly funded through private contributions. Michigan-based Penske Corp. was the primary sponsor of Sunday’s grand prix.

 







Actors with Fox Sports Networks played Abraham Lincoln and Thomas Jefferson as race car drivers. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

title: Ruston girl, 8, dies from brain-eating amoeba infection
description: Lillian Smart, who health officials believe contracted a brain-eating amoeba from swimming in a North Louisiana lake, died Saturday at a Ruston hospital from an infection linked to the pathogen. She had turned 8 years old a day earlier. “The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from,” the […]
text:
Lillian Smart, 8, of Ruston died Saturday, Aug. 22, 2026, after being infected with Naegleria fowleri, an amoeba that feeds on brain tissue. State health officials believe she was exposed while swimming in Lake Claiborne. (Photo courtesy Smart family)Lillian Smart, who health officials believe contracted a brain-eating amoeba from swimming in a North Louisiana lake, died Saturday at a Ruston hospital from an infection linked to the pathogen. She had turned 8 years old a day earlier.
“The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from,” the Smart family said in a statement posted Sunday morning on Facebook. “Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?”
In a news release Wednesday morning, the Louisiana Department of Health reported a state resident had been hospitalized after becoming infected with Naegleria fowleri, an amoeba that feeds on brain tissue. State officials have yet to confirm Lillian was the infected patient, but the Smart family confirmed on social media she was in the pediatric intensive care unit of a Ruston hospital and encouraged prayers for her recovery.
The health department said the infection was likely acquired when the girl was swimming in Lake Claiborne shortly before her illness.
This is believed to be the fifth death attributed to Naegleria fowleri in Louisiana since 2011.
The most recent fatality occurred in St. Bernard Parish in 2013, when a Drake Smith Jr., 4, contracted the amoeba while playing on a slip-and-slide. Officials confirmed presence of the amoeba in the household’s water, but tests for the pathogen in the water system were negative. However, the parish did detect low levels of chlorine and immediately treated the water system.
Two years earlier, a St. Bernard Parish man died from an infection after using tap water for a sinus rinse, and a DeSoto Parish woman perished after using tap water there for similar treatment.
Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, an extremely rare brain infection that can happen when water travels up the nasal canal and reaches the brain. The amoeba cannot cause an infection if it is swallowed.
Naegleria fowleri is not found in saltwater or in properly chlorinated pools. Infection symptoms typically begin with headache, fever, nausea and vomiting before progressing to a stiff neck, seizures and coma before death within about a week or two. Symptoms typically appear within about five days after an infection and are fatal in 97% of cases, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and prevention.
Nationwide, the CDC reported two cases of primary amebic meningoencephalitis last year. The U.S. count has exceeded six cases just twice since 1937, according to the agency.
Of the 173 infections documented in the past 90 years, nearly 91% have occurred during the months of July and August.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s cybersecurity program is running out of time, money as local governments face attacks
description: Pennington County residents haven’t been able to access some services since a cyberattack knocked out county computer systems in July. The attackers did not access its […]
text:
(Getty Images)Pennington County residents haven’t been able to access some services since a cyberattack knocked out county computer systems in July.
The water system in Rapid City, which is part of Pennington County, was among the first of dozens of utilities targeted in a nationwide wave of cyberattacks this summer. The attackers did not access its network in Rapid City, city officials said.
Mitchell, meanwhile, is recovering from its own breach, which left city staff without computer access.
The three incidents — all hitting South Dakota local governments within weeks of each other — underscore a vulnerability that state officials have spent years and millions of dollars trying to address.
Local governments hold sensitive taxpayer data, but often lack the staff, budget or expertise to protect it from cyberattacks. A 2025 report by the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center found that 68% of state, local, tribal and territorial governments lack the budget to address major cybersecurity priorities, and that small and rural communities are especially vulnerable.
A state-funded program in South Dakota is working to close that gap — but time and money are running short.
State funding in place of declined federal funding
SecureSD is a $7 million program run by the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office and Dakota State University that delivers cybersecurity tools, training and technical support to local governments.
Lawmakers launched the program with funds in 2024 in response to Gov. Kristi Noem rejecting a piece of $1 billion in cybersecurity grants to states. Noem spokesman Ian Fury told South Dakota Searchlight at the time that the grants were “wasteful spending,” adding the administrative burden of the grant “would have far exceeded the allowable administrative cost.”
That 2022 four-year federal grant program, part of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, faces an uncertain future. Congress extended the program through next month, but did not provide new funding. Efforts to reauthorize the program haven’t cleared both chambers.
After Noem turns down federal cyber money, lawmaker suggests using state funds

South Dakota’s SecureSD program is led by Mike Waldner, who previously directed South Dakota’s centralized education email system.
The program reviews regular vulnerability reports from the Department of Homeland Security for local governments that sign up for the program, which flag issues like outdated software or misconfigured firewalls. It also helps transition local governments to more secure data and email, purchases equipment or contracts with information technology companies to monitor cybersecurity needs, and trains local employees. SecureSD also runs Project Boundary Fence, in which cybersecurity experts test local governments’ defenses and report back on weaknesses.
Most counties have participated in at least one aspect of the program, including Project Boundary Fence, and participation has “ramped up” in recent years, Waldner said.
“It’s like walking through a parking lot and checking doors. We’re not there to steal anything, but we’ll tell people when their doors are unlocked so they can fix it,” Waldner said.
The “hands down number one priority” of SecureSD, Waldner said, is moving local governments onto professionally managed email systems that meet federal security standards — a step up from the patchwork of local setups many counties currently rely on. 
More than half of county-level email addresses, based on a South Dakota Searchlight analysis of county auditor email addresses, are not on government domains, making them more vulnerable to attacks and impersonation. Only verified U.S.-based public sector organizations, including state and local governments, can get a .gov email address, and agencies must have advanced security protocols that make it harder for scammers to copy or fake official government messages.
“We’re working our tails off to remedy that and fix that, for a number of reasons,” Waldner said.
Mislabeled electrical wiring sparked two-day state network shutdown

Rapid City is transitioning to a government, cloud-based email system using SecureSD funding, said Jim Gilbert, the city’s director of information technology. Katy Urban, public information officer with the Pennington County State’s Attorney Office, said the county is in the process of the same transition.
The $7 million in state funding for SecureSD expires June 30, 2028. Waldner said all of it will be spent — but once it runs out, local governments will have to absorb the cost of maintaining any improvements themselves. That uncertainty is “one of the biggest reasons an entity pauses” when considering cybersecurity upgrades, he said.
Waldner has had to prioritize the secure data and email transition as the expiration date nears. He said additional funding could eventually allow the program to expand into other areas, including cybersecurity management and data backup.
“My hope is we can secure funding and not only pay for the data and email solution, but pay for additional cybersecurity functions I know are needed,” Waldner said.
Future of state help for local governments
Sen. Randy Deibert, R-Spearfish, was among the lawmakers who championed the $7 million appropriation in 2024. A former Lawrence County commissioner, he said the program’s upcoming funding deadline was a built-in inflection point for the Legislature.
“It’s probably time to take a good look at that local government cybersecurity program and get an update on it for lawmakers: what’s working, what’s not, what should work,” Deibert said. “We should have some recommendations after a couple of years.”

Sen. Randy Deibert, R-Spearfish, speaks in the Senate chamber at the South Dakota Capitol in Pierre on March 9, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Deibert said the original vision wasn’t just funding — it was to offer state-level IT support to counties that couldn’t afford their own, similar to how the state helped school districts move onto secure email systems. He noted that Lawrence County has been fortunate to have a strong IT person on staff, but acknowledged not every county is in that position.
“I’m not certain that throwing dollars at it is the key,” Deibert said.
Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen leads the Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force. That group is evaluating South Dakota’s critical infrastructure — energy, water, data networks and more — and identifying vulnerabilities to natural disasters and cyberattacks. The task force discussed SecureSD at its August meeting and plans to recommend legislative proposals next session, including how to expand and continue the program.
“We haven’t made a final decision on what to propose, but it’s clear the need is still there and is going to still be there to continue to serve local governments in this way,” Venhuizen said.
The task force is also considering how much the state should require local governments to participate in cybersecurity programs, rather than leaving it voluntary.
Gov. Larry Rhoden recently awarded $500,000 to the task force to primarily fund research by Dakota State University and South Dakota Mines. The money is meant to build a map of the state’s critical infrastructure systems to identify vulnerabilities and redundancies. The funding will also support public education on cybersecurity and how residents can prepare for disruptions.

name: VTDigger
title: The catch in Noah Kahan’s charity concert for Vermont
description:
A worthy cause comes with a ticket price that leaves ordinary fans out.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The catch in Noah Kahan’s charity concert for Vermont.
text:
Dear Editor,
I have been a Noah Kahan fan since 2021. I heard a Vermont Public feature about him on the radio in the car with my grandma and have been hooked ever since. I got my mom into him. I cried on my bedroom floor listening to the original “Stick Season” album and again, even harder, when I heard “The Great Divide.” All of this is to say that I really love Kahan. 
As someone who grew up in Vermont and now goes to Providence College in Rhode Island, I love having Kahan as a point of reference. Before him, it was just Ben & Jerry’s ice cream and Sen. Bernie Sanders. Now there is a tangible piece of media attached to Vermont for my generation. I am proud to be from the same state as him, and Kahan has built his brand on being from Vermont. So, why does it now appear that he is ignoring the cost-of-living crisis in his home state?

READ MORE

Specifically, I am referring to the announcement of his charity event supporting The Busyhead Project: a two-day golf tournament and acoustic show at Spruce Peak. Fans had the chance to enter a ticket lottery, and if they won, even with a Vermont resident discount, they still had to pay almost $350 per ticket. Those tickets are general admission, standing room only. Not even for my favorite artist would I shell out $350 and not have a seat. This is also the only stop in Vermont that Kahan has made since the release of his third studio album in 2022. The closest that we got was a four-night run at Fenway. 
Almost $350 for a single-night ticket is a lot anywhere, let alone in a place where the average monthly cost of living is 14% above the national average. Our effective property tax rate is among the top five highest across the country. Even groceries and utilities are higher here than in other regions. This kind of money is not small potatoes to the average Vermonter.
I am not against the event at all. My family is a monthly sustainer of The Busyhead Project. Rural mental health saves lives and is a pillar of many communities. I sincerely hope that Kahan’s foundation never goes underfunded. But is this really the way to do it? In my opinion, the golf tournament should be made a true luxury. Pay hundreds of dollars to play with Kahan and support a local charity. But if you really want to reach the average Vermonter who composes your fan base, the prices have to be lower. A fair price would be $100 a ticket. Concerts are a luxury, something to look forward to, but for someone who claims to be supporting the community that raised him, I think Kahan is overlooking the struggles of the people who live here. 
Gracie Batsie
Jericho, Vt.

name: VTDigger
title: Meet three Vermonters whose histories are lesser known
description:
“The majority of people throughout history have been common people whose stories have not been highlighted,” said Angie Grove, executive director of the Ethan Allen Homestead.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Meet three Vermonters whose histories are lesser known.
text:
An illustration of a mass revival during the Second Great Awakening. The image is a depiction of what Charles Bowles’ congregation might have looked like. Image courtesy of American History Central

Kyle Neece is a reporter with the Community News Service, part of the University of Vermont’s Reporting & Documentary Storytelling program.This summer marked the 250th anniversary of the United States, and many Vermont towns and cities celebrated residents who played important roles in the fight for independence.
But there are many other notable Vermonters who lived in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Their names may be lesser known, but their stories reveal the realities of life at the time.  
Charles Bowles, founder of the first Baptist Church in Huntington 
Charles Bowles was born in Boston in 1761. His father was “an African, In the humble capacity of a servant,” and his mother was the daughter of a Revolutionary War hero named Col. Morgan, according to a biography by John W. Lewis. At the age of 12, Bowles became a servant in a Loyalist household.
When the Revolutionary War kicked off, Bowles joined the Colonial army as a waiter. In 1776, Bowles served in a New Hampshire regiment as a private. After the war, in 1779, Bowles was honorably discharged in Newburgh, New York. Shortly after, he moved to Warren, New Hampshire, and began preaching in nearby communities. 
A few years later, Bowles moved to Vermont, where he continued preaching.
Author and historian Elise Guyette researched and wrote about Bowles for her book “Discovering Black Vermont.” 
“This was during the Second Great Awakening, which is a very important movement in our country,” said Guyette, referring to a major religious revival around the start of the 19th century. “But usually you don’t read about people like Charles Bowles, even though he was a very important part of it.”
Bowles lived in Huntington, where he was a successful preacher with a congregation of about 60 people, according to Guyette’s research. He also preached across central and northern Vermont and upstate New York. He founded Free Will Baptist churches in Huntington, Hinesburg, Shelburne and Duxbury. 
“He held huge revivals all over the state, and hardly anybody remembers this man,” Guyette said. 
Bowles eventually moved to Malone, New York, where he purchased small farmland and settled down with his daughter, Eunice. He died March 16, 1843, at age 81. 
The church Bowles built in Huntington still stands today. The building became the town hall, then the first volunteer fire department. According to Guyette, the town has been working to preserve the building.
Joseph Susap, Indigenous Revolutionary War veteran 

Two handmade dolls of Joe and Molly, made by a woman in Morristown, were sent to President Eisenhower. Photo by Kyle Neece/Community News Service

Joseph Susap was born circa 1739 in Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island in Nova Scotia, a member of the Mi’kmaq people. When he was only 6 years old, the British set siege to Louisbourg and killed his family, according to Jill Mudgett, an independent historian who has researched Susap’s life.
Susap, along with other Indigenous people, fled to Odanak, Quebec, where he was taken in by a group of Abenaki. This is where Susap grew up and met Molly, an Abenaki woman with two sons, whom he would eventually marry.
However, trouble followed Susap as he escaped death a second time. In 1759, British Army Officer Robert Rogers and his rangers attacked the Odanak village. Susap and Molly fled south and lived in a variety of places ranging from Derby at the northern Vermont border down to Cabot, Morristown and as far south as Newbury. 
When the Revolutionary War started in 1775, Susap enlisted to fight for the Colonies.
“He had strong opinions about the British,” Mudgett said. 
Susap served as a scout for Gen. Jacob Bayley and helped map out the Bayley-Hazen Road, which was ordered by George Washington to connect the Connecticut River Valley with Canada. 
After the war, Susap traveled far and wide within northern Vermont. He had a reputation for being kind to settlers and was known as “Indian Joe.” 
In one story, Susap shared moose meat with a family before feeding himself. In another, he killed a catamount to protect a group of settlers. Mudgett said Susap’s friendly actions left a complex legacy. 
“He unintentionally and culturally gave the sense that (settlers) have the go-ahead to colonize due to his friendly nature,” Mudgett said. “It’s not so much that he is literally doing that, but he is symbolically used to do this. The settlers used his actions as one guy as a stand-in for Indigenous people.” 
As he grew older, Susap was taken care of by a group of Vermonters. He died in 1819 and is buried in Oxbow Cemetery in Newbury. 
Joe’s Pond, which straddles Caledonia and Washington counties, is named after Susap.
According to Mudgett, Susap’s story has persisted with Vermonters because of his “friendly” attitude toward white settlers. But she said Susap’s tale is a reminder that other Indigenous peoples’ stories are not as popular. 
“The communities that claim him as their own have always historically embraced him because he’s Joe the ‘friendly Indian,’” Mudgett said. “And if it’s more complicated than that, then these stories get erased.” 
Martha Powell, a woman on the frontier 

A map of early land lots of Burlington, where the Powells would eventually settle. Photo by Kyle Neece/Community News Service

Martha Winslow Powell was born in 1724 in Gloucester, Massachusetts. In 1748, at age 24, she married John Felix Powell. Shortly after their marriage, they had their first child, who died as an infant. In 1761, she gave birth to a son, Felix Powell Jr.
In 1768, the family moved to Dorset, Vermont, where Felix Powell is credited as the first settler; Martha Powell was left unmentioned in the land deeds, according to Angie Grove, executive director of the Ethan Allen Homestead, who has researched Martha Powell’s life. 
In 1770, the Powells moved to Pittsford, where Martha Powell gave birth to a second daughter, only for her to die as an infant as well. 
Martha Powell’s life “reflects the hardships, displacement and active contributions of working-class women who helped settle the frontier and establish the state of Vermont during the Revolutionary period,” Grove said during a panel discussion in April.  
The Powells eventually settled in Burlington, where the family purchased property in 1774. 
Martha Powell helped with her husband’s trade activities, managed household financial accounts and spending, and performed various tasks like cleaning, cooking and maintaining gardens. 
When the American Revolution began, both Felix Powell Sr. and Felix Powell Jr. left to serve in the war. In September 1777, forces aligned with the British attacked and burned down the Powells’ home during a raid. 
“The American Revolution was experienced by everybody. It was not just soldiers on battlefields; the chaos, fear, and drama were experienced by everyone on every piece of land. 
People’s experiences differed vastly and were heavily influenced by their demographics and personal relationships,” Grove said. 
According to Grove, Martha Powell, who was pregnant at the time, escaped into the surrounding woods. While hiding from the raid, she went into labor and delivered her baby alone in the forest. This baby, too, didn’t survive. 
Martha Powell did not live to see the conclusion of the war, as she died sometime between 1777 and 1780 in her early to mid 50s. In October 1780, her father wrote a revised will leaving portions of his estate to his surviving daughters and “to my grandchildren born of Martha Powell, deceased.” 
Grove said that researching stories like Powell’s takes a lot of time and resources but that the histories of everyday people are essential. 
“The majority of people throughout history have been common people whose stories have not been highlighted,” she said. “Most people today would relate more to these untold stories than to the political leaders whose stories are commonly told.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Secretary of State urges voters to update state records before ballots get mailed out
description:
Despite rampant national claims to the contrary, mail-in ballots are a safe and secure way to vote, Secretary Sarah Copeland Hanzas said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Secretary of State urges voters to update state records before ballots get mailed out.
text:
A ballot drop box outside the Randolph Town Clerk’s office in October 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The Vermont Secretary of State’s office is urging voters to make sure they have a current address on file with the state before ballots get mailed out for this fall’s general election.
After Sept. 1 — which is in less than two weeks — whatever voter addresses the secretary’s office has listed will be used to mail ballots. The state will start sending out ballots late next month ahead of the election on Tuesday, Nov. 3, said Sarah Copeland Hanzas, the secretary of state.
Despite rampant national claims to the contrary, mail-in ballots are a safe and secure way to vote, she said. Recent state data shows they are widely used in Vermont. In the 2024 election, nearly two-thirds of people who voted did so by mail, also known as voting absentee.
Checking addresses
In Vermont, state law requires that every registered voter be mailed a ballot for the biennial general election. Voters can fill out their ballot at home and return it by mail or at a drop-off location. They can also disregard the mail ballot entirely and vote in person on election day.
The state does not mail out ballots for primary elections, like the one held earlier this month. If a voter has moved since the 2024 election, though, they should update their address with the state as soon as possible, Copeland Hanzas said.
“We want to make sure that ballots are going exactly where the voter lives,” she said. 
Voters who will be away from home this fall should submit an absentee ballot request, which will direct their ballot to the address they’ll be at instead. That’s a good option for college students and members of the military who will be overseas, she said. 
Voters can verify or change the address that’s on file — or request an absentee ballot — at the online Vermont Voter Portal, which is vote.vermont.gov. They can also contact their local town or city clerk.
Voter rolls, mail delays
Copeland Hanzas said Vermont puts multiple sets of eyes on every stage in the vote-by-mail process to make sure it’s as accurate and secure as possible.
She explained that since last fall, officials in every city and town have completed a legally-mandated review of their local voter checklists to identify anyone who they believe has moved, passed away or otherwise cannot vote there. That review is done by each town’s Board of Civil Authority.
Any people who are flagged by the board will not be automatically mailed a ballot this fall unless that person clarifies with local officials that they are listed correctly, Copeland Hanzas said. That means it’s highly unlikely that someone would be mailed a ballot who was not registered to vote in a given city or town.
At the national level, President Donald Trump is trying to limit access to mail voting, in part with an executive order in March directing the U.S. Postal Service to only deliver ballots from people who are on a federally-approved list. That followed another order last year attempting to prohibit counting of mail ballots that are postmarked by Election Day but arrive afterward, among other changes. (In Vermont, election officials must get mail-in ballots back before polls close on Election Day in order to count them.)
Federal courts have so far blocked implementation of both orders in response to legal challenges from states, including Vermont, and national voting rights groups. The president continues to disparage mail-in voting, though he has voted by mail himself, including in Florida’s Republican primary earlier this month.
Even if Vermonters aren’t concerned about the security of mail-in voting, they may be worried about the timeliness with which their ballot will be delivered. Mail delivery delays are well-documented, especially in the state’s most rural communities. 
More than 2,000 people have made complaints to the three members of Vermont’s congressional delegation about mail service so far this year, according to a letter the lawmakers sent Friday to U.S. Postmaster General David Steiner.
Copeland Hanzas said that voters should feel confident they will receive a ballot in the mail this year. If they’re concerned about it getting back in time, they can use a ballot dropbox, locations of which are listed online. They can also turn in a filled-out ballot up until polls close on Election Day.

name: VTDigger
title: What’s next for Vermont? Meet the reporters covering politics, elections and health care
description:
Join VTDigger at the Manchester Community Library for a free, public conversation with the journalists following some of the biggest decisions facing Vermont this fall.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  What’s next for Vermont? Meet the reporters covering politics, elections and health care.
text:
VTDigger’s Shaun Robinson and Ethan Weinstein at an event with historian Jill Lepore at the Manchester Community Library on Thursday, September 5, 2024. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
State government can be difficult to follow. Major policy decisions take shape through legislative debates, agency actions, elections and negotiations that often happen far from public view.
On Thursday, September 10, VTDigger is bringing the journalists who follow those decisions to Manchester for a candid conversation about what they’re seeing, what they’ll be watching this fall and how their reporting helps Vermonters understand how consequential decisions are made.
The panel will be moderated by Editor-in-Chief Sue Allen and feature Senior Editor Ethan Weinstein, Health Care Reporter Olivia Gieger and State Government & Politics Reporter Shaun Robinson.




Ethan Weinstein, senior editor




Olivia Gieger, health care reporter




Shaun Robinson, government & politics reporter


The reporters will discuss the November election, state politics and the forces shaping Vermont’s health care system. They’ll also pull back the curtain on their work: how they develop sources, scrutinize public officials’ claims, navigate complex policy debates and uncover information the public needs to know.
Attendees will leave with a clearer understanding of the issues and decisions VTDigger’s reporters are following, how those decisions could affect Vermont communities and what it takes to bring readers accurate, independent reporting from the Statehouse and beyond.
VTDigger’s new CEO, Brendan Kinney, will open the evening, share how the organization is working to bring more reporting to more Vermont communities and offer a look at what’s ahead for the newsroom. 
Event details
When: Thursday, September 10, 2026, from 5–7 p.m.Where: Manchester Community Library, 138 Cemetery Ave., Manchester CenterAdmission: Free and open to the public; registration is required.
Doors open at 5 p.m. The program will begin at 5:30 p.m. Hors d’oeuvres will be provided, with beverages available by donation. The venue is wheelchair accessible, and onsite parking is available.

Reserve your seat

What do you want VTDigger’s reporters to address?

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont wants to train the next generation of physicians. How much should insured Vermonters be paying for it?
description:
Commercial insurance payouts subsidized about $82 million in graduate medical education costs at UVM Medical Center last year. That number is only expected to increase. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont wants to train the next generation of physicians. How much should insured Vermonters be paying for it? .
text:
The University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington in Nov. 2020. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Teaching and training the next generation of physicians is expensive work. And commercial insurers are footing more than half that bill in Vermont through their payments for care, according to an independent analysis. 
Nearly $82 million of commercial insurance dollars went toward the $161 million cost for UVM Medical Center to run its medical education programs last year, analysts said in a recent memo. That number is on track to reach $88 million for 2026, the memo estimates. 
The question of how Vermont pays for medical education is a complicated one with few clear answers. With one medical school in the state, the cash flow from Vermonters to the state’s student doctors is more pronounced here than in many states, though the way commercial payers support medical education is not unique to Vermont. 
Still, it is difficult for insurers and the insured to know just how much they are paying for medical education. With renewed attention to this relationship recently, regulators, independent analysts and the medical school itself agree this financial relationship should be more transparent and more responsive to the needs of Vermont’s physician workforce.
The problem is one of a balance Vermont has long struggled to strike: Vermont needs to recruit clinicians, especially for primary care, but it also wants to curb commercial insurance premiums, which are some of the highest in the nation.
“Medical education is incredibly important. We need doctors,” said Rep. Alyssa Black, D-Essex Town, who chairs the House’s healthcare committee, in an interview with VTDigger. “I just wonder: Do Vermonters know that when they pay their insurance premium that a part of that is paying for medical education … of someone who probably will never practice here?”
‘Black box’
Medicare, Medicaid and other federal sources cover a big portion of medical education, but payments from commercial insurers make up most of the difference. This support is not in explicit line-item sums passing from insurers to an academic medical center; rather it is built into the charges an insurer pays for clinical care — a small fraction of the amount that the hospital charges an insurer for, say, a CT scan.
“It’s not specified that you’re paying for medical education as well as clinical care,” Nancy Kane, a health policy professor at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, told VTDigger. 
Kane is a member of the three-person independent liaison group that wrote the memo detailing how much commercial money goes toward medical education, as part of the team’s assignment to oversee the UVM Health network’s budget-setting process. Kane specifically dug into the medical education issue.  
“I’m kind of obsessed with how we’re funding academic medicine, because I actually think the model we’ve used in the past is about to implode,” she told the Green Mountain Care Board, which regulates hospital spending, during an early August hearing.
Kane expects the costs to fall more heavily on commercial insurers in coming years, because Medicaid matching funds for medical education are predicted to decline for 2027. Unless the cut in Medicaid funds is matched with a decline in academic expenses, she estimates that commercial insurers’ support to UVM Medical Center’s medical education could rise to $92 million for 2027.
Medical education at UVM encompasses the training at the Larner College of Medicine; the residency and fellowship programs at the University of Vermont Medical Center; and education  for nurses and other clinicians. Part of this broad umbrella — and the distinction between the medical center and the medical college — is what makes the movement of money so murky. 
Kane said she spent nearly six months determining how UVMMC subsidizes medical education.
Even after running the numbers, the process that UVM Medical Center and the medical school take to decide how money moves from the hospital to the school is still a bit unclear to her. She told regulators, in an Aug. 3 care board hearing, that ultimately it seems to come down to private conversations among the leaders of each of those related entities: Dr. Steven Leffler as president of UVMMC, Dr. Ramsey Herrington as president of UVM Health’s physician group and Dr. Richard Page at the head of Larner.
“These aren’t numbers they keep track of,” Kane told VTDigger. “Not because they’re derelict, but because people don’t think of them that way.”
In 2022, the university and the health network renewed a 10-year affiliation agreement, updating a relationship that has been in place since 1995, Herrington told VTDigger.
In that most recent agreement, the two bodies established a flow of money from the medical center to the college of medicine, increasing 2% every year or at the rate of the consumer price index, whichever is higher, Herrington said, but he didn’t provide dollar figures. 
The costs of providing medical education include payments for faculty to supervise; resident and intern stipends; the “oversight infrastructure” required for teaching doctors; and indirect costs that can come from more novice patient care — such as if a doctor in training orders a more expensive test than necessary.
Tuition to the medical school covers a slew of classroom costs separate from the medical center’s. But the medical center needs to come up with the funds to cover its costs, Kane said. Medicare and Medicaid pay a portion through federal earmarks for graduate medical education. Last year, Medicare paid $13 million and Medicaid paid $66 million toward graduate medical education at UVM Medical Center and Larner College of Medicine, Kane found. 
“And then — you have the rest,” she said in an interview with VTDigger. “And where does that come from? That’s the black box. The only major other source that’s coming from is commercial payers.”
Those payments, embedded in the costs of patient care, make up the $82 million figure Kane found for 2025. Still, it’s a small fraction of what commercial insurance pays overall: The medical center’s current commercial revenue, according to its presentation to the care board, is nearly $1.07 billion.
Herrington told VTDigger that he and his colleagues collaborated closely with Kane and the liaison group. Although he couldn’t say the team’s numbers were “exactly right,” they were “directionally pretty close to right,” he said.  
‘Vermonters are healthier’
Herrington emphasized how important it is that the medical school and the medical center are training physicians who can fill gaps in Vermont’s healthcare ecosystem. He said it’s something he did when he led UVMMC’s emergency department and established its residency program in 2019, which has yielded a fresh crop of Vermont-grown emergency doctor hires. He wants to replicate that in gastroenterology, obstetrics/gynecology, psychiatry and oncology, he said. 
“Our educational training strategy should match what it is that we’re looking to do for the state of Vermont as we look forward, and I’m here to put those things together,” he said.
About one-third of physicians currently practicing in Vermont graduated from Larner College of Medicine or did their residency at UVM Medical Center, according to a report from the Department of Health. Each year, the medical school graduates about 120 doctors and trains more than 320 residents and fellows. Over the past five years, nearly half of UVM Medical Center’s residents and fellows have stayed to practice in Vermont, the school says.
Beyond its ability to produce local doctors, the academic medical center has a value to Vermonters simply because it is an academic setting. Its teaching mission attracts specialists and highly regarded clinicians to the state, Leffler told regulators recently.
“We do believe strongly that Vermonters are healthier and have greater access to specialty care due to our (graduate medical education) programs,” he said. “You would not be able to have specialties and subspecialties available in Vermont without being an academic medical center.” 
Basil Waugh, a spokesperson for the University of Vermont, echoed the importance of being able to combine the missions of the medical center and the college of medicine. 
“The opportunity to combine clinical practice with teaching, research and training future physicians helps Vermont attract physicians and sustain a breadth of specialty care that would otherwise be very difficult for a state our size to support,” Waugh wrote in a statement to VTDigger.
‘Don’t squander this asset’ 
Still, as insurance premiums in Vermont — and across the country — reach new, unaffordable highs for so many, Kane thinks commercial insurers will eventually need to cap what they contribute to the medical school. Representatives at the state’s largest insurer, BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont, declined to comment to VTDigger about the funding of the medical school. 
At the very least, Kane and her colleagues on the liaison team say that if Vermonters are contributing so much to support UVM’s medical education, there should be more ways to ensure that the medical education supports Vermont back.
The team’s memo calls for more public accountability for the cost and benefits of medical education that so many Vermonters are paying into through their premiums to insurers. The authors suggest that the state develop a governance model more strongly linking medical education with the state government’s health planning. 
Nearly 20 states already have some version of a statewide graduate medical education strategy, housed in a state agency, workforce organization or academic institution, the liaison group said in its memo.
“Everyone is being challenged right now by the supply and demand mismatch for clinician workforce,” Herrington said. “The state should really lean on the (UVM Health) Medical Group to meet that need and solve the problem of getting care to Vermonters as close to home as possible. But you can’t lean on us to do that job without the backbone of the college of medicine or our (graduate medical education) programs.”  
Mike Smith, who leads the three-person liaison team, said the state should develop a more formalized way for those beyond the UVM network to weigh in on how the medical center and medical school use Vermonters’ money to train new doctors, in ways that meet the state’s specific gaps in care.
“What does the state need? How can we get there?” Smith asked. “Don’t be so closed in the process. We’re not talking about not funding medical education. We’re talking about how to fund it in a more transparent and efficient way.” 
“If there’s transparency and accountability, it’s a great opportunity to do things for the state of Vermont,” Smith continued. “What we’re saying is this (medical education) is an asset; use it as an asset. Don’t squander this asset.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Now that we’ve adopted Right to Read legislation for our schools, we must revamp teacher preparation to match it
description: In order to be sure our state's new literacy legislation has the most impact on our students, we need to ensure that we have the same laser focus on teacher training  that this bill has brought to our students.
text:
ON SEPTEMBER 16, 2025, when the Right to Read Act was being debated at the State House, I testified before the Joint Education Committee in support of this crucial legislation. This was nerve-racking, but I had to do it because I strongly believe that all students should get appropriate reading instruction. It felt good to see legislators listen to me, a teacher of 23 years.  
During my two-plus decades in the first- and then second-grade classroom, I have been responsible for teaching hundreds of students how to read. I realized long ago that the content I had learned way back when in my teaching program, and even in my masters of literacy and language program, was not enough to help my most struggling kids. 
I had to independently find ways to supplement my teaching. Fortunately, my school district embraced the importance of teaching our students how to read using evidence-based reading instruction, which is now universally known as the science of reading. More than once, I was witness to the difference it made for the students in my school.
In early June, when Gov. Healey signed the Right to Read into law, it was an exciting day for me. Now school districts like mine would be required to shift to evidence-based literacy curriculum to teach reading to students in kindergarten through third grade, including explicit instruction in phonics, phonemic awareness, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension. They would no longer use the three-cueing method.
While this is certainly a victory for students in Massachusetts, the law is only as successful as the teachers who can implement it. In this, crucial gaps remain. One of the most important is that most of the teacher preparation programs in the state do not teach the science of reading methodology. It is not enough for the Right to Read to work great in theory. It must work in practice. 
Our state must overhaul teacher preparation so that new teachers entering the profession are properly trained to teach reading. The good news is that Massachusetts has a precedent we can follow. When the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education established the requirement for a license endorsement for teaching students for whom English is not their first language, student teaching programs immediately adapted to this and made sure new teachers studied the best practices of teaching English language learner students. These new teachers then left college with an English language learner license endorsement and armed with the most recent strategies to be able to teach ELL students in their classroom.  
The ELL license endorsement also meant that longstanding teachers like me received the required rigorous training to work with students learning English. Every five years when I renew my teaching license, I again have to prove that I’m up to date on ELL learning. My ELL students have directly benefited from this teaching license endorsement. We can provide the same benefit to our struggling readers by requiring that teachers in the classroom and teacher training programs obtain a literacy license endorsement. 
I have been an elementary school teacher since my daughter Carly was a kindergartener. She has now been an elementary school teacher for five years. Although our graduation dates were 22 years apart, much of our college preparation programs, especially in regard to literacy, were very similar.  
We both had just one class that covered the general aspects of reading, and we both learned to use a reading curriculum that has now been debunked. A quarter of a century without meaningful improvement in teaching aspiring educators how to teach reading is a very long time for Massachusetts students to wait. It is past time for a change. 
All teachers encounter students with reading challenges, whether they are actively teaching students to read or are a 10th grade math teacher with a student struggling to understand a word problem. Both the initial license endorsement and the licensure expectations would enable all teachers to be more successful in meeting the needs of all of our struggling readers. 
In order to be sure our state’s new literacy legislation has the most impact on our students, we need to ensure that we have the same laser focus on our teachers that this bill has brought to our students. The right to read can only become a reality for our students if all teachers in our state are properly trained. 
Donna Thayer is a 2nd grade teacher at Mason-Rice Elementary in Newton and a Teach Plus Massachusetts Policy Fellowship alumna.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: UNO grad’s aim to soar as U.S. pilot dashed by immigration status, despite Rep. Bacon’s intervention
description: OMAHA — Ever since she can remember, Mariana Juarez wanted to fly. A commercial pilot’s license seemed a distant dream, though, when family hardships in her home in Guerrero, Mexico, drove her out of school at age 14. Two years later, she and her mom fled to the United States without authorization. They were allowed to […]
text:
Mariana Juarez earned her private pilot license in the U.S., a step in a journey to be a commercial pilot. The University of Nebraska at Omaha graduate, who entered the U.S. from Mexico without authorization, lost a battle to remain in the country and said she bought an airline ticket to return to her homeland. (Photo courtesy of Mariana Juarez)OMAHA — Ever since she can remember, Mariana Juarez wanted to fly.
A commercial pilot’s license seemed a distant dream, though, when family hardships in her home in Guerrero, Mexico, drove her out of school at age 14.
Mariana Juarez clocking in flight hours. She earned a private pilot license on a quest to be a commercial airline pilot. (Photo courtesy of Mariana Juarez)
Two years later, she and her mom fled to the United States without authorization. They were allowed to stay while the federal government weighed their cases. But shortly afterward, Juarez said, depression gripped her mom and she returned to Mexico, leaving her daughter with relatives in Omaha.
With the help of a cousin, Juarez enrolled in high school, won a full-ride private scholarship and this year graduated from the University of Nebraska at Omaha with honors and an aviation degree. Along the way she worked full time, obtained a private pilot’s license and, at age 24, was in the process of achieving certification as a commercial pilot.
But her plan has been thwarted by immigration legal problems. When she was a teen, unbeknownst to her until later, an immigration judge had ordered her removed from the country.
Despite the weight of a well-known legal team — and intervention from a Republican congressman — Homeland Security officials have declined to reverse course and allow her to stay legally.
Juarez plans a September return to the homeland she hasn’t seen in eight years. She chose to buy a one-way ticket out rather than risk detention amid President Donald Trump’s mass deportation push, which he argues protects U.S. jobs, public resources and public safety.
Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska’s Omaha-heavy 2nd District said he met Juarez and went to the top seeking a different outcome, twice speaking to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. He said he was told — most recently this past week — there’d be no exception.
U.S. Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska speaks at a Ukrainian Appreciation Dinner hosted by the House of Prayer in north Lincoln. Nov. 7, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“It’s an unchristian policy we’re seeing here,” Bacon said in an interview with the Examiner. “I get it, we wanted to secure the borders. I think we’ve done that. We don’t want dangerous people here, I get it. But what’s going on here is a terrible overreach, a terrible injustice.”
Bacon, a retired Air Force brigadier general wrapping up his fifth term, said he’s armed with examples of other constituents, and is calling on Republican colleagues to support immigration reform that “makes sense.”
Teen steered her own path in foreign land
Juarez launched her U.S. education in 2018, in the halls of the largest high school in Nebraska’s most populated city.
By the time she enrolled in Martha Omar’s senior English class at Omaha Central High, the teen had learned a second language and had become a “bridge” helping other immigrant students adjust.
“She was a student that struck me as someone navigating high school by herself,” said Omar, a teacher of 20 years. “She was getting herself to school and home on her own, and was always working a job during high school.”
Omar said Juarez impressed her to the point that after her 2022 graduation, she hired her former student to tutor her two sons in Spanish. Years later, Juarez remains a close family friend, picking the boys up sometimes for adventures such as Sky Zone. Omar called the predicament heartbreaking.
Mariana Juarez graduated in 2022 from Omaha Central High before her UNO studies leading to an aviation degree. (Photo courtesy of Mariana Juarez)
“As a teacher we pour into our students and our dream is they go on to thrive in our community,” she said. “When you have kids like Mariana that have this incredible talent and bravery and drive … what’s better to have in a community than that?”
While at Central, Juarez knew she wanted to go to college, the first in her family to do so, and dived into research.
What she didn’t know until it was too late, said her attorney Roxana Cortes-Mills, was that in the fall of 2018 an immigration court had sent notice of a hearing to a residence she had shared with her mom.
Cortes-Mills said she found the notice in Juarez’s official immigration file marked as undeliverable and “return to sender.”
Juarez did not show up at the hearing, and an Omaha immigration judge on Oct. 24, 2018, ordered her removed from the country.
“She was 17 years old,” a minor under Nebraska and federal law, said Cortes-Mills, legal director for the Center for Immigrant and Refugee Advancement. “That hearing happened. She didn’t attend. She didn’t know.”
No lawful status, no pilot’s license
As Mariana explored her dream career, she said she learned she could not obtain a U.S. pilot’s license without a lawful status.
In 2022, she sought assistance from CIRA (formerly known as Immigrant Legal Center) and the nonprofit’s legal experts explained consequences of the removal order. They said she was beyond eligibility for special immigrant juvenile status for minors deemed by a court to have been abused or abandoned by a parent.
 A subsequent effort to reopen Juarez’s case due to not receiving the hearing notice was denied April 24, 2024, according to Board of Immigration Appeals records. Cortes-Mills said the legal team did not pursue a further challenge based upon a new high court ruling that at the time seemed to rule out a chance.
A woman apprehended and detained by immigration agents in Omaha in 2025. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)
That year, federal officials did offer a form of relief to Juarez  — a temporary stay of removal, which she said allowed her to obtain work authorization while in college and cleared the way for a private pilot license in 2025. She said a private license is a step toward her commercial license.
This summer, however, immigration officials denied Juarez a third extension on the stay of removal.
Homeland Security officials, in response to a request for comment, offered a three-paragraph statement that pointed to the immigration court’s 2018 removal order. A spokesperson’s email said Juarez and her mother had applied for admission through the San Ysidro Port of Entry and that neither had legal documents to enter the U.S.
The department, which oversees Immigration and Customs Enforcement, in January claimed “an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations and more than 675,000 deportations” in the first year since Trump returned as president in 2025. Homeland Security said the crackdown set the stage to break more records and save taxpayer dollars. 
Juarez — faced with a U.S. future without a work permit, driver’s license and risk of detention — said her $400 Mexico-bound ticket is set for early September. 
Tearing up, the UNO grad who had started working at CIRA greeting clients, said leaving is not her preference but that she knew each renewal of a stay of removal was uncertain. She said she appreciates the friends she’s made and her U.S. education.
University of Nebraska at Omaha, in front of the Milo Bail student center, September 2024. (Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Her UNO degree reflects a concentration in air transport administration, and she hopes while in Mexico to validate her training thus far and resume her quest to be a professional commercial pilot.
Juarez, whose roots are in the southwest Mexican state of Guerrero, recalls visiting an airport as a child and seeing the joy on people’s faces as a plane connected them to family or adventure.
“Since I was a kid, I didn’t see myself being anything else,” she said. “I wanted to be in the sky.”
Sitting in university aviation classes dominated by males strengthened her resolve. Juarez said she became more motivated.
One “extreme” to the next? 
Bacon — who has been in the national spotlight as one of a small number of  Republicans in Congress critical of the president, but who also said he has learned to pick his battles — said he sees “no goodness” in ousting Juarez. Bacon said his staff worked many hours on her case.
He cited a recent Gallup poll, which showed that 73% of Americans believe immigration is a “good thing” for the country.  That share slipped from a record high of 79% last year, but remains above the 25-year trend average of 67%, the pollster in July said of its June telephone survey.
Bacon said the “real issue” is an outdated system of immigration laws and policies. He said “we went from one extreme” under Joe Biden to “another extreme” under Donald Trump. 
Bacon believes the current extreme will hurt his party in the midterms.
A backer of the stalled Dignity Act of 2025, Bacon wants Congress to create a path for working migrants to legally stay. That bipartisan bill, championed by Rep. Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, and Rep. Veronica Escobar, a Texas Democrat, drew support from across party lines and multiple states, offering border protections, asylum and immigration reforms but no amnesty or citizenship to those who entered illegally.
“We can put a little common sense and humanity into the equation,” Bacon said.
Mariana Juarez was in flight training in Omaha before Homeland Security officials declined to extend a stay of removal. (Photo courtesy of Mariana Juarez)
Bryan Slone, former chief executive of the statewide Nebraska Chamber of Commerce & Industry who currently is a pilot trainee, continues to work on workforce issues and touts an overhaul of the immigration system as a way to help the state’s labor shortage.
A registered nonpartisan, Slone considers undocumented migrants schooled in Nebraska an attractive recruitment and retention pool, and he urges bipartisan solutions. 
“We still have the ‘brain drain’ issue and we still have the declining birth rate issue that we’ve been talking about for four or five years,” he said.
Ariel Ruiz Soto, senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, a Washington, D.C., nonpartisan think-tank, said part of the conversation often missing is what happens to migrants after they return or are removed to their homeland.
He said brain drain, or exodus of young educated talent, can be viewed as “brain gain” for the other side.
Ruiz Soto said the Mexican government, for example, has tried to “make the most of this brain gain.” Among reintegration resources it offers is the “Mexico te abraza” (Mexico embraces you) program. Returning or deported nationals at various reentry points can access support ranging from food to employment assistance.
Juarez said she hopes her journey will inspire young immigrants with voting power to speak out on issues facing their community. 
With her eye on a flight program in Mexico, she said she will “keep chasing my dreams,” albeit in a country other than the U.S.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Andy Gipson’s Muslim rhetoric doesn’t match the Woodie Guthrie classic he sings
description: State Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson, the first candidate to officially announce a run for Mississippi governor in 2027, gives a stump speech at the Neshoba County Fair on Wednesday, July 30, 2025.
text:
Andy Gipson, Republican agriculture commissioner and gubernatorial candidate, sings a Woody Guthrie song on his latest compact disc – “God Bless America!”
Gipson, who is also a part-time country crooner and a Baptist minister, belts out Guthrie’s iconic song “This Land Is Your Land.” The decision of Gipson to include folk legend Guthrie’s song amongst his patriotic collection of music is of note considering his recent comments about Muslim Americans.
Not long after social media expressed outrage as only social media can do that the tiny Delta town of Benoit had appointed Assama Ali, an American citizen lawyer and Mulsim, to serve as municipal judge, Gipson weighed in multiple times on the topic while never mentioning her by name.
Gibson went to social media to renew his call to ban Sharia law, which provides the moral and religious guidelines for many Muslims. He didn’t mention that no one is trying to enact Sharia Law in the American judicial system and that the Mississippi Legislature passed a bill in 2015 when Gipson was a member to ban Sharia law from the state judicial system and that he voted for the proposal.
In his social media posts, Gipson didn’t acknowledge that Assama Ali was a fellow graduate of the Mississippi College School of Law, now known as Mississippi Christian University, and was a licensed attorney in the state of Mississippi who as a judge had the duty to uphold state laws.  
Instead, he stated on social media “If you are among those who think Sharia law is not an issue in Mississippi, you’d better think again.”
He then asked, “But did you know that in our own capital city, in Mississippi, there is a Center for Muslim Culture at the Planetarium in Jackson? Billed by its founders as the first Muslim Museum in America, it includes displays complete with this exhibit featuring Muhammed as ‘The Messenger.’”
Gipson who served as an attorney in a prominent Jackson law firm went on to pledge on social media, “I will defend our Constitution and our Christian values.”
As a Baptist minister, no doubt, Gipson has often proclaimed Jesus Christ as the savior and one true way to heaven. No doubt, the United States Constitution defends Gipson’s right to make that proclamation. Does it not defend Muslims’ rights to their proclamation?
The social media posts beg the question of whether Gipson was comprehending the lyrics he sang in the Woodie Guthrie classic.
     This land is your land, this land is my land
     From California to the New York island,
     From the redwood forest to the Gulf Stream waters;
     This land was made for you and me.
When Gipson sang “for you and me,” did he not mean for “you” to be all inclusive?
According to various sources, Guthrie wrote this song as a critical response to Irving Berlin’s “God Bless America,” which he believed did not paint a true picture of America. Guthrie had been “roaming” the country seeing the pain and suffering of the 1930s’ Depression era.
Two verses, known as the lost verses, depict that pain and suffering and what many saw as the unfairness of the country.
Not surprisingly, Gipson did not include the two “lost” verses in his rendition of “This Land Is Your Land.”
In fairness to Gipson, Guthrie’s recording of the song during World War II also did not include the two verses. Many speculate that the omission was made to limit criticism of the country during war time.
But surprisingly, Gipson also chose not to include the rousing final verse of “This Lsnd Is Your Land” in his version.
     Nobody living can ever stop me,     As I go walking that freedom highway;     Nobody living can ever make me turn back     This land was made for you and me.
The phrase “freedom highway,” penned by Guthrie, later became the title of an album and song by the Mississippi-rooted Staple Singers written for the historic 1965 Selma to Montgomery march for voting rights for Black Americans. The song references the violence of the Civil Rights era, including the murder of Black teenager Emmett Till by white men for allegedly flirting with a white woman.
That Staple Singers song, also covered by the North Mississippi Allstars, asks a critical question.
     March the freedom highway      March each and every day      March the freedom highway      March each and every day      Made up my mind, and I won't turn around      Made up my mind, and I won't turn around      There is just one thing      I can't understand, my friend     Why some folks think freedom      Is not designed for all men

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s statewide ban on cellphones in schools starts this year
description:
As districts take different approaches, some observers say the policies don’t go far enough.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s statewide ban on cellphones in schools starts this year.
text:
Sam Blair demonstrates the use of a magnetically-sealed cell phone pouch at Harwood Union High School in Duxbury in August 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Kids across Vermont will be banned from using smartphones during the school day this year as a new state law takes effect. 
Although schools are newly required to have policies on banning phones from the classroom, many schools around the state have tried out the ban for the last year or two. And staff in those districts say students have been more attentive in class, more social and less likely to engage in cyber bullying. 
“We’ve had overwhelming positive responses from families, from students, from teachers,” said Ryan Heraty, superintendent of the Lamoille South Supervisory Union. This is the third year the district will restrict phones in schools, he said. 
Vermont passed its law banning cellphones from schools in 2025 amid a nationwide movement concerned about the cognitive and emotional impacts of social media and smartphone use among youth. 
Vermont’s law prohibits students from using cellphones and other personal electronic devices, such as tablets and smartwatches, during the school day unless necessary for their healthcare or academic accommodations. 
School districts have discretion, though, over how they enforce the prohibition. This school year they’re required to have district policies that are at least as restrictive as the model policy released by the Vermont Agency of Education. 
In some schools, students are required to leave their phones in their lockers or at home, while students at other schools must keep them in magnetically sealed pouches throughout the day. And at others, kids can keep their phones quietly stored in their backpacks. 
Advocates and lawmakers who supported the state’s law say that certain schools’ policies that are compliant with the law still don’t go far enough. 
“It’s not setting kids up for success,” said Rep. Angela Arsenault, D-Williston, referring to policies that allow kids to keep their phones in their backpacks or close by. 
Arsenault, who spearheaded the provision in the legislature, said research shows that as long as a student’s phone is nearby, the temptation to use it is there.
What schools are doing 
Some school districts, like the Lamoille South Supervisory Union, were ahead of the curve. 
The district’s movement to ban phones from schools started two years ago when teachers across the district grew concerned about students using their phones in class, according to superintendent Heraty.
After hearing complaints from teachers, the district surveyed parents and found overwhelming support for restricting phone use in classrooms, Heraty said. 
Rather than collecting students’ phones or providing locked magnetic pouches, schools simply require kids to leave their phones in their lockers, cars or at home, Heraty said. With that method, the school doesn’t have to spend money on methods to store phones, and school staff don’t have to be responsible for the devices. 
“Really, this is a trust situation, and we’re going to have high expectations for students,” Heraty said. 
Since restricting phones from the classroom, Heraty said that cyberbullying has decreased, students are less distracted and student achievement has improved. 
Jay Nichols, the executive director of the Vermont Principal’s Association, described similar reports from principals and superintendents across the state. Most schools leaned into the phone ban last year, he said, and he’s heard overwhelmingly positive results. 
Across the state, different schools are trying out different methods to help keep kids away from their phones, Nichols said. Some schools, like Harwood Union High School in Duxbury, have invested in magnetically sealed cell phone pouches. Others have created small cubbies or lockers made for phones, he said. 
Wendy Baker, superintendent of the Addison Central School District, said that her district’s approach to restricting devices can vary depending on the student. Some kids are allowed to keep their phones with them during the school day, while others are expected to leave their phones in the school’s office, she said. 
“It really just depends on what the student needs in order to support them,” Baker said. 
Lasting concerns 
Laura Derrendinger, an advocate for passing the law, said that she — like Arsenault — takes issue with kids being able to keep their phones within reach throughout the school day. 
Derrendinger’s 15-year-old daughter, A.M. Derrendinger, formerly attended a Waldorf school in Vermont before attending the Sharon Academy. At her former school, she said, kids were given magnetic pouches to hold their phones throughout the school day. 
Still, A.M. Derrendinger said kids would break into the pouches. She would walk into the bathroom to find other girls were on their phones, she said. Some students would find ways to talk to Siri through the pouches, she said. 
They were still a distraction. 
Laura Derendinger said the advocacy organization she helps lead, called VT-IRL.org, is grading schools around the state based on their compliance with a model policy that her advocacy organization supports. 
Schools will only receive an A grade from her organization if students have to store their phones in a central location for the entire school day, she said. It’s the only model in which “there’s no risk of a child being tempted even,” she added. 
“That is the least expensive and most effective solution,” she said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas led the way on vaccinations. It shouldn’t follow Trump backward in time.
description: Anger and policy aren’t always good combinations. Betty Bumpers, however, proved that there’s an exception to that rule. The former first lady of Arkansas was dismayed when her husband, Gov. Dale Bumpers, took office and she learned the state had one of the lowest childhood vaccination rates in the country. That changed after she spearheaded […]
text:
Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy on Jan. 26, 2015 in Mill Valley, California.  (Photo by Illustration Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Anger and policy aren’t always good combinations. Betty Bumpers, however, proved that there’s an exception to that rule.
The former first lady of Arkansas was dismayed when her husband, Gov. Dale Bumpers, took office and she learned the state had one of the lowest childhood vaccination rates in the country.
That changed after she spearheaded a successful campaign to get more Arkansas kids vaccinated, an effort she later took nationwide with former first lady Rosalynn Carter.
Bumpers told the Los Angeles Times in 1994 that her campaign with Carter to get every child younger than 2 immunized was “fueled by anger.”
“Anger that we can’t figure out a way to care for our children,” she said.
Arkansas could use a little more of Betty Bumpers’ anger. President Donald Trump’s recent executive order on childhood vaccinations threatens to reverse decades of progress on public health that Bumpers helped secure. 



Let us know what you think...


 


Trump’s order advocates splitting up the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three separate single-disease shots. It also recommends that all childhood immunizations be administered in separate medical visits. 
Following such a recommendation poses logistical challenges and would create new burdens for families. Carrying it out would require drugmakers to build new manufacturing plants to produce more vaccine doses. For families, it would require multiple trips to the doctor and could strain pediatricians further.
The Trump administration is also issuing the recommendation as the president and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. continue promoting widely discredited claims linking childhood vaccines to autism.
Experts say the order has questionable legal authority, but it threatens to add to the confusion and misinformation surrounding vaccines. It also comes as measles cases in the U.S. are reaching record highs. 
Arkansas’ public health officials and elected leaders have an opportunity to speak out against the recommendations. History shows that Arkansas can be a leader on vaccinations and in battling misinformation about them.
Arkansas was the first state in 1916 to introduce a mandatory smallpox vaccination program for all children starting school. Bumpers’ efforts as first lady helped give Arkansas one of the highest immunization rates in the country, and her campaign was used as a national model.
“Because of Mrs. Bumpers’ efforts, more than 95% of American children today are protected against what once were the most dreaded childhood diseases,” then-Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Robert Redfield said when Bumpers died in 2018.
More recently, former Gov. Asa Hutchinson showed the value of elected officials standing up to vaccine misinformation. The Republican governor endured jeers at times as he spoke out in favor of the COVID-19 vaccine, and even received his COVID vaccine booster shots on livestream to demonstrate their safety.
Arkansas has also seen the dangers of not getting vaccinated. A decade ago, a mumps outbreak in Springdale grew to nearly 3,000 cases and was one of the largest the U.S. had seen in decades. The outbreak accounted for 41% of the mumps cases in the country that year. 
Bumpers showed how one person’s anger about the government not doing enough to protect children can translate into meaningful action. Imagine the anger she would have displayed at an order that won’t just undermine her legacy but threatens to reverse decades of progress in protecting children.
