name: Florida Phoenix
title: Angie Nixon shrugs off the Florida GOP attacks that are just beginning
description: Although Florida Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon’s ties with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) appear limited, the Republican Party of Florida appears determined to use that association to paint her as unelectable. Nixon is a member of the “I hate America DSA Party,” Sen. Ashley Moody told reporters in Tampa Thursday night. She […]
text:
Florida Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon in St. Petersburg on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Although Florida Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon’s ties with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) appear limited, the Republican Party of Florida appears determined to use that association to paint her as unelectable.
Nixon is a member of the “I hate America DSA Party,” Sen. Ashley Moody told reporters in Tampa Thursday night. She went on to decry the DSA’s stance on defunding the police and defunding and abolishing prisons.
“This stuff is anti-American,” Moody said.
Nixon rejected Moody’s assertions on Friday.
“Ashley Moody needs to stick to the facts,” she told a Phoenix reporter in an interview on WMNF 88.5 FM radio in Tampa. “She’s just continuing to demonize me. What has she done for our country and our state, besides making it more unaffordable?”
Nixon made it clear she’s never called for defunding law enforcement.
“What I have called for is a people’s budget and a people’s agenda, which is what I will continue to call for, because I believe that hardworking everyday people should get to shape what our communities look like and what our economies look like.”
Nixon said earlier this week that she does not support abolishing prisons, but does support abolishing for-profit prisons.
Her reputation as one of the most liberal members of the Florida House far preceded any association with DSA, which she did join this summer. When asked if her link to the biggest socialist organization in the United States makes it harder to defeat Moody, she said it didn’t really matter.
“So, they’re going to associate me with DSA or socialists or communism anyway,” she said Friday. “They were already doing that. And so, the reason I joined the organization was because they believe we should have access to quality healthcare. They believe that we should have quality access to quality housing and fully funded public schools.”
During her six years in the Florida House, the Jacksonville representative sparked several controversies on the floor of that chamber. None were considered as incendiary as when she introduced a resolution calling for a cease-fire in the Middle East a month after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
She brought up the incident unsolicited Friday.
“When I called for that cease-fire, I upset some members of the Jewish community. Guess what I did when I ran for office? Every week I had a different community on a Zoom, on a line with me asking me hard-hitting questions. I did it for the Jewish community. I did it for the Muslim community. I did it for the LGBTQ community. I did it for kids. I did it for Black men. Black women. I talk to people. 
“And the problem is, you have politicians that are so uptight and just want to try to stick to these same talking points and they’re just afraid to go out and be a normal person. No one wants to continue to elect people who live in this, like, ivory tower. They want regular, everyday people who understand what it’s like to struggle.”
The mother of five says she has had her struggles.
“I was a single momma for 12 years, right? I know how to make a dollar stretch, but we shouldn’t have to do that. I know what it’s like to make a decision around, ‘Oh, my God, my daughter needs her asthma pump, but I gotta make sure to have enough money to feed her and keep a roof over our head.’ 
“People are making decisions like that each and every day, and it is because Ashley Moody, Ron DeSantis, Donald Trump, Rick Scott, it is because they have been in power for so long and so now people want something different. They are tired of the corruption. They are tired of the lies.”
Hope Florida
Nixon also criticized Moody’s involvement in the Hope Florida scandal.
Several weeks ago, Alex Vindman, Nixon’s now vanquished Democratic Senate opponent, began calling on Moody to request the grand jury report (or “presentment”) on what happened with Hope Florida. Shortly thereafter, the Florida Democratic Party did the same thing. That grand jury investigation examined how $10 million from a state Medicaid settlement was diverted to the Hope Florida Foundation, connected to First Lady Casey DeSantis. That money was then sent to a political action committee chaired by DeSantis’ then-chief of staff, James Uthmeier.
Moody approved the transfer of the $10 million to the Hope Florida Foundation as part of a larger $67 million agreement the Florida Agency of Healthcare Administration (AHCA) signed with Centene Health Plan, one of several managed care providers the state contracts with to provide health services to the poor, elderly, and disabled. The other $57 million went to the agency.
A spokesperson for Moody’s Senate campaign issued a statement saying, “The Senator has had no role in any grand jury proceedings and would certainly have no issue with the public release of any report.”
“I cannot get over this lady allowed $10 million that was supposed to go towards the most medically needy kids to be diverted,” Nixon said. “I am someone who had a child that was on KidCare. Like, I would not have been able to ensure that my child had the medicine that she needed.”
Who’s the ‘big-tent party’?
Byron Donalds and Ashley Moody in Tampa on Aug. 20, 2026 (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix).
While Nixon will use that issue and others against Moody, Republicans seem united in using socialism as a scarlet letter against her.
“I think it divides Democrats,” GOP gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds said about the DSA while speaking with reporters in Tampa Thursday night. 
“They don’t even know what party they are on Capitol Hill. I think it puts more pressure on them here in Florida. Are they going to continue down the line of socialism? Is that where Democratic voters want to go? And I’ll tell you, I don’t think that’s all Democratic voters. I think you have a lot of conservative-leaning Democratic voters. Longstanding registered voters, who are JFK Democrats or Bill Clinton Democrats. And they do not recognize this party. And so, we are a common sense party. We’re a big-tent party.”
“I know people are trying to box me in, but, like, we are a big-tent party as far as the Democratic Party,” Nixon said. “And all of the Republicans who are fighting for higher office, Byron Donalds, Ashley Moody, they don’t have a leg to stand on because they are the reason that we are in the mess right now. People are working harder than ever and they’re just struggling just to stay afloat.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: After five theft convictions, nursing home worker faces licensing sanctions
description: An Iowa nursing home worker who has been convicted of theft on at least five occasions is now facing sanctions from state licensing officials. The Iowa Board of Nursing has charged licensed practical nurse Sam Justin Cook, 47, of Ankeny with failing to notify the board of a criminal conviction within 30 days and with […]
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Nursing)An Iowa nursing home worker who has been convicted of theft on at least five occasions is now facing sanctions from state licensing officials.
The Iowa Board of Nursing has charged licensed practical nurse Sam Justin Cook, 47, of Ankeny with failing to notify the board of a criminal conviction within 30 days and with failing to respond to or comply with a board investigation or subpoena.
Sam Justin Cook of Ankeny. (Photo from Iowa District Court records)
The board has released no information on the circumstances that gave rise to the charges. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for Oct. 15, 2026.
Court records show Cook, who has worked at the Bethany Life care facility in Story City and other Iowa nursing homes, has been convicted of theft on at least five occasions.
In December 2024, police charged Cook with theft after he allegedly entered a Casey’s General Store in Story County, stole three charging devices worth roughly $54, then traveled to a different Casey’s where he returned the items for a “refund.” He later pleaded guilty to a charge of fifth-degree theft and paid a fine of $105.
Within days of that arrest, police again charged Cook with theft, alleging he had entered a Hy-Vee store, selected an $18 can opener off the shelf, then walked to the customer-service area of the store and returned the item for a “refund” of $18. He later pleaded guilty to a charge of fifth-degree theft and paid a fine of $105.
Two weeks after the Hy-Vee arrest, Cook was again charged with theft, with police alleging he had entered a Hy-Vee store, taken a decorative pillow from the floral department, then collected a $24 “refund” from the store’s customer-service staff. The theft charge was later dismissed by Story County prosecutors.
Three months later, in March 2025, Cook was employed by one of ManorCare’s Iowa facilities when he was again charged with theft. Police alleged he entered a Menard’s store, selected three Dremel-tool products, then took them directly to the customer-service center, where he obtained $65 in store credit for the “returned” items. He was later convicted of third-degree theft and sentenced to one year of probation.
In court records related to that case, Cook acknowledged other, previous convictions for theft in 1998 and 2002.
State records indicate Cook has been a licensed practical nurse since 2005. In 2019, the Iowa Board of Nursing charged Cook with repeatedly leaving a nursing assignment without first ensuring the safety and welfare of patients and ordered Cook to complete 4.6 hours of educational training on professional responsibility and legal liability.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Cook for comment.

name: VTDigger
title: Fed-up White River Junction bar owner posted explicit security footage, then apologized
description:
The emoji-censored video showed two people engaging in sexual behavior in the bar’s patio area. Similar incidents, ranging from drug use to theft, have become daily occurrences, she said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Fed-up White River Junction bar owner posted explicit security footage, then apologized.
text:
Patrons visit Putnam’s vine/yard in White River Junction, Vt., on Thursday, March 23, 2023. (Valley News / Report For America – Alex Driehaus) Copyright Valley News. May not be reprinted or used online without permission. Send requests to permission@vnews.com. Credit: Valley News / Report For America
This story by Marion Umpleby was first published in the Valley News on Aug. 21, 2026.
WHITE RIVER JUNCTION — In the early hours of Aug. 5, Kelsey Rush awoke to an alert from a security camera on the exterior of Putnam’s Vine/yard, her cafe and bar on South Main Street.
The footage showed two people engaging in sexual behavior behind a wooden bench in the bar’s patio area. 
About four hours later, Rush posted clips of the footage to Putnam’s Instagram using snake or eggplant emojis to cover the people’s genitals, along with captions such as “When someone replies five stars, and you have to remind them that lasting for two min does not make for five stars.” 
She also posted footage captured two nights before that showed two people using drugs on the bar’s property. 
Similar incidents, ranging from drug use to theft, have become daily occurrences, Rush said in an interview, and she was fed up. 
“I was definitely triggered by the idea that this gentleman and his partner were … trespassing, being lewd, leaving behind fluids on places customers sit,” Rush said.
She soon deleted the videos after receiving criticism from viewers about her decision to post footage of people having sex without getting their consent, which is illegal under Vermont state law. 
The Hartford Police Department declined to disclose if Rush was facing legal repercussions for posting the videos. 
While it’s unclear whether the people having sex in the video were unhoused or using drugs, the incident — and Rush’s decision to post footage of it — sparked ongoing discussion about the prevalence of drug use and homelessness in White River Junction and how the village can support people grappling with these challenges as well as the businesses affected by them.
“The way people view unhoused people, people dealing with substance issues, it’s awful,” Jordyn Lich, a production manager and producer at the White River Junction community media center JAM (Junction Arts and Media), said in a recent interview.
Lich, who provided screenshots of Rush’s posts to the Valley News, recently drafted a letter urging Rush to apologize for her actions, agree to never again distribute security camera footage on social media, and to engage with a local organization to “repair the harm they have caused in the community.”
“Putnam’s chose to publicly humiliate these community members and tag the Hartford Police Department on social media, the least appropriate avenues to deal with the situation,” the letter read. 
As of Monday, the letter had received 65 signatures. 
Rush received the letter after she issued an Aug. 12 apology on Facebook stating, “We are sorry that the way we shared these stories contributed to fear, hurt, or stigma in our community.” 
The post went on to say that Putnam’s had joined a “community watch set up by a neighborhood business” and made donations to the Upper Valley Haven and H2RC, a group that organizes needle clean-ups. 
“I’m sorry. I took them down,” Rush, a resident of Hanover, New Hampshire, said in a Thursday interview. But, she added, “when you trespass … you’re giving up your right to privacy.” 
Rush, a Dartmouth graduate who opened Putnam’s in 2022, has noticed an increase in theft and drug-related incidents on the bar’s property in the past three months. 
She estimates she’s spent several thousand dollars replacing stolen patio furniture and extension cords. She’s also invested in protective gear to clean up human feces and needles, and her employees frequently have to wash drug residue from the bar’s outdoor tables, she said.
Stephanie Waterman, who owns Growpro, the dispensary and plant store located in the same parking lot as Putnam’s, has noticed similar incidents. 
“The last year we have seen this incredible degradation downtown with a significant increase of drug activity,” Waterman said in a Thursday interview. 
She often sees people passed out in the parking lot, and her staff have found “dozens of needles on the ground.” 
Waterman didn’t see Rush’s posts, but she considers them “a hysterical and interesting PR move,” she said. 
“There’s no right to privacy in a public space, so if you’re having sex in a public space, you have no right to privacy,” Waterman said, echoing Rush’s sentiment. 
At the same time, “I’m glad she took it down,” Waterman added. “Obviously it’s a little crass.” 
Instances of drug use and theft at Putnam’s coincide with steep housing costs in White River Junction and a growing need for food and shelter among the village’s unhoused population. 
“White River Junction to me is like the most textbook example of gentrification I have ever witnessed,” said Lich, adding that Putnam’s, where a 5-ounce glass of wine can cost $35, is “part of the problem.”
Larry Blake Harvey, executive director of the Hartford Community Restorative Justice Center, which offers community housing and employment opportunities to people seeking a fresh start, said he’s noticed an increase in people visiting the nonprofit for snacks, water and a hot shower who aren’t part of its programs.
“We don’t have the funding to support all these people,” said Harvey, who recently had to put away many of the center’s free snacks because the demand was growing too high. 
Supporting White River Junction’s unhoused population also came up at the Aug. 18 Hartford Selectboard meeting, where Lich criticized Rush’s Instagram posts.
“In these posts, Putnam’s mocked, demeaned and posted nude, explicit content of these individuals without their consent,” Lich said in the public comment section of the meeting.
Selectboard member Miranda Dupre acknowledged that issues of homelessness and addiction go beyond the scope of White River Junction. 
“I don’t think the town is going to solve this problem. I think all we can do is harm reduction and kind of like putting band-aid fixes wherever we can …,” she said at the Aug. 18 meeting. 
But that’s not enough, and it’s not sustainable for the town as a whole, she added. 
She urged the selectboard to demand the state and federal government fund healthcare and other services.
Lich had their own ideas, too. 
“Perhaps plan free community workshops around harm reduction” and “what it means to live in a surveillance state,” they said. 
The Hartford Community Restorative Justice Center, for its part, has been working on ways to include unhoused people and those struggling with addiction in discussions about how the village can better support them. 
One avenue could be a public “circle of support,” where unhoused people can voice their needs and experiences. 
“This is a challenge that every major city is facing without a lot of answers, so as a rural community the cards are kind of stacked against you,” Harvey said.

title: Measles spread in Wisconsin; almost everyone made ill is unvaccinated, health officials say
description: An outbreak of measles in two counties reported earlier this month has spread and is affecting 48 people, the state health department reported Friday. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services has identified a total of 41 confirmed cases and seven “probable” cases, reported in Grant, Iowa and Lafayette counties. They include two cases in Grant […]
text:
A young child with measles. According to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, 12% of the measles cases in Wisconsin this year are in children age 4 or younger. (Getty Images)An outbreak of measles in two counties reported earlier this month has spread and is affecting 48 people, the state health department reported Friday.
The Wisconsin Department of Health Services has identified a total of 41 confirmed cases and seven “probable” cases, reported in Grant, Iowa and Lafayette counties. They include two cases in Grant County, which were reported earlier this week, and 35 in Iowa County.
In Lafayette County, the count is now four confirmed measles cases and seven probable cases. One of the confirmed cases is new, along with the four probable cases, DHS reported in an updated announcement. 
So far DHS has not found evidence of public exposure to the virus, meaning the cases identified so far appear to have been spread between people who knew each other.
State health officials are recommending that people check their vaccination status. The MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine is the best protection against measles, health officials say.
DHS is recommending that anyone who isn’t sure whether they have the MMR vaccine check their vaccination status at the Wisconsin Immunization Registry or with their local public health department or healthcare provider.
A federal report in July found that nationwide, measles cases have reached their highest level in 35 years. The reemergence of the viral illness, which public health experts said had been eliminated by 2000, coincides with declining vaccination rates in the U.S.
Since Jan. 1, the number of Wisconsin measles cases has grown to 50, according to DHS, and with one exception, everyone who has taken ill was not vaccinated for the disease. 
DHS operates a Measles Dashboard and a webpage for Outbreaks and Investigations that supplies more public information about public health conditions, with 12% of cases in children age 4 or younger, 44% in children ages 5 to 17, and 44% in adults 18 or older.
This report was updated with additional information from DHS.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Residents voice concerns over Mandan data center during town hall
description: Infrastructure costs, potential for constant noise and close proximity to local schools were a few of the concerns raised Thursday by Morton County residents during an informational meeting regarding a proposed data center. The Stark Power data center and natural gas generation campus in Mandan is still in its planning phase, but the location seems […]
text:
Attendees view promotional signs and talk with project members of a proposed Stark Power data center during an informational open house in Mandan on Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Infrastructure costs, potential for constant noise and close proximity to local schools were a few of the concerns raised Thursday by Morton County residents during an informational meeting regarding a proposed data center.
The Stark Power data center and natural gas generation campus in Mandan is still in its planning phase, but the location seems to be set. The facility would be built north of Interstate 94, between Highway 1806 and Old Red Trail, a short distance from Red Trail Elementary, Mandan Middle School and Mandan High School.
That’s too close for Terry Mastel of Mandan who lives off Old Red Trail, near the proposed site. He worries about the destruction of the natural environment for future generations and school kids, including his granddaughter who will attend school near the project area.
“We have sunshine. We have quiet. We have a river that’s clean, and all of these things are going to affect us,” Mastel said. “I feel that sometimes it’s hard to stop a train, but I think that we have to not quit trying to stop the train.”
Michael Wahlen, managing director of digital infrastructure for Stark Power, said in an interview that the company is not looking at alternative sites for the project. The company has not submitted a zoning application since city and county officials are evaluating data center ordinance proposals.
Michael Wahlen, left, managing director of digital infrastructure for Stark Power, speaks to attendees about a proposed data center during a Mandan informational open house on Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“We want to give the city and the community time to be thoughtful and deliberate about the things that are important to them and make sure those are reflected in the ordinance,” Wahlen said. “And then we’ll move forward with a project application, if we determine that the ordinance is workable once we have it finalized.”
State lawmakers have data centers on their radar, too – forming a new committee to look into the issue and including a bill draft banning nondisclosure agreements involving industrial projects during a special session that starts Sept. 2. The Mandan project will not use nondisclosure agreements, according to posters displayed at the event.
North Dakota is seen as an attractive state for data center developers, with a cool climate, access to power and rural space to build in. Members of Legislative Management discussed data centers as part of multiple bills proposed by Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, on Monday. 
One of Mathern’s bills would have temporarily banned North Dakota counties, cities and townships from issuing construction permits for data center projects through June 2027, but that proposal did not advance out of the committee.
“Data centers developing across America have dramatic impacts on communities, the energy grid and infrastructure demands,” Mathern said Monday. “Data centers create potential economic benefits, but also great stressors, and, if not done correctly, great harm.”
Sen. Brad Bekkedahl, R-Williston, one of the lawmakers who opposed a moratorium, argued that it would prevent a community that wants a data center from moving forward with a project.
Sen. Keith Boehm, R-Mandan, who attended the Mandan data center open house, said letting the state decide issues before local subdivisions would be a “bad idea.”
“Local control is always best,” Boehm said. “I think of these industrial projects as an opportunity, but you better mitigate the determinants.”
He added issues surrounding water use, noise and infrastructure need to be addressed by Stark Power to reassure the community.
The Mandan project would generate about 1,000 construction jobs and about 150 full-time positions once completed, according to the project website. The company estimates the facility could generate $40 million to $50 million in annual economic benefits to Mandan public schools, the city of Mandan and Morton County.
No pause on data centers but North Dakota special session to debate nondisclosure deals

The company plans to hold more informational sessions with Mandan and Morton County residents, Wahlen said. 
On Thursday, residents filled Mandan’s Signature Events Center and lined up outside waiting to get in and talk to the project team. 
Lee Fleischer of Mandan said he wants to see upfront payments from Stark Power to cover the costs of city and county infrastructure improvements needed for the data center, if the project should fail.
“If they start the project and then find out it’s not going to go the way they want, we’ve got the money,” Fleischer said. He added he also wants to see a definitive amount on how much tax revenue the project will generate for the city and county, not estimates of economic benefits provided by the company, and a fully-funded decommission plan for the facility before construction starts.
Blaine Engelstad of Mandan said he doesn’t support the project and worries about the noise that could be caused by the facility.
“Inevitably, we probably need them, but not right here,” Engelstad said. “We don’t have any superfund sites around here, but we have some reclaimed coal mine areas. Put them there.”
The company is taking steps to minimize noise, including installing mechanical equipment in the center of the facility, using sound-dampening materials and installing engineered sound walls, according to the project website.
Data center concerns dominate public comment for new legislative committee

Wahlen said the project team appreciates the comments from Mandan and Morton County residents and hopes the community gives them a chance to address their issues. He said Stark Power is going to propose a community benefit agreement that would be funded by the company, but controlled by a group of community members to support initiatives in Mandan and Morton County.
“Between our commitment to being good neighbors and the intentionality that the city has put into the ordinance development, there’s a recipe here for a project that works well for everyone, and that’s what we’re hopeful for,” he said.
The city of Mandan will review its data center ordinance during a meeting of the Planning and Zoning Commission on Monday, and the Morton County Planning and Zoning Commission is expected to discuss its ordinance on Wednesday.
The legislative Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee moved its next meeting a day earlier than originally scheduled to 9 a.m. Aug. 31, ahead of a special session of the Legislature. Lawmakers also will take public testimony on Sept. 1 about special session bills, including the proposal related to nondisclosure agreements.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Fentanyl seizures plummeted as Trump administration shifted focus to immigration
text: WASHINGTON — Fentanyl seizures decreased by 39% during the first year of the second Trump administration after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shifted the Department of Homeland Security’s criminal investigations arm to conducting immigration enforcement, according to a report government investigators published Friday. Agents with Homeland Security Investigations, a subagency of DHS’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement, reported an “all hands-on deck” environment toward immigration enforcement began in January 2025, according to the DHS Office of Inspector General report.“With ICE dedicating more staff hours to immigration investigations, staffing hours for fentanyl investigations declined,” the report said.The report found that the hours dedicated to fentanyl investigations for fiscal 2025 declined by more than 250,000 hours, or 31%, compared to fiscal 2024.“At the same time, immigration enforcement saw the largest increase across all investigative categories, rising more than 1.7 million hours (over 800 percent),” according to the report.Inspectors interviewed more than 100 agents from 11 HSI field offices for the report.At one HSI office, approximately 99% of work was dedicated to immigration, leaving almost no capacity for fentanyl investigations, the watchdog found. A drug investigation team of seven agents was reduced to about three and the rest of the personnel was reassigned to work on immigration cases, according to the report.  Fentanyl is a highly addictive synthetic opioid that is the main driver of overdose deaths in the United States. HSI plays a key role in countering fentanyl smuggling in the U.S. by targeting routes, laboratories and collaborating with law enforcement to investigate smuggling operations.    ICE agreesThe inspector general recommended that HSI review staffing levels “to ensure an appropriate level of coverage commensurate with the relative priority of fentanyl investigations.”Inspector general reports are presented to the affected agency for comment ahead of publication. ICE agreed with the recommendations in the DHS OIG report.“Homeland Security Investigations will review staffing levels, and determine and implement next steps, as needed, to ensure an appropriate level of coverage commensurate with the relative priority of fentanyl investigations,” ICE’s comments in the report read.ICE estimated that recommendation would be completed by June 2027.The report also found that the technology HSI agents and analysts used had limitations during fentanyl investigations and their missions were “hindered by delays in agents obtaining funds to purchase information and evidence (i.e., drugs) during an investigation; a lack of independent authority to investigate fentanyl-related offenses; and low, inconsistent referral of fentanyl cases from U.S. Customs and Border Protection to HSI.”

name: WyoFile
title: The BLM may stop notifying landowners about drilling under private land. Wyoming ranchers are alarmed.
description:
Western cattlemen are poised to lose almost all opportunity to comment on oil and gas development underneath their property.
The post The BLM may stop notifying landowners about drilling under private land. Wyoming ranchers are alarmed. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Joe and Nancy Rankin’s ranch, just north of Douglas, has been in the family for 80 years. As Joe Rankin manages the ranch, he keeps track of any oil drilling underneath their land. But, due to a controversial federal proposal, his ability to influence or even comment on such operations may soon evaporate. His property and others nearby are already impacted by drilling. 
“Some spots in my area right now look like a spaghetti bowl from all the pipelines that are going through,” Rankin said.
Tracking drilling, for Rankin, also means managing environmental consequences and personal headaches. Leaks from abandoned or “orphaned” wells affect his cattle and cause bovine health issues, he said. At one point during a blizzard, his herd ended up stranded in a ditch where developers were trying to build a pipeline. Another time, he found Bureau of Land Management officials driving across his pasture and had to convince them that they should not be there.
Rankin’s property is a “split estate,” meaning that he and many of his neighbors do not own the rights to the minerals underneath their ranches. The mineral rights — which are owned, in this case, by the BLM and leased to interested oil and gas companies — are separate from surface rights to the ranch’s grass, soil and buildings. And mineral rights are dominant over surface property rights, meaning that the companies that acquire them often have the ability to access surface property and house equipment there, even if the landowner objects. 
A drilling rig stands against the sunset Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2014, in Wright. (Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile)
Historically, the public has been given a total of 90 days to weigh in on any leasing of BLM-managed minerals. Oil and gas companies were also required to identify surface owners whose land may be impacted by proposed underground development, and the BLM was required to notify them. But soon, Rankin and other Western landowners may lose that right: In a June leasing proposal, the BLM proposed reducing the general public comment period to 10 days and eliminating the landowner notification requirement for split-estate land. Separately, the agency also wants to reduce the minimum bonds companies are required to pay in case drilling is abandoned without environmental cleanup. The changes would apply to oil and gas as well as to other subterranean natural resources managed by the agency.
The public comment window for the BLM’s proposed changes ends Monday. Comments are accepted here. 
Industry interests praised the proposal as beneficial for smaller companies and important for growth. But many landowners and local government officials say the proposal will remove public input, impede landowner rights and jeopardize community health. 
Wyoming’s influential ranching lobby opposes the changes to public comment, and Douglas Mayor Kim Pexton, Montana state Rep. Shelly Fyant and New Mexico rancher Don Schreiber penned a joint op-ed in WyoFile criticizing the split estate proposal and the other two changes. All told, there are nearly 58 million acres of split-estate land across the U.S., an area roughly the size of Wyoming. Montana and Wyoming have the two largest amounts: over 11 million acres, an area five times larger than Yellowstone National Park and the Wind River Reservation.
‘Count your fingers’
The division of land rights is common in the rural U.S., especially in the West. It’s partly a relic of early 20th-century policy intended to promote Westward expansion while preserving underground minerals for extraction. North of Douglas, most landowners own split-estate land, according to Rankin. Wyomingites and other Westerners have spent decades in state legislatures and courts battling over whose rights take precedence: companies’ or landowners’.
The proposed changes in split-estate management align with the Trump administration’s long-stated goal of bolstering and deregulating the energy industry. In a press release announcing the proposal, the Interior Department, which oversees the BLM, said it expects the change to benefit small oil and gas companies. 
“These targeted updates cut through the red tape that has historically deterred investment, ensuring our public lands remain a reliable engine for economic growth and innovation,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said.
U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum speaks in June 2025 at the Western Governors’ Association conference in Santa Fe, New Mexico. (Ellen Jaskol)
Rural communities will be impacted the most, according to Gwen Lachelt, founder of Western Leaders Network, which advocates for conservation and democracy. She added that the proposal represents a notable change from the BLM’s previous values. 
“This has always been an agency that has been difficult to work with, but it has been an agency in the past that has valued the input of the public and has respected landowner rights,” Lachelt said.
For the most part, Rankin said, working with the BLM and with drilling companies has been amicable. But the experience can vary depending on the company.
“One company just falls over backwards to take care of us,” he said. “Another company, when you shake hands, you count your fingers when you’re done to make sure you have them all.”
Public comment
When companies express interest in leasing and extracting underground minerals, the BLM currently requires firms to identify surface landowners who may be impacted. The BLM is then required to notify those landowners, often ranchers, with a letter or a phone call.
Separately, the agency currently offers three 30-day periods for public comment on all leasing: during the initial scoping period, after an environmental review and then a final opportunity to protest. The proposed changes would reduce the public input period to 10 days by eliminating the first two comment periods and cutting the final protest window by two-thirds.
Jim Magagna, a rancher from Rock Springs and executive vice president of the Wyoming Stock Growers Association, called the proposed public comment reduction unreasonable. 
“Our people are out busy,” Magagna said, occupied with “haying, or they’re feeding cows, or they’re calving, or they’re shipping. And a 10-day comment period?” 
By ending landowner notification requirements and slashing the comment window, the BLM is essentially removing landowners’ right to comment, Magagna said. At a minimum, he added, surface owners should “definitely” be notified before minerals are put up for lease.
The BLM, meanwhile, says it doesn’t plan to notify landowners because the Mineral Leasing Act, which governs extraction on public land, doesn’t require the agency to do so. Notification, the BLM says in federal documents, “imposes undue burdens on the oil and gas industry.”
Jim Magagna, 80, tries to guide a separated lamb back to its flock while it’s unloaded from trucks at his ranch on July 3, 2023.(Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Public comment doesn’t just benefit landowners with concerns, Lachelt said. It is also good for companies that may have overlooked details of their drilling plans.
“I’ve worked with really incredible federal personnel with the BLM who take every single comment to heart, and they have improved applications immensely based on public feedback, because no one knows their land better than those people who are being directly drilled on,” she said.
BLM officials said the reduced comment period is designed to eliminate repetitive review, and that the concerns raised in public comment periods can likely be addressed through other elements of the leasing process, like larger-scale land-use planning.
“Shortening the protest period from 30 to 10 days streamlines the lease‑sale process while preserving opportunities for public input at other stages,” a BLM spokesperson told High Country News in a statement.
Bond levels
The June announcement also proposed a change to the bond levels implemented by the Biden administration, which received widespread media coverage at the time. In contrast, the recent Trump administration proposal has received far less fanfare; many Douglas landowners had not even heard of the proposal several weeks after its release. Bonds act as collateral, charged in case a company abandons a drilling site without proper environmental cleanup. The bond money is used to plug orphaned wells and repair any environmental damage.
“That is a worst-case scenario, and it is something that we work hard within our organization, within our industry to avoid,” said Aaron Johnson, vice president of public and legislative affairs with the Western Energy Alliance.
A 2023 U.S. Geological Survey analysis documented over 1,000 orphaned wells in Wyoming alone, with thousands more scattered across the West, though the study found that the rate of “orphaning” appeared to decline with newer wells. In federal documents, the BLM acknowledges that reducing the bond amounts may delay orphaned well reclamation.
From 1951 to 2024, the federal government set bond levels at $25,000 for statewide leases. In 2024, the Biden administration raised that amount to $500,000 to address inflation and prioritize covering the costs associated with cleanup.
Bill West walks toward one of about 100 orphan coal-bed methane wells on his family’s ranch near Arvada on April 8, 2015. (Ryan Dorgan)
If adjusted just for inflation, the U.S. Government Accountability Office estimated in a 2019 report that statewide bond amounts would be around $198,000. Rankin, the Wyoming rancher, supports a higher bond level.
“It gives them more incentive to care,” Rankin said, speaking of private companies. 
But the Western Energy Alliance’s Johnson called the Biden-era bond increase excessive, adding that the Trump administration’s proposed reduction would likely benefit small- and medium-sized companies.
“Going from $25,000 to $500,000 is punitive, and that half a million dollars is just sitting idle,” Johnson said.
The BLM agrees.
“Returning minimum bond levels to $10,000 for leases and $25,000 statewide reduces barriers for smaller operators while continuing to ensure adequate reclamation coverage,” the agency spokesperson said.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: US senator from South Dakota subjects Postal Service to multiple pressure points
description: About two years ago, U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, started hearing increasing complaints about slow mail delivery. Veterans weren’t receiving their prescriptions on time, he said, or medications got lost on the way. Some people said they received bills on the day payments were due. Newspaper publishers said it took over a week for […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, speaks during a Downtown Sioux Falls Rotary event on Oct. 28, 2024. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)
https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/rounds-postal-service-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
About two years ago, U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, started hearing increasing complaints about slow mail delivery. Veterans weren’t receiving their prescriptions on time, he said, or medications got lost on the way. Some people said they received bills on the day payments were due. Newspaper publishers said it took over a week for papers to travel less than 100 miles away, and some reported lost deliveries.
Rounds took his frustrations to the postmaster general, who resigned not long after their meeting. Rounds then brought his complaints to the new postmaster general, “who basically pooh-poohed our concerns” and said “the bigger problems were in the bigger cities,” Rounds recalled.
Growing increasingly frustrated, Rounds concluded a letter about the matter to fellow senators in June by writing “I am forwarding this to you via email because if I mailed it, you may not receive this letter in a timely fashion.”
The senator’s recent actions in response to the problems include supporting an investigation into the Postal Service, proposing legislation to remove bonuses for Postal Service executives, and placing a hold on Senate confirmations of new members for the Postal Service’s executive board.
Investigation underway
In December, Rounds asked the Inspector General of the U.S. Postal Service to investigate the state’s mail delivery problems.
“They cautioned us that they would have to do this somewhat in a clandestine manner because they couldn’t trust that the post office wouldn’t try to hide mail if they knew they were coming in to inspect,” Rounds said, “which is exactly what we have found out to be true.”
Rounds said he’s heard from post office workers who say when there’s a potential for the inspector general to show up, employees are directed to hide undelivered mail.
“So, we’ve really appreciated the help from postal employees who have been frustrated by the inability of the post office to honor the commitment that they’ve made in the past,” Rounds said.
A report from the investigation should be available in September, according to Rounds.
Legislation introduced
Recent changes to processing procedures have deprioritized rural America in an effort to save costs, Rounds said.
Two years ago, Postal Service leaders decided to move all non-local mail processing from the Huron, South Dakota, processing facility to Fargo, North Dakota. Rounds and fellow South Dakota Republicans Sen. John Thune and Rep. Dusty Johnson pushed then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy to reconsider. Due in part to that effort, the Postal Service announced last year that it would keep some processing at the Huron site.
In 2025, the Postal Service began its Regional Transportation Optimization initiative. That means mail dropped off at post offices more than 50 miles from a regional hub will only be transported to processing centers once per day, instead of two or more, which means some mail is delayed. The initiative is expected to save millions of dollars, according to the National Association of Postal Supervisors.
The Postal Regulatory Commission, an independent oversight agency, found the new initiative negatively impacts rural communities. In 2025, about 64% of rural communities were anticipated to experience slowed service.
Small-town newspapers say mail delays are crippling their business

Rounds said he has tested the speed of mail delivery in South Dakota. He sent a letter from his office in Rapid City to his office in Pierre. It left the state and passed through Colorado, Nebraska, Iowa and North Dakota before being delivered at his Pierre office over a 10-day stretch of time, he said.
“It was evident that they had not counted on the length of time it takes to truck over long distances that amount of mail,” Rounds said. “First-class mail is supposed to be delivered in three days. It’s taking closer to 10 for a lot of the mail in South Dakota.”
Continued problems with mail delivery led Rounds to introduce the Executive Benefit and Bonus Removal Act, which would eliminate bonuses for Postal Service executives.
“Incompetent bureaucrats should not get bonuses when the mail does not run on time,” Rounds said. “If the Postal Service were serious about cutting costs, it should cut costs inside its own ivory tower before passing costs on to the American people who are still receiving terrible service.”
Hold on nominations
In addition to his legislation, Rounds has placed a hold on all Senate confirmations of nominees for Postal Service Board of Governor positions.
Senators can hold bills and nominations, sometimes out of process-related concerns or to gain leverage while negotiating with agencies or colleagues. The decision to honor a hold request ultimately rests with the majority leader — Thune. Rounds’ move is known as a “blanket hold,” objecting to the approval of all nominations for a specific government agency.
“It is my intent to only release this blanket hold when my concerns are fully resolved by USPS leadership and service returns to levels at least equal to the days of the Pony Express,” Rounds said in a letter.
The Board of Governors acts as a board of directors. A full board has 11 members, but there are five unfilled positions. President Donald Trump nominated one person last June and announced three nominations in March.
Issues facing the Postal Service
In a June Senate hearing on the “Postal Service’s broken business model,” Postmaster General David Steiner reviewed the Postal Service’s challenges and said “levers available to private sector enterprises and to government agencies are unavailable to the Postal Service.”
“In a normal business model, if 70% of routes are losing money, you would adjust the routes. In a normal business model, if 60% of the stores you had were losing money, you’d close them,” Steiner said. “We’re not allowed to do either. That is a broken business model.”


 To learn more about Rounds’ involvement with the Postal Service and other priorities in the U.S. Senate, listen to his interview on Searchlight Report, a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight.

Without help from Congress to raise the price of stamps and packages and increase the amount of money the Postal Service can borrow from the federal government, Steiner said the post office’s ability to deliver mail is threatened.
Meanwhile, the Postal Service is under pressure from President Trump to participate in his proposed restrictions on voting by mail. His March 31 executive order told the post office to refuse to deliver ballots in states that don’t provide lists of voters and to only send and receive ballots that include tracking barcodes, but courts have blocked the order and the Trump administration is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to consider an appeal.
The Postal Service did not immediately respond to South Dakota Searchlight’s request for comment on Rounds’ legislation, nomination holds and criticisms.
Brian Bengs, an independent challenging Rounds in the Nov. 3 election, called former Postmaster General DeJoy the “worst postmaster general in history,” and told Searchlight that Rounds “sat by for years” while DeJoy “laid the foundation of today’s problems.”
“It’s past time for Postal Service management and the board of directors to be held accountable, and I find it convenient Mike has only come around to that idea during an election year,” Bengs said.



For broadcasters

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Electric Boat cheers move into new campus at former Crystal Mall
description: Officials said the new campus marks a new economic opportunity for southeastern Connecticut, one that could usher in a wave of growth.
text:
Windy skies and a steady downpour weren’t enough to dampen spirits in Waterford on Friday morning as local officials, construction workers and business leaders gathered to celebrate the groundbreaking of General Dynamics Electric Boat’s new campus. 
Work on the roughly 800,000 square foot facility, which will reuse the former Crystal Mall complex, is well underway. The majority of the mall was acquired last year, and the remaining tenants moved out of the building in the spring. 
When renovation work is completed, the campus will house office and software development space as well as facilities for training and workforce development. Some 4,000 to 5,000 employees are expected to work at the campus, which is expected to open in 2027. 
The facility will make Electric Boat, a defense contractor responsible for supplying the military with submarines of varying sizes, the largest employer in Waterford. The company recently celebrated a $76.6 billion contract with the U.S. Navy, one of the largest shipbuilding contracts ever awarded. 
The contract, which comes amid a hiring push for the company, further cements the need for Electric Boat’s expansion, speakers said Friday. 
“This groundbreaking signifies our long-term commitment in Connecticut but also in  all of you and all the workforce,” said Electric Boat President Mark Rayha. 
But speakers also acknowledged that the campus marks something even greater for southeastern Connecticut: a new economic opportunity, one that could usher in a wave of growth and once-in-a-generation investment in the local workforce. 
It’s a new chance for revitalization and commercial activity in the region, built using a space that supported earlier waves of development. Now, as renovation work begins, supporters say that the reused mall will become the backbone of the region’s economic comeback. 
“For decades, the Crystal Mall was part of the fabric of our community. We shopped here, we worked here, we brought our families here,” said Waterford First Selectman Rob Brule. “Today we aren’t here to talk about what this property used to be. We’re here to celebrate what it’s about to become.”
Crystal Mall is trying on something new
The mall redevelopment, DECD deputy commissioner Matt Pugliese noted, is one of the largest reuses of an existing property in the state. The redevelopment work comes as DECD looks to support projects around the state that will breathe new life into old buildings, part of a larger effort. 

Rob Brule, Waterford first selectman, speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall, on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

A place like the Crystal Mall, speakers said, is a natural fit for this work. 
“Malls simply cannot meet the kind of commerce that we see today in the United States of America,” said U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal. “Electric Boat, with typical ingenuity and innovation, is, in effect, putting new wine in old bottles.” 
When completed, the Waterford campus will complement submarine production efforts by providing additional space for administrative staff, software developers and new trainees. Submarine production work will continue in nearby Groton, where Electric Boat’s shipyard is located. 
As renovations continue, parts of the Waterford campus will house temporary training spaces for new employees. A more permanent location on the campus known as SAIL, or the Shipbuilding Advanced Institute for Learning, is set to open in the near future. 
When fully operational, SAIL is expected to support close to 400 shipbuilders and will also include support for welding, advanced technology work and additional innovations. 
“We’re really celebrating bringing this place back to life,” said Courtney Murphy, Electric Boat’s director of talent acquisition, workforce development and compensation. “Seeing this plan take shape and now become reality is truly inspiring because it is more than just a groundbreaking. It’s the start of a new chapter in how we grow, train and support the shipbuilders who carry our mission forward.” 
The growth comes as the company continues a larger expansion, including hiring a projected 8,000 workers this year, more than double what it hired in 2025.
And in a region that has long struggled to find stable economic footing, the hope is that Electric Boat’s growth will have effects that will be felt across Connecticut more broadly. 
“This is just going to be one of those milestones that our children and grandchildren are going to experience,” said U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney. “It’s a big deal.”
A deeper economic shift
The hoped-for economic transformation, coming to a region that has long relied on the manufacturing industry, is expected to bring significant change, and thousands of new workers, to the area. 
Local officials are gearing up to meet the demand and figuring out how to support the workers expected to flood into the region in the coming years. The region is facing a housing shortage, with low stock and rising costs squeezing the market further. The area needs thousands of new homes to support the expected workforce. 
Still, the hope is that the influx will usher in a larger wave of economic activity in the region, rippling out from Electric Boat and driving increases in tourism, recreational activities and other industries. 

Rep. Joe Courtney speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall, on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Electric Boat says that for now, its focus is on meeting its hiring and workforce goals.
Local officials, meanwhile, say they are prepared to do their part as the region looks ahead. Hundreds of new housing units are in development, with more on the way. 
“We’ll support responsible housing. We’ll invest in infrastructure. We’ll continue to work closely with DECD. We’ll support our businesses and schools,” Brule said. “Growth isn’t about getting bigger; it’s about getting it right.”

name: WyoFile
title: Cheyenne Roundup: Decision 2026 | Wyoming primary results
authors: WyoFile staff and Wyoming Public Media
description:
Freedom Caucus candidates took a beating in Wyoming’s primary election. But MAGA Republicans found success in congressional races.
The post Cheyenne Roundup: Decision 2026 | Wyoming primary results appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Freedom Caucus candidates took a beating in Wyoming’s primary election. But MAGA Republicans found success in races for federal office. Plus, Democrats envision a new direction; details TBD.
Download the podcast episode.
Maggie Mullen: This is the Cheyenne Roundup: Decision 2026, a look at the candidates vying for Wyoming’s top elected positions, from Wyoming Public Radio and WyoFile.  
Jordan Uplinger: I’m Jordan Uplinger with Wyoming Public Radio.
MM: And I’m Maggie Mullen with WyoFile. 
JU: The primary was on Tuesday. We’re recording this on Thursday afternoon, Aug. 20.
MM: We finally got to hear from voters about the tug-of-war happening within the Republican Party. More than a dozen incumbent Freedom Caucus members and allies lost to challengers, stripping the bloc of its majority in the state House and failing in its goal to grow its members in the Senate.
JU: In the governor’s race, Eric Barlow beat out Trump-endorsed Megan Degenfelder and Brent Bien, who was backed by the Wyoming Republican Party in its first-ever round of endorsements.
MM: Voters swung the other way when we look at the federal races, where a founding member of the state Freedom Caucus took the GOP nomination for Congress, and Trump-backed Harriet Hageman found success in her bid to move from the House to the Senate.
JU: Let’s swan dive right into it.
MM: So, did the Freedom Caucus grow its power? Nope — much the opposite. It looks like the caucus will have about 10 reliable votes in the House. Some notable oustings include former caucus chairman John Bear of Gillette, founding member and Majority Floor Leader Scott Heiner of Green River, Ann Lucas of Cheyenne and Ocean Andrew of Laramie. Plus, Jeanette Ward of Casper and Mark Jennings of Sheridan, who previously served in the Legislature and were part of the caucus, also lost their bids to return to the House. 
Members and allies of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, including, from left: Reps. Ann Lucas, Nina Webber, Scott Heiner, Bill Allemand, Joel Guggenmos and John Bear, as well as Ken Pendergraft, Pepper Ottman and Joe Webb (in back row, not visible), Rachel Williams and Darin McCann hold a press conference on the opening day of the 68th Wyoming Legislature’s budget session in Cheyenne. All pictured except for Bill Allemand and Pepper Ottman, who was uncontested in the primary election, lost their seats to challengers. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
JU: The caucus also failed to pick up any new seats in the House, and nine newcomers that would’ve likely carried the torch of their Freedom Caucus predecessors came up short.
MM: Bottom line is the caucus voting bloc is no longer big enough to thwart bills on introduction during budget sessions. That’s a tactic we’ve seen various voting blocs use to block legislation. 
JU: As a little bit of framing, Tuesday’s results come after the Freedom Caucus held a press conference in the Capitol rotunda toward the end of this year’s legislative budget session. They made a call for reinforcements to adopt a statewide library book policy, prohibit touchscreen voting machines, strengthen legal recourse if parents feel their rights have been violated and better public access to court documents.
MM: Which all failed, even with the caucus’ majority.
JU: Looking at the state Senate, voters rejected several prominent Freedom Caucus members’ attempts to move up from the House. Chip Neiman, current House speaker, came up short against Sen. Ogden Driskill in a closely watched race in Northeast Wyoming. Ken Pendergraft and Paul Hoeft also failed to move up. And Sen. Bob Ide lost his reelection bid.
MM: This leaves five reliable Freedom Caucus votes in the upper chamber, well below the 16 needed for a majority. My colleague, Maya Shimizu Harris, talked to Gail Symons, a long-time Wyoming politico and Freedom Caucus critic. She likened this year’s results to the flip in the opposite direction that happened in 2024. But she said this is a way larger scale than that.
Gail Symons: I think what happened is they weren’t paying attention to whose ox was being gored.
JU: The team at Wyoming Public Radio and KHOL in Jackson were talking to voters all day and we kind of heard inklings of that from the polls.
Jeanene Esterholt: I’m not sure I completely agree with the Freedom Caucus.  I’m glad they’re conservative. On the other hand, I don’t like the fact that there’s out-of-state places that are swaying our state officials to vote one way or another. 
Bob Woodall: In name only, that’s all they are, that they’re an out-of-state group that is trying to usurp Wyoming and bring their outside influence into our state. In the state Legislature, they’re changing all the rules. That’s why I had to vote, change my affiliation and make myself a RINO [Republican in name only] for the day.  
Kendra Cross:  We’re losing young people. We are losing people having the ability to pay their bills, to have services. We absolutely need strong, stable, reasonable leadership and no more extremism.  
JU: I was also bopping around a few watch parties in Cheyenne, and after some races were called, I made some calls myself. Jessica Crowder is a political newcomer with a career in ag. She beat out Freedom Caucus Rep. Ann Lucas with roughly 63% of the vote. Crowder told me a common question she heard on the campaign trail was, “Are you part of the Freedom Caucus?” 
Jessica Crowder: So it’s certainly on everyone’s mind, and it looks like there’s a shift across the state just based on the results of the night.
MM: For Wyoming’s top five statewide offices, again voters chose traditional Republicans.
JU: In the secretary of state’s race, current Freedom Caucus Chair Rep. Rachel Williams lost by more than 10 points to Converse County Commissioner Robert Short. Where Williams campaigned as a successor to the current secretary’s approach to managing elections and business filings, Short said he wanted to “make the office boring again.” 
Republican candidate for Wyoming Secretary of State Robert Short on Wednesday, July 15, 2026, during a candidate forum at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
MM: Rep. Steve Harshman took the Republican nomination for superintendent of public instruction. He had about 60% of the vote over caucus ally Rep. Tom Kelly’s 31%. Chad Auer, who previously worked as Gov. Mark Gordon’s senior policy advisor, came in third place. 
JU: Worth mentioning: This race also saw a Democratic primary between political newcomer Ana Cordova and former Northern Arapaho Tribal Education Director Sergio Maldonado. Cordova took it with about 63%.
MM: For state treasurer, Curt Meier will have a third term after staving off a challenge from Lingle Rep. Scott Smith, who is listed as a member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus and who earned the state GOP’s endorsement.  
JU: The governor’s race was an interesting one. You may remember from the many political ads flooding our TV, phones and YouTube, President Trump backed current Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder. While the state Republican Party put its weight behind retired civil engineer and military officer Brent Bien. 
MM: They both garnered about a quarter of the vote, well behind rancher-slash-state Senator Barlow’s 45%. Barlow campaigned on protecting public lands, funding education and solving Wyoming’s healthcare access and affordability issues.  
Republican gubernatorial candidate Eric Barlow speaks during a primary election candidate forum organized by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming on Wednesday, July 22, 2026 at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
JU: The last two times the governor’s seat was open in Wyoming, the Republican nominee handily won the general election. But Barlow will have competition in November.
MM: That comes from Democrat Kenneth Casner of Casper and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel of Jackson. You may remember earlier this year, Bextel hand-delivered campaign donation checks to lawmakers on the House floor after they’d adjourned for the day. 
JU: Ah yes, I think that was called “Checkgate.”
MM: That’s right. To close that loop: Nine out of the 10 lawmakers who received the $1,500 checks from Teton County donor Don Grasso lost their seats.
JU: Moving on up to the federal races, where Wyomingites had a lot of choices, especially in the congressional race.
MM: Current Secretary of State Chuck Gray carried the day over eight Republican competitors by a slim margin. 
JU: Didn’t we guess this race could be won with something like 25% of the vote?
MM: We sure did, and that’s exactly what happened.
JU: Gray was closely followed by Jackson conservative activist Steve Friess with 20%, Army vet Kevin Christensen with 17% and former Superintendent of Public Instruction Jillian Balow with 10%.
MM: This race really showcased the “big tent” of the Republican Party. Several candidates tried to position themselves as Trump acolytes, though the president did not make an endorsement in the race. Others ran more middle-of-the-road campaigns while a couple voiced opposition to some Trump administration policies, like Trump’s latest funding request for the war in Iran. 
JU: Despite that, after the race was called, candidates were quick to get voters to rally behind Gray.
MM: This was a spendy race, boosted by the candidates’ own money. Four loaned themselves over a million dollars. Gray said that he, like Trump, had to make that kind of investment to take on “the insiders and the media.”
JU: On the Senate side of things, Republican Harriet Hageman and Democrat James Byrd both won by landslides.
MM: Voters first elected Hageman to Congress in 2022 over Liz Cheney and again in 2024. This year she ran a $2 million MAGA campaign eight times larger than her closest competitor, Sam Mead. Mead is the nephew and great-grandson of two former Wyoming governors. He campaigned under the banner of protecting public lands. That struck a contrast with his opponent, who signed onto a Utah lawsuit that claimed the U.S. government’s ownership of land in Wyoming amounted to a justification for war. 
JU: I was at a watch party with Democrat James Byrd, a former state lawmaker and son of the first Black woman elected to the Wyoming Legislature. With MSNBC on a big TV and LED lights flashing, Byrd gave a speech to a small but energetic crowd, talking about a new Democratic Party approach, but I didn’t hear specifics on that idea.
MM: Byrd easily won over his opponent, Billy Benavidez, a greenskeeper from Sheridan. 
JU: If history tells us anything, Byrd has an uphill fight in the general election. The last time this seat was open in 2020, current U.S. Sen. Republican Cynthia Lummis handily won with about 73% of the vote over Democrat Merav Ben-David. But Byrd is undeterred.
MM: A quick programming and process note: We’ve been talking about unofficial results. The state canvassing board still needs to meet on Aug. 26 to certify the results. 
Jordan: It’s unlikely we’ll see any changes in the winners. This is really the process that counties and the state use to cross their Ts and dot their Is. It also gives counties time to run post-election audits. 
MM: For recounts, any race where the winner won by less than 1% will have an automatic recount. Candidates can also request a recount for their race by Aug. 24.
JU: I want to go back to audits, just for a second. This year’s primary and general elections also have a hand-count audit requirement. Clerks will assemble teams to count, by hand, about 5% of ballots cast in certain races. Election clerks we’ve talked to said they think this will be a good chance to show the machine tabulators that counties use are accurate.
MM: So, where does this leave us for the general election?
JU: Republicans are still likely to have a supermajority in the state House, as only 20 Democrats are running out of the 62 House Districts.
MM: We might see some Independent candidates file to run, too. There could also be minor and provisional party candidates, but that list hadn’t been posted by the time we recorded.
JU: A couple seats could see exciting contests come November. 
MM: I’m really curious to see whether this rebuke of the Freedom Caucus and its cut-and-slash budget approach carries over into November’s general election when voters will decide whether to approve a 50% property tax cut. 
JU: Thinking in the long term, I’m interested in the direction of the Democratic Party. James Byrd talked a lot about being a “new Democrat” [and] the state party has gone through some leadership changes. Even if they win all their races in the state Legislature, I don’t think they’re going to be driving policy anytime soon, but it will be interesting to see how they operate without the Wyoming Freedom Caucus majority in the Capitol.  
MM: Another thing I’ll be looking out for: The 69th Wyoming Legislature is gonna have a lot of freshman lawmakers, especially in the House. And there can be a steep learning curve to lawmaking, so they’ll have their work cut out for them when the next legislative session kicks off in January. 
JU: I’ll also be watching to see if the Freedom Caucus will keep up its tradition of wearing red jackets, their way of bringing attention to a potential budget deficit down the line, which was also the justification for the large quote “Spending Reductions” they wanted to make to the governor’s proposed budget earlier this year. 
MM: I’ll also want to point out that our current lawmakers — a lot of whom are losing their seats — are the ones currently working on committee bills that’ll be voted on in next year’s legislative session. They’re the ones shaping policy, so it’ll be interesting to see how the next few months go and how that legislation comes together.
JU: And I also want to point out: Ballpark, 150,000 Wyomingites voted in the primary. That’s about 55% of registered voters, but somewhere like 33% of voting-age Wyomingites.
Poll workers signal to voters as they enter the polling station during the 2026 Wyoming primary elections at North Christian Church on Tuesday, Aug. 18, in Cheyenne. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
MM: The raw turnout numbers were second only to the 2022 midterms, the last time Wyoming’s top five elected positions were on the ballot and when Harriet Hageman successfully challenged Liz Cheney for Wyoming’s U.S. House seat. 
JU: We’re expecting to see more people at the polls for the general election on Nov. 3.
MM: We’ll be back with more Cheyenne Roundup before that, so check our feed.
MM: Thanks, as always, for listening to the Cheyenne Roundup: Decision 2026, a preview of Wyoming’s primary election races, from Wyoming Public Radio and WyoFile.
JU: Make sure to like this episode and subscribe wherever you get your podcasts.
MM: Editing and producing by Nicky Ouellet and Tennessee Watson. 
JU: Keep following our politics and state government reporting at wyomingpublicmedia.org and wyofile.com. Thanks for listening.
