text:
A sign directs voters inside a west Bentonville polling site to cast ballots on March 31, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussions of domestic violence. If you or someone you know needs help, please call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.
A special election to fill the House District 8 vacancy resulting from Austin McCollum’s resignation following domestic violence charges will coincide with the Nov. 3 general election, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders announced Friday. 
The Bentonville Republican stepped down earlier this month, just days after being arrested on charges of aggravated assault against his wife. Sanders and other top Republicans urged him to resign after the arrest.
Arkansas state Rep. Austin McCollum resigns after domestic violence arrest

McCollum, who served in the House since 2017, was not running for reelection and won the Republican nomination for Benton County judge in March. 
Parties shall issue certificates of nomination by noon Aug. 28 and candidates must file by 5 p.m. that same day, according to a press release from the governor’s office. Independent candidates must submit petitions to the secretary of state’s office by noon Aug. 28. Petitions can be circulated from Monday through noon Wednesday. 
The winner of the special election will serve the remainder of McCollum’s term, which ends in January. McCollum’s resignation leaves Republicans with a 79-20 majority in the House.
Republican Brian Armas, who serves on the Benton County Quorum Court, is running unopposed in November’s general election for a new two-year term to represent House District 8, which includes a portion of northeastern Benton County. 
McCollum’s vacancy is the fifth that will be filled in 2026. Republican Sen. Brad Simon and Democratic Rep. Alex Holladay won special elections in March to represent Senate District 26 and House District 70, respectively. 
Republican Bill Teeter won the House District 44 special election earlier this month to replace the late Republican Rep. Stan Berry.  
Harrell Wilson won the Republican nomination for the Senate District 1 seat Tuesday. He’ll face Eudora Mayor Tomeka Butler, the only Democrat who filed to run for the seat, in November’s special general election. 
The candidates are vying to replace former Republican Sen. Ben Gilmore who resigned in June to work for Attorney General Tim Griffin. The winner of November’s general election will serve until the end of Gilmore’s term in 2029, and represent a district that includes Ashley, Bradley, Chicot and Cleveland counties, and parts of Drew, Grant, Jefferson and Lincoln counties.
Republicans hold a 28-6 majority in the Senate with the vacancy.

title: Indiana marks America’s 250th year with commemorative highway signs
description: Indiana motorists will soon see new reminders of America’s 250th birthday along two of the state’s busiest highways. Gov. Mike Braun unveiled one of the commemorative Freedom 250 signs Friday at an Interstate 70 rest area near Plainfield. The Indiana Department of Transportation plans to install 20 signs along I-70 and U.S. 30 over the […]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun and Indiana transportation officials mark the rollout of Freedom 250 signs Friday near Plainfield. The signs will remain along I-70 and U.S. 30 through the end of 2027. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana motorists will soon see new reminders of America’s 250th birthday along two of the state’s busiest highways.
Gov. Mike Braun unveiled one of the commemorative Freedom 250 signs Friday at an Interstate 70 rest area near Plainfield. The Indiana Department of Transportation plans to install 20 signs along I-70 and U.S. 30 over the next week.
The signs were created in partnership with the U.S. Department of Transportation and the White House Freedom 250 initiative. They will remain in place through the end of 2027, according to the governor’s office.
“For generations, Indiana’s highways have served as a central hub connecting Americans to family, communities, businesses and opportunities across our nation,” Braun said in a statement. “As we celebrate 250 years of American freedom, these signs are a fitting tribute to Indiana’s proud legacy as the Crossroads of America.”
Indiana going all out to celebrate America’s 250th birthday

The markers also recognize the 70th anniversary of the Eisenhower Interstate System and 100 years of the Lincoln Highway. U.S. 30 follows the route of the Lincoln Highway, the country’s first transcontinental road.
Similar signs and flags are appearing in other states through the federal “Freedom Moves You” campaign, part of the White House’s broader celebration of 250 years since adoption of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
Indiana Secretary of Transportation and Infrastructure Matt Ubelhor called the project a “unique opportunity” for the state.
“I-70 and U.S. 30 are main thoroughfares traveled by thousands of Indiana residents and visitors each day,” Ubelhor said at Friday’s unveiling. “Both are significant in the history of transportation.”
Braun said Indiana’s location makes the state a fitting participant in the national campaign.
“You can reach more commerce in two days of ground transportation from our great state than any other place in the country,” he said. “We are the center of the world’s economy.”
Hundreds of other events and programs have been organized across Indiana for the semiquincentennial. A bipartisan state commission has coordinated the celebrations intended to highlight Indiana’s role in U.S. history.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lt. Gov. Hosemann ousts top Senate Democrat from redistricting committee
description: Republican Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann presides over the Senate in a special legislative session at the Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, July 15, 2026.
text:
Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann has removed Senate Democratic Leader Derrick Simmons of Greenville from a select committee on redistricting that is tasked with advising the full chamber on redrawing electoral maps after the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision. 
Republican Hosemann did not respond to a question on why he removed Simmons from the committee. But he did replace Simmons with another Democrat, Sen. Albert Butler of Port Gibson. 
The lieutenant governor’s removal of Simmons from the committee comes after Simmons, House Minority Leader Robert Johnson and Legislative Black Caucus Chairman Kabir Karriem wrote a letter to Hosemann and House Speaker Jason White saying they did not believe lawmakers should redraw political districts now. 
“The Legislature cannot and should not revert to lines or schemes that have already been determined to dilute Black voting strength, which would constitute intentional discrimination,” the letter reads. “Indeed, it does not need to draw new lines at all.” 
Sen. Derrick Simmons, D-Greenville, asks a question about a bill in the Senate chamber at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, April 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Simmons, in a statement, said he respects the lieutenant governor’s authority to appoint senators to committees, but he still believes the Legislature should not redraw political lines right now. 
“My position on mid-decade redistricting remains unchanged,” Simmons said. “I continue to believe that any consideration of redistricting should be legally justified, transparent, and accompanied by meaningful public input.” 
The Legislature typically redraws congressional and state legislative districts once every 10 years after U.S. Census data is released. But the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent Louisiana v. Callais decision gave state legislatures more freedom to redraw districts for partisan reasons. 
A joint House and Senate redistricting committee is currently holding hearings across the state to gather voter input on how legislative and congressional districts should be redrawn. Republican Gov. Tate Reeves is expected to call lawmakers into special session on redistricting before year’s end.

title: Governor seeks expedited federal disaster aid for 54 Indiana counties
description: Indiana has asked the federal government to expedite a major disaster declaration that could unlock additional aid for Hoosier residents and communities across 54 storm-damaged counties. Gov. Mike Braun signed and submitted the request to President Donald Trump on Thursday night, earlier than state officials had expected to complete their damage assessments.[...]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun, left, surveys flood damage in Noblesville on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the governor’s office)Indiana has asked the federal government to expedite a major disaster declaration that could unlock additional aid for Hoosier residents and communities across 54 storm-damaged counties.
Gov. Mike Braun signed and submitted the request to President Donald Trump on Thursday night, earlier than state officials had expected to complete their damage assessments.
Braun said Friday that a federal decision would typically take at least a week, but his administration is seeking a faster review by the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
“I would hope that it doesn’t take seven to 10 days,” Braun told reporters. “That is typical, and the other issue will be: does it reach the threshold of what other recent similar disasters have had to reach in terms of whether we get it or not? I’m optimistic.”
Indiana seeking federal storm assistance at time when Trump wants to scale it back

The request seeks both individual and public assistance. Individual assistance can help residents with uninsured or underinsured losses, while public assistance can help governments and certain nonprofit organizations pay for debris removal, emergency work and repairs to damaged infrastructure.
It follows a federal emergency declaration Trump previously approved for 53 counties. That declaration supports immediate response efforts but is capped at $5 million. The major disaster declaration would make substantially more federal help available.
Recent storms and flooding displaced more than 1,000 families and contributed to at least seven deaths around Indiana, according to officials.
Central Indiana experienced widespread flooding, while powerful winds caused heavy damage and prolonged power outages in the northwestern part of the state.
“This is a more granular approach that’ll help entities, families that were displaced, losing their home, underinsured, no insurance, that type of stuff,” Braun said of the latest request.
The governor’s office said Braun has also pressed utilities to restore power in northwest Indiana, directed additional relief money to affected families and secured more time for eligible residents of Lake and Porter counties to seek replacement Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits for food lost during outages.
State emergency grants of up to $5,000 are available for displaced families to cover immediate needs such as food and clothing. Braun said earlier this week that Indiana had restored its State Disaster Relief Fund to $5 million using state reserves.
“If granted, this declaration will mean significantly more resources to accelerate Indiana’s recovery from the recent severe weather. I will do everything in my power to ensure Hoosiers have the resources needed to recover,” Braun said in an additional statement on X. “My commitment to every impacted Hoosier is that the state will continue working alongside them in the weeks and months ahead, deploying the resources they need to recover and rebuild.”

Lashley will be paid $220,000, plus benefits, to head the university system, which serves […]
text:
East Central University's Memorial Student Union in Ada is pictured on Dec. 4, 2024. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The board that governs six of Oklahoma’s regional universities has hired its third new chief executive officer in two years. 
Kent Lashley will assume the role of CEO for the Regional University System of Oklahoma beginning Sept. 1. Lashley will be paid $220,000, plus benefits, to head the university system, which serves over 40,000 students, according to RUSO’s offer letter. 
Kent Lashley, the new CEO of the Regional University System of Oklahoma, is pictured. (Photo provided by RUSO)
He currently serves as executive vice president and chief financial officer at Rose State College and has held various senior leadership positions at the school for about 17 years.
“I am grateful for the opportunity to serve RUSO and work alongside the board, our presidents, staff and partners,” he said in a statement. “Higher education has been the focus of my career because of the difference it makes for students, families and communities. … I look forward to strengthening the pathways that connect RUSO students with Oklahoma’s workforce and its future.”
Lashley, who will serve as a liaison between RUSO’s governing board and its universities, will be the university system’s third CEO appointed since June 2024.
He replaces Ellen Buettner, who was appointed to the role in October. Brandon Tatum, who had served as Gov. Kevin Stitt’s chief of staff, announced his resignation in August 2025 after a little more than a year in the position. Debra Lyon, RUSO’s general counsel, has been serving as interim CEO since June.
The system governs East Central University, Northeastern State University, Northwestern Oklahoma State University, Southeastern Oklahoma State University, Southwestern Oklahoma State University and the University of Central Oklahoma 
Lashley previously practiced corporate law with The ServiceMaster Company and taught as an adjunct professor at Rose State and UCO. 
He earned a Juris Doctor from the University of Memphis School of Law as well as a masters in education and a bachelor’s degree in social science from Harding University. 
“Kent brings a depth of higher education experience, sound judgment and a clear commitment to public service,” RUSO Board Chair Lake Carpenter said in a statement. “He understands the opportunities and challenges facing our regional universities, and he is committed to furthering RUSO’s mission.”

name: Delaware
title: School Boards Face Bigger Literacy Decisions Under Delaware’s New Funding Model
description: Greater local flexibility will require boards to balance student needs, community priorities and evidence about what improves reading Editor’s note: This is the final installment of a three-part Delaware LIVE series examining Delaware’s literacy challenge, the state’s 2028 goal and the changing responsibilities of local school boards. By George D. Rotsch, Ed[...]
text:
Caption: A major shift in school funding and School Board decision making come as Delaware attempts to raise third-grade reading proficiency from 40% to 53% by 2028.

Greater local flexibility will require boards to balance student needs, community priorities and evidence about what improves reading
Editor’s note: This is the final installment of a three-part Delaware LIVE series examining Delaware’s literacy challenge, the state’s 2028 goal and the changing responsibilities of local school boards.
By George D. Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s new school funding model will give local school boards greater influence over how education resources are used, placing more responsibility for literacy decisions closer to students, parents and communities.
That shift comes as Delaware attempts to raise third-grade reading proficiency from 40% to 53% by 2028 and as school boards have more information available to understand where students are performing, whether they are making progress and where additional support may be needed.
For school boards, those two changes are connected.  Assessment results provide a lagging measure of where students ended the year. Leading indicators collected throughout the year can show whether students are on track and whether the district’s strategy is working. Together, that information can help boards evaluate whether district spending is aligned with the needs of students and the outcomes the district is trying to achieve.
“The opportunity is to make a much clearer connection between what we know about student performance and where we invest our resources,” said Julia Keleher, executive director of First State Educate. “What are the results telling us? What does the district believe is driving them? What is the strategy for improving them? And does our budget put resources behind that strategy?”
From approving budgets to aligning investments with outcomes 
School boards have always approved district budgets. Greater funding flexibility makes it even more important for boards to understand what need an investment is intended to address and what result it is expected to produce.
In literacy, for example, annual assessment results may show where proficiency remains low, while screening, student progress, attendance, intervention participation and other leading indicators can provide more current information about where students are struggling and whether existing strategies are working.
The superintendent and district team use that information to diagnose needs and recommend how resources should be used. The board’s role is to determine whether the proposed investments are aligned with the district’s student outcome goals, whether there is evidence supporting the strategy, and what information the board will receive to know whether the investment is producing the intended result.
Those decisions could include investments in classroom instruction, intervention for struggling students, professional learning, staffing, student supports or other strategies identified by the district.
“The budget should tell the same story as the district’s student outcome goals,” Keleher said. “If third-grade reading is a priority, the board should be able to see how resources are supporting the district’s strategy for improving it. Then, throughout the year, the board should be looking at the indicators the district has identified to understand whether that investment is helping move students toward the goal.”
Local flexibility creates different choices
Not every Delaware district faces the same literacy challenge.
One district may need to strengthen reading instruction across all elementary schools. Another may find that its greatest needs are concentrated in a small number of schools. Some districts may need to focus on students entering school without foundational skills, while others may need stronger intervention for children who have fallen behind.
The new funding model gives boards an opportunity to respond to those differences rather than applying the same solution everywhere.
But local flexibility also carries risk. Boards could spread resources across too many priorities, continue programs without sufficient evidence or focus on activities that are visible to the community but have little effect on reading.
The central question is not whether a district spends more. It is whether the board can connect its spending choices to a clearly identified student need and a measurable academic objective.
Parents can help define the problem
Greater local control also creates an opportunity for parents and community members to become more involved in setting education priorities.
Assessment data can show where students are struggling, but it may not explain why. Parents can help boards understand whether families receive clear information about reading performance, whether students can access additional support, and whether attendance, transportation, language, scheduling, or other barriers limit participation. That information can help a board evaluate whether the district’s proposed spending responds to the needs behind the data.
“Community engagement should help shape the decision, not simply react to it,” Keleher said. “Parents can help boards understand barriers and student needs that may not be visible in a spreadsheet. When resources are limited, that perspective matters in deciding where an investment is most needed and what problem it should solve. “Meaningful engagement would occur before the district commits to a strategy, not only after administrators have presented a finished proposal.
Complex decisions require the right expertise 
Greater flexibility does not mean boards or districts are expected to have every type of expertise internally. Decisions about how to improve literacy and where to invest limited resources can involve student performance data, instructional research, implementation evidence, financial analysis, community input and governance considerations.
Districts can draw on the expertise needed to strengthen those decisions, whether from state education officials, educators and literacy specialists, researchers, financial experts, community organizations or others with relevant knowledge and experience. The question is not whether outside perspectives should influence the decision, but whether the district has assembled the information and expertise necessary to make a well-supported investment.
For boards, that expertise should strengthen, not replace, their governance role. The board still must understand what student need the investment addresses, why the proposed approach is expected to help, what it will cost, what results are expected and how progress will be monitored.
Measuring whether the decision worked
The new funding model also will require boards to think more carefully about results.
Annual state testing remains an important measure, but boards cannot wait until the end of the school year to determine whether students are progressing.
They will need regular, understandable information showing whether the district’s strategy is reaching the intended students and whether reading performance is moving in the right direction.
That does not require board members to manage daily instruction. It requires them to agree with district leadership in advance about what progress should look like, when it should be visible and how the administration will respond if improvement does not occur.
A literacy investment should begin with several broad questions:

What student need is the district trying to address?
Why is the proposed approach appropriate?
How did parents and educators help shape the decision?
What result should the board expect?
When will the board know whether the strategy is working?
What will change if progress falls short?

Those questions preserve the distinction between governance and management while creating meaningful accountability.
A test of local governance
Delaware’s new funding model is based partly on the idea that local leaders can make better decisions when resources and authority are placed closer to students.
Literacy will provide an early test of that premise.
Experts such as First State Educate can help boards understand data and strengthen their decision-making processes. Administrators can recommend strategies. Educators can explain classroom needs. Parents can identify barriers and community priorities. School boards must bring those perspectives together and make choices that reflect both local needs and the state’s larger academic expectations.
By 2028, the public will be able to judge the new funding model by more than the amount of money distributed or the percentage placed under local control. Its most important measure will be whether substantially more Delaware children can read at grade level.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Strafford County food pantries raise alarm about increasing hunger and food insecurity
description: New Hampshire families are struggling to put food on the table and the problem is only getting worse, according to a new report from Feeding America and a group of local charity leaders who gathered to discuss the issue in Rochester this week. Feeding America, a national nonprofit, reported that food insecurity in New Hampshire […]
text:
New Hampshire Food Bank Executive Director Elsy Cipriani (center) speaks about her concerns that recent state policy changes will harm the state’s already low SNAP enrollment rates. On her left and right, respectively, are Annie Hayes, executive director at the Portsmouth food pantry Gather NH, and Marion Harris, also with the New Hampshire Food Bank. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)New Hampshire families are struggling to put food on the table and the problem is only getting worse, according to a new report from Feeding America and a group of local charity leaders who gathered to discuss the issue in Rochester this week.
Feeding America, a national nonprofit, reported that food insecurity in New Hampshire rose from 10.7% of residents in 2023 to 11.7% in 2024 in its recently released annual report. Among children, the problem is even more severe. Child food insecurity rose in the state 6% during that time period, from 14.4% to 15.5% of New Hampshire children.
Data for 2025 and 2026 isn’t available because of delays in federal data reporting. However, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which had been providing this data for around 30 years, canceled its annual Food Security Survey last year. Hunger nonprofits and others are concerned that without the survey they’ll lack an accurate picture of the state and national landscape.
Food insecurity rose from 2023 to 2024, according to the most recent data available from Feeding America. This Bulletin graphic shows the breakdown of that data by county. (Canva graphic by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“These redundant, costly, politicized, and extraneous studies do nothing more than fear monger,” the Trump administration wrote in a press release announcing the cancellation. “For 30 years, this study — initially created by the Clinton administration as a means to support the increase of SNAP eligibility and benefit allotments — failed to present anything more than subjective, liberal fodder.”
Elsy Cipriani, executive director of the New Hampshire Food Bank, told the Bulletin she’s confident food insecurity has only worsened since 2024.
During a roundtable on Tuesday, food pantry and food bank officials described an increasing number of sign-ups from people concerned about the economy, as well as a rise in homelessness among those they help. Others have been asking if they can visit the pantry after hours because they’re working jobs during operating hours, which don’t pay enough to cover expenses, they said.
Officials also lamented the rising cost of food, fuel (which adds to delivery costs), and other necessary resources, which is inhibiting their ability to meet the growing demand. They said inflation is also hitting their benefactors’ wallets and decreasing donations.
Cipriani said last year it cost the food bank 90 cents per meal to provide food to its partner organizations, such as local food pantries, but this year that’s risen 8 cents per meal.
“Which a lot of people think, ‘Now, doesn’t sound like a lot. That’s only eight cents,’” she said. “But you multiply that for 20 million pounds of food.”
U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who organized the roundtable, took aim at federal cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program implemented by Republicans in their One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
That new law, among other things, capped future SNAP funding increases at the rate of inflation; restricted the factors that can be taken into account when deciding a family’s benefit amount; banned many legal migrants (specifically refugees and asylees) from benefitting from the program (people in the country without legal status were already ineligible); and implemented stricter work requirements. Those measures have been going into effect in a piecemeal schedule since the bill was signed into law in July 2025.
“This was done as a deliberative design to try and reduce the number of people who are getting assistance,” Shaheen said. “And that’s part of the problem because people are dealing with the increased cost of everything from energy to groceries to rent, and we should be doing everything possible to ensure that people have enough to eat.”
The nonprofit leaders also discussed how other issues, such as homelessness, are compounding the problem. Rochester Mayor Chuck Grassie said the city is struggling to build shelters because neighbors oppose them.
“Everybody says, ‘Oh yeah, we need more of that, but no, we don’t want it in my neighborhood or not here. Do it there,’” Grassie said. “Hopefully, working with the county, we’ll be able to get some more of that stuff, because I think they’re in a good place to try to promote that.”
All the nonprofit leaders were most concerned about the youth going hungry in the state.
“I just learned that we’re serving 46 homeless high school students,” Annie Hayes, executive director of Gather, a food pantry in Portsmouth, said.
U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (left) and Rochester Mayor Chuck Grassie (right) listen to food bank and food pantry officials during a roundtable discussion in Rochester on food insecurity, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

title: 150 people evacuated as crews battle wildfire in south Arkansas
description: About 150 people in Union County have been evacuated as crews worked to contain a wildfire that’s grown to 2,000 acres, Arkansas authorities said Friday morning. The Arkansas Department of Agriculture said in a post on X that the fire at Pine Tree Road has been burning since Thursday night. “Ten bulldozers are currently working […]
text:
(Getty Images)About 150 people in Union County have been evacuated as crews worked to contain a wildfire that’s grown to 2,000 acres, Arkansas authorities said Friday morning.
The Arkansas Department of Agriculture said in a post on X that the fire at Pine Tree Road has been burning since Thursday night.
“Ten bulldozers are currently working the fire, and we are preparing replacement crews from other parts of the state,” the department’s post said. “A detection flight over southeast Arkansas is planned this morning. Air tankers are scheduled to begin aerial operations immediately.”
Shelters have been opened in El Dorado at the Municipal Auditorium and Immanuel Baptist Church, according to the Union County Sheriff’s Office.
Union County Judge Mike Loftin said by mid-morning Friday aircraft had dropped water on the fire about five or six times. Loftin said there were no reports of any injuries or homes lost from the fire.
“The wind was changing direction on us,” Loftin said. “Today the wind has died down.”
Arkansas launches online wildfire tracker as drought continues

A months-long drought has left a third of Arkansas at high risk of wildfires and all but a handful of counties are under burn bans. 
As of Friday, there have been 1,120 wildfires in Arkansas so far this year affecting more than 29,000 acres, according to an online tracker launched by the state earlier this week. 
The agriculture department has warned that fire risk is expected to go up across the state in the coming weeks. 
“It’s probably been a month since we had a measurable rain in this area,” El Dorado Mayor Paul Choate said. “The woods were primed for a fire.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: $10M in grant funding will expand in-district special education in CT
description: Funds from CT's High-Quality Special Education Incentives Grant Program will largely go toward hiring more specialists in several districts.
text:
A series of grants first set in motion in 2025 is making its way to schools across the state.
The High-Quality Special Education Incentives Grant Program originated in the biennial budget proposal Gov. Ned Lamont released at the start of the 2025 legislative session. State legislators kept the idea and wrote it into law (along with some bigger special education funding boosts the governor wasn’t quite as enthusiastic about). 
Now that fiscal year 2027 has officially begun, the first round of grant money is ready to go out.
In total, the state is sending $10.6 million to 41 school districts. The grant was competitive, with over 100 districts submitting proposals, and the money was awarded based on the strength and specificity of the application. Individual districts could qualify for a maximum of $350,000, while collaborative projects could qualify for $500,000.
The general aim of the grant is to get schools to build more in-district special education programming. 
It’s common for schools to send students with disabilities to outplacement facilities, which can be extremely expensive. Until recently, however, those were also the only costs the state would (partially) reimburse. The idea behind the new grants was that by boosting in-district services, costs for both schools and the state should go down.
Plus, students receiving in-district services can spend more time with their general education peers. That’s a major goal of special education advocates in the state and throughout the country. 
Lamont acknowledged as much in a statement announcing the release of the grant funds.
“It is important that school districts have the resources to support special education programming that allows more students to learn alongside their peers in their own communities,” Lamont said.
What exactly schools will do with the money will vary, though it generally involves hiring staff. For example:

Hartford is using its $350,000 to hire two special education teachers and a social worker; those staffers will expand the district’s RISE Academy into Bulkeley High School, where they will serve an estimated 30 students. 
Putnam is receiving $315,000 to hire a specialized program coordinator and a special education coach; the former will provide much-needed administrative support, while the latter will train teachers on implementing IEPs and providing quality services.
West Hartford is using $350,000 to hire two special educators and a board certified behavior analyst as part of its “push-in” model — sending extra hands into classrooms to support students with high needs rather than pulling them out into isolated settings.
Simsbury already opened a new building earlier this year for its New Path program, which supports students grades 9 to 12 with high behavioral needs. It’s using $350,000 to expand that to grades 7 and 8 by hiring a new teacher and paraeducator. The money will also support the purchase of a van to transport students back to the main school, giving them more time to spend with general education peers.
New Haven will spend part of its $350,000 to create one new specialized classroom program for children in kindergarten through 5th grade with autism. The district came under fire earlier this year after a state complaint alleged it had failed to staff such a classroom with a special education teacher. The rest of the money will go toward professional development.

Some proposals also involve opening or expanding new facilities. That includes Bethel and Brookfield, one of two pairs of districts to win $500,000 through a collaborative proposal. In their case, the money will go to support the creation of a “living laboratory” for students aged 18 to 22 who need additional support mastering activities of daily living and transitioning to the workforce. The house is located near downtown Bethel, with multiple job sites in walking distance.
Bethel’s director of special education services, Meghan Stabile, said the district already had a robust program before the grant, but the space it was using lacked important amenities for daily living activities, such as a full kitchen. Moreover, it wasn’t big enough to accommodate the growing need; Bethel, like most districts in Connecticut, has seen a steady rise in special education students in recent years.
“The community here in Bethel is pretty amazing and we have so many local businesses that employ our students, and so they’re going to be able to keep those job sites … it’s pretty amazing, actually,” Stabile said.
A full list of grant awardees can be found here.
Grant money aside, the issue of special education funding remains far from resolved in Connecticut. 
Special education is not factored into the state’s main funding system — a problem when the population of special needs students keeps growing. The SEED grant — also passed in 2025 — aimed to fill in the gap, but it remains underfunded by about $150 million. That’s far more than what the High-Quality Special Education Incentives Grant provides.
Lamont has signaled he’s aware of the problem. On various occasions speaking with educators and state leaders this year, he has brought up the idea that the state could step in to provide or negotiate for services with more leverage than individual districts can muster. 
His ongoing Blue-Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability is also looking at special education as part of its larger effort to reimagine the state’s relationship to its public schools.
The commission aims to release its recommendations at the end of the year, in time for the 2027 legislative session.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Prediction markets, facing no Mississippi regulations, are  targeting college campuses, policy expert warns
description: The growing prediction markets face limited regulations and are increasing in popularity on college campuses.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.

This month, Mississippi parents will pack their 18-year-olds off to campuses across the state and worry about the usual things – homesickness, roommates and that first shaky attempt at independence.
But there is a new risk many parents don’t know exists. Their child can now place real-money bets on sports from a dorm room, despite Mississippi’s prohibition on online sports gambling.
So-called “prediction markets,” popular platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket, let users as young as 18 all across the country gamble on everything from sports to what word might be mentioned at a press conference.
It doesn’t matter what the laws are in Mississippi or any other state. Unlike traditional online sports betting apps, these platforms don’t abide by state age minimums or bans, nor do they provide problem gambling resources to prevent addiction.
Emily Stack Credit: Courtesy photo
Instead, these companies insist they are federally regulated financial exchanges – investment tools – not sportsbooks. But for a college freshman with a Venmo balance and a favorite team, the distinction is meaningless. It is sports gambling.
Most parents assume the guardrails are in place. Almost three in four voters in Mississippi believe that prediction markets should be required to follow the same state gaming laws as licensed sportsbooks, according to Morning Consult polling conducted earlier this year.
But prediction markets claim they cannot be regulated by states. Working with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), they argue they are akin to the New York Stock Exchange but for sports. That has opened up sports gambling to anyone as young as 18, including college students in Mississippi even though statewide mobile sports betting remains illegal.
These platforms are also reportedly targeting college campuses with aggressive marketing, sponsoring college clubs and paying student influencers to popularize them with peers. The NCAA has called for the CFTC to pause prediction market offerings on college sports until safeguards are enacted, but that request has fallen on deaf ears.
As students head off to campus this fall, they will face hundreds of betting opportunities every week and an advertising blitz already ramping up. Freshmen will see ads during game breaks in dorm lounges. They will watch classmates open the apps between lectures. And they will be told, over and over, that they are not gambling – they are “investing.”
That framing is the most dangerous part. Investing is about ownership, long-term growth, and building a future. Wagering on whether the Ole Miss Rebels cover the spread on Saturday is not investing, no matter how sleek the interface.
Wrapping a bet in the language of Wall Street does not change what it is. It only makes it easier for smart, financially inexperienced 18-year-old students to talk themselves into it.
The science is clear. The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that governs impulse control and long-range judgment, is not fully developed until the mid-twenties.
That is why we do not let 18-year-olds walk into a casino. It is also why the American Psychiatric Association classifies gambling disorder alongside substance addictions, and why young men in college are among the highest-risk populations for developing one.
As you zip up that last suitcase, smooth the comforter one final time and hug your child goodbye, you’ll be thinking about all the things you hope for the child – that he or she will find lifelong friends, stay safe, work hard and make choices that lead toward a bright future.
We can’t walk with our children every step of the way, but we can have honest conversations about the world they’re entering. This fall, make sure one of those conversations is about sports prediction markets and the risks of conflating gambling with investing.

Emily Stack is senior director of policy and executive director of Moms for America Action, a national movement of over half a million moms whose stated mission is to empower moms, promote liberty and raise patriots to heal America from the inside out.

name: Michigan Advance
title: ‘Nobody who knows the Legislature better’: Brinks would bring active legislative approach as LG
description: Michigan Senate Democrats are expressing their enthusiasm at the possibility of the next Senate president being someone who already has experience leading the chamber following Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson’s announcement of Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) as her running mate. The role of lieuten[...]
text:
Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) endorses Jocelyn Benson at a campaign event. Jan. 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Michigan Senate Democrats are expressing their enthusiasm at the possibility of the next Senate president being someone who already has experience leading the chamber following Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson’s announcement of Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) as her running mate.
The role of lieutenant governor is often one of ceremonial leadership, both in the Senate chamber and outside of it — but Brinks seems to see her potential position as taking on a more significant role in promoting the agenda put forward by a Benson-Brinks administration.
Sen. Dayna Polehanki (D-Livonia), who serves as majority caucus chair for Senate Democrats, said that she believes Brinks would bring to the position someone who knows exactly how to execute ideas that Benson might bring forward to propose to the Legislature. 
“Winnie will know the path of how to get that done, who to talk to, who to get on board, and I think Jocelyn made a wise pick in Winnie,” Polehanki told Michigan Advance on Thursday. “There’s nobody who knows the Legislature better than Winnie, and I can see a scenario where Jocelyn will be able to rely on her, if she wants to, heavily in terms of passing her ideas.”



Quotation







When things get to the highest level is when Winnie closes these deals. She’s a closer.


– State Sen. Dayne Polehanki (D-Livonia) on Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks legislative abilities.


Brinks herself has made the same indication that she would intend to take on a more present role in the Legislature if elected in November, with a campaign spokesperson telling the Michigan Advance that she would bring an “active governing approach to the job.”
Speaking to reporters following Benson’s announcement of Brinks as her running mate, Brinks said that she believes it is a strength to have pre-existing strong relationships with legislators. 
“I think that will help us move our agenda. It will help us find common ground, and it will also help us work out differences,” she said. “I’m confident that those strong relationships will serve both the governor’s agenda well and the state Legislature’s agenda.”
She also told Gongwer News Service that she is “really excited to bring the depth of my experience at the Legislature to the table,” as a part of that more active legislative role. 
Brinks’ colleagues in the Senate Democratic caucus cited her work ethic — Polehanki said her car is always one of the first in the parking lot — and her negotiating skill as key benefits to helping govern effectively if elected.  
“When things get to the highest level is when Winnie closes these deals. She’s a closer,” Polehanki said. “I can see her suiting up, being on time, running everything efficiently, and to the extent Jocelyn wants to use her expertise, she’s going to have a whole book of knowledge that she can rely on to guide Jocelyn through reaching her legislative goals.”
And Polehanki is not alone among her Democratic colleagues in celebrating Brinks as the pick for the role.
Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton), the assistant majority leader for Senate Democrats, wrote on X, “I know as LG, she will continue to help us as we bring more positive change in 2027,” while Majority Whip Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak) posted, “She’ll be a tremendous partner to help our next Governor get real, meaningful things done for Michigan families.”
Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay Township) speaks at a House Judiciary Committee hearing. Dec. 17, 2025. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance
Benson and Brinks will face a Republican ticket of U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) and state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay). 
Much like Brinks, DeBoyer brings state-level legislative experience that James does not have — something that Dennis Lennox, a Republican public affairs consultant, said makes him “a governing partner, not a geographic or demographic box-checker” on the ticket. 
Brinks, on the other hand, seems to fulfill both sides of that statement — along with her strong legislative background, she is the only statewide candidate for either major party from West Michigan, and with Benson makes the first all-female gubernatorial ticket in the state’s history.
Brinks, who was term-limited from running for re-election in the state Legislature, will be officially nominated into the lieutenant governor position at the Michigan Democratic Party’s convention on Aug. 29.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky judge allows case arguing period product tax is unconstitutional to proceed
description: Kentucky is one of 18 states that still tax period products, according to Period Law.
text:
Kentucky is one of 18 states that still tax period products, according to Period Law. Two women are trying to change that. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)A lawsuit arguing that Kentucky’s tax on menstrual products is unconstitutional will be allowed to proceed through the courts, Jefferson Circuit Court Judge Melissa Logan Bellows ruled Thursday. 
This comes roughly a month after the judge heard arguments over the state’s motion to dismiss the case that Alex Baldon and Skylar Davis filed in March. 
These women assert that Kentucky is discriminating against women on the basis of sex by taxing period products like tampons and pads when no comparable product for males is thus taxed. 
When Bellows heard arguments over the motion to dismiss the case, Lucas Roberts, representing the state through the Office of Legal Services for Revenue, argued not against the merits of the case, but said the women had not exhausted their administrative recourses. They should have first lodged complaints through the Department of Revenue and Board of Taxes, Roberts told the judge. 
Kentucky women sue to end ‘arbitrary, irrational’ sales tax on tampons, period products

The lawyers representing the two women who filed the lawsuit countered, saying the administrative option would not be appropriate since the board can’t consider the constitutionality of a tax and because the women are not seeking refunds. 
In her Thursday ruling denying the motion to dismiss, Judge Bellows acknowledged that “exhaustion is the ordinary rule in tax disputes and that an as-applied challenge often requires agency process so the constitutional injury can be framed by administrative action.” 
But, she said: “Kentucky also recognizes that exhaustion is not required — and would be futile — where the complaint attacks a statute as void on its face and the agency cannot decide that constitutional question.” 
“The Department and the Board of Tax Appeals enforce and review tax determinations; they do not sit as constitutional courts to invalidate statutory classifications,” Bellows wrote. “Sending every menstruating consumer through a refund pipeline the complaint does not invoke would not produce the declaration sought and would not conserve judicial resources.” 
Kentucky is one of 18 states that still tax period products, according to Period Law. 
The Lantern has asked the Finance and Administration Cabinet for comment on the ruling. 
This story may be updated.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska 2nd District candidates try to paint each other as extreme
description: Republicans plan to paint Denise Powell as ‘out of touch,’ as Dems will point to Brinker Harding’s Trump’s endorsement.
text:
Denise Powell speaking during a campaign event in Omaha on July 20, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — On a hot July day, Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District Democratic nominee Denise Powell spoke alongside Rahm Emanuel, local union leaders and Premier-Midwest Beer & Beverage workers on strike to make the case for why the district should elect a Democrat for the first time in a decade.
“The momentum is huge … people are ready. They’re tired. They’re frustrated,” Powell said after her event. “I think Brinker (Harding, the GOP nominee) just keeps proving that he is not gonna be any better than what we have. … I think the choice is clear.”
As in other election cycles, Democrats — and election analysts — view the slightly red-leaning 2nd District as a pickup for the blue column to make gains in the U.S. House, as midterm elections often don’t go the way of the party that controls the White House. 
Republicans are looking to defend the state’s most politically divided and diverse congressional district without retiring Republican U.S. Rep. Don Bacon. 
Bacon told the Examiner in June that Republicans can keep the seat because Harding is “a pragmatic, smart Republican” who can compete for independent voters in the district. 
“Denise comes from the more left wing of the party. … Her challenge is going to be how she can also compete in the middle, because in the end, District 2 — it’s about who wins the middle vote,” Bacon said. 
Harding and Powell have tried to paint each other as the extreme of their party. 
Harding and Republicans seek to tie Powell to a string of wins for the progressive and Democratic socialist wings of the Democratic Party across the country and contend that she is “out of touch” with the district. 
Meanwhile, Powell and Democrats want voters to think of Harding as a Republican who has embraced the MAGA label, pointing to President Donald Trump’s endorsement and Harding’s support of Trump’s policies. 
Second District voters got a taste of the Republicans’ game plan for the next three months when U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson and Majority Leader Steve Scalise came to campaign for Harding. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Johnson described the 2nd District race as a contest between “common sense and crazy” during his visit at a crowded Omaha cafe. Harding joined in by saying that communists are coming for Nebraska, pointing to Democratic socialist Melat Kiros’ June 30 victory over outgoing U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado’s 1st District Democratic primary.
“We cannot fool ourselves to think that they’re not trying to get here to Nebraska,” Harding said. “We’re going to make sure that we do everything we can to get our message out that we will keep those heartland values and take them to D.C.” 
Brinker Harding (left) with U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson in Omaha on July 18, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Harding, in the same July campaign visit , said Powell won’t represent the entire district because she campaigned on anger and “Trump derangement syndrome.”
“I work for everyone, Republicans, Democrats, independents alike. That’s how I worked on the City Council,” Harding said. “That’s the same way I will treat my term in Congress.”
The Republican Congressional Committee has amplified a story from Fox News about Powell’s opposition to Omaha state Sen. Kathleen Kauth’s successful 2023 push for a bill that restricted minors from accessing puberty blockers or cross-sex hormones for gender-related care and prohibited gender reassignment surgery before age 19. The Nebraska Republican Party has posted about a Daily Wire story about Powell with the headline “Dem Candidate Tied To Revolutionary Org That Pushes Sex Ed On Kindergarteners.”
Powell has worked behind the scenes of state politics as co-founder of a group that coached local women to run for office and helped with recent Nebraska ballot initiatives. One pushed to codify abortion rights and failed; the other, to repeal a publicly funded voucher program for private K-12 schools, succeeded.  
After her July campaign event with Emanuel, Powell told the Examiner the GOP strategy shows that Republicans have nothing of substance to offer voters in this election. Powell called the Republicans’ attacks “easy jabs that they’re trying to get in because they don’t have anything more substantial to hit me on.”
“Nebraskans are pragmatic, centrist, commonsense folks, and that’s how I’m showing up,” Powell said. “I think when voters meet me … they’re like, ‘Oh, she’s a working baseball mom. She’s not some crazy extremist.’
Powell, during her heated Democratic primary, was viewed as the more moderate candidate by national outlets. 
Powell, during her speech when former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg visited Omaha earlier this year, said Harding has embraced the Trump administration’s tax and spending law “even after it dumped thousands of our neighbors off their health insurance.” 
“He thinks this war in Iran that is jacking up everyone’s gas prices … that is putting American and civilian lives at risk … he thinks this is great,” Powell told the crowd at Metro Community College. “Mike Johnson and Donald Trump know Brinker Harding is just a rubber stamp for their agenda.”
Buttigieg, who served as U.S. secretary of transportation under former President Joe Biden, said he traveled to Omaha because Powell is a leader. He said the district “can do better” than Harding.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has also tried to paint Harding as “MAGA” with press releases about Trump’s policies on taxes and spending. They even point to some of his votes as a city councilman: one example the DCCC highlighted was his vote against a motion to override former Mayor Jean Stothert’s veto of fire department funding in 2024, saying his vote put “Nebraska’s firefighters and working families’ lives at risk.”
“Brinker Harding is an avowed extremist whose views and policy stances are wildly out of step with everyday workers and families in Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District,” one of the DCCC memos said.  
Washington Rep. Suzan DelBene, the DCCC chair, echoed similar criticism to the Omaha World-Herald this week during a quick visit to Omaha.
Harding has been on the Omaha City Council since 2017. During his first reelection bid in 2021, he pointed to what one would expect for a city council race — improving city services and promoting public safety during his first term in office. 
He easily defeated his 2021 opponent; he ran unopposed last year for another term. Harding told Roll Call that Trump’s endorsement will “be a benefit to our campaign.”
“To have his endorsement, knowing what this district is, says a lot about the confidence that the White House and leadership have in me and our campaign,” Harding said to Roll Call. 
Another wrinkle in the race could be two new political parties — who are still dealing with litigation. It is unclear which races the Nebraska Working People Party and the America First Party will put candidates in if the two become official.
Libertarian Eric Michael Foreman is also running for the 2nd District seat.
Whoever wins this November will have to balance representing the Nebraska swing district. 
In her first campaign ad for the general election, Powell doesn’t mention her party affiliation but focuses on affordability and fighting corruption. Harding’s general election campaign ad with his family said he “will work with both sides to bring down the cost of living.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Surging book demand leaves NC libraries struggling with long waitlists, pricey content
description: If you’re someone who frequents a North Carolina public library — especially in an urban area like Raleigh or Charlotte — you might be all too familiar with searching the catalog for a buzzy book, only to find the waitlist is hundreds, if not thousands, of people long. Local library employees say the entire country […]
text:
A library search for one of the most popular book titles of 2026, "Yesteryear." Long waitlists for popular books have become a common feature at North Carolina public libraries. (Photo: Kate Denning / Carolina Public Press)If you’re someone who frequents a North Carolina public library — especially in an urban area like Raleigh or Charlotte — you might be all too familiar with searching the catalog for a buzzy book, only to find the waitlist is hundreds, if not thousands, of people long.
Local library employees say the entire country faces this issue, but North Carolina’s booming population and the growing number of library patrons in the state make it especially challenging.
Even worse than the waitlist for physical copies is the one for e-book and audiobook versions. E-content has unique barriers, including costing libraries up to three times the price of a physical book, that make it difficult to keep up with the heightened demand.
Population, library and book usage trends
“Yesteryear,” a 2026 novel by a debut author that examines “tradwife” influencer culture on social media, has been a viral sensation since its spring release. As of mid-August, all 232 of Wake County’s physical copies are checked out, and more than 1,700 people are on the waitlist between standard and large print copies. At Charlotte Mecklenburg Libraries, 376 print copies are checked out and almost twice as many holds are in place.
If waitlists get so long that the ratio of holds to total copies exceeds a certain threshold, Selection Manager for Wake County Public Libraries Dan Brooks told Carolina Public Press, the libraries decide to purchase additional copies. For children’s books, that’s about one copy for every five holds, but the ratio is a bit higher for adult titles. Harold Escalante, Charlotte Mecklenburg Library’s Assistant Director of Collections and Access, told CPP its ratio for print titles is four to one.
Celebrity book club picks like Jenna Bush Hager’s “Read with Jenna” and Reese Witherspoon’s “Reese’s Book Club” consistently generate long waitlists, especially if they’re thrillers, Brooks and Escalante said. Others can go viral any day and take library managers by surprise.
“Some titles, like ‘The Correspondent’ or ‘Yesteryear,’ which did end up being one of the book club picks, just sort of build more slowly over time, but then just keep building and building with higher momentum,” Brooks said. “We just have to keep buying more copies until we get to that ratio.”
WCPL patrons might be familiar with the branch’s “Lucky Day Collection.” Each month WCPL chooses four to six books to buy an extra 75 to 125 copies of that aren’t used to fill holds. Instead, they are distributed among the 23 locations to be put on the Lucky Day display, available for checkout then and there.
It’s a way for readers to get their hands on the most sought-after titles without having to wait for their turn on the hold list — and it helps shorten the waitlists, even if by a small margin.
But the e-content waitlists often go above and beyond. In the case of “Yesteryear,” more than 5,000 patrons are waitlisted for a copy of one of the 452 e-books or audiobooks in Wake County. In Charlotte, for 585 e-book and audiobooks, there are over 4,500 holds.
With around 66 people moving into Wake County per day, the libraries subsequently have new patrons coming in to register for a library card every single day, Brooks said. This heightened demand can be noticed most by the surge in e-content checkouts.
“We’ve definitely seen a huge increase in our digital e-book and downloadable audiobook usage,” Brooks said.
“From 2019 to 2026, it’s been a 200% increase. We circulated about 1.1 million in fiscal year 2019, and then over 3.5 million in fiscal year 2026. The whole issue with e-books and long waits and more demand than libraries can satisfy is not unique to Wake. It’s a national phenomenon happening.”
Through migration alone, 135 people move to the Charlotte region per day on average, with Mecklenburg County leading the pack. Charlotte currently ranks as the United States’ 14th-largest city, and it could move up the list if growth trends continue.
Population growth can impact the resources libraries have available, however not every new resident will become a cardholder, Escalante wrote in an email. It’s something Charlotte-Mecklenburg considers, but it’s not always a driving force for purchasing decisions.
While population growth is part of North Carolina’s story, President and CEO of the Urban Libraries Council Brooks Rainwater told CPP there’s generally been more usage of libraries since the pandemic, so local libraries could still be seeing an increase in patrons even if their area isn’t experiencing significant population changes.
Research the ULC released in 2024 found that while in-person visits were still lower than they were pre-pandemic, they were rising again quickly — responding libraries reported a 24% increase from 2022 to 2023. And in the same timeframe, use of meeting rooms and digital resources increased by 52% despite the lower attendance.
“If you look at baseline numbers from coming out of the pandemic to now, we’ve been seeing more and more people return to the library,” Rainwater said.
“We’ve also been seeing usage patterns change, where more people are renting rooms within the libraries. It can be really difficult in some library branches and central libraries to actually find room rentals because everybody is going there to work remotely or using them to meet with friends or other things.”
‘Disappearing, limited-access content’
Demand for digital items has steadily risen, especially since the pandemic, Escalante wrote. The challenge for keeping e-content available consistently is “always going to be the increasing cost of digital licenses.”
The ULC and other national library organizations recently spoke out about the strain the licensing process and cost of e-content is putting on local branches. An open letter to book publishers says while individuals pay $13 for an e-book on average, which they maintain access to in perpetuity, libraries often spend upwards of $55 for a singular two-year license.
“Many libraries are now spending 50% or more of their collections budgets — taxpayer funds — on disappearing, limited-access content, giving them less ability to support lesser-known authors and smaller publishers,” the statement reads.
“Meanwhile, wait times for readers of all ages have exploded, as libraries spend more to get less in our digital collection.”
Audiobooks of thrillers from popular authors like Stephen King or Ruth Ware can be more than $100 per copy, but most others are between $50 and $75, Brooks said. E-content is usually provided with metered access, meaning libraries can distribute the book for 12 to 24 months or up to a certain number of checkouts.
Licensing is set by publishing houses, namely the “big five” — Penguin Random House, HarperCollins, Simon and Schuster, Macmillan Publishers and Hachette Book Group — as well as e-book distributors like Hoopla, Overdrive and Libby. Copyright laws function differently for digital content versus physical books, which is why the pricing structure varies, Rainwater said.
Just keeping up with expiring titles and purchasing additional copies to bring the wait down to a reasonable timeframe takes up about 75% of WCPL’s weekly spending, leaving around 25% of the budget for new titles, Brooks said.
The cost can lead libraries to remove e-content from its collections if they aren’t getting enough use. At WCPL, they track how many checkouts content receives and use that to help determine whether it’s worth renewing for another cycle.
“If it’s a title we’ve owned for three or four years, but it was only checked out 20 times last year, that might not be high enough to renew it, given the demand of the newer, more popular titles,” Brooks said.
“So we will have to remove things from the collection on the digital side, versus, if you get print copies, they’ll last until they fall apart, so they can stay in much longer than 26 checkouts or 12 months.”
One advantage of digital items is that they are returned to the library and fill the next hold automatically, Escalante wrote. Plus, they are never lost. This helps patrons move through the hold list more quickly than print titles. But still, they have to think and buy strategically.
“To overcome some of the challenges of high-cost licenses, we make sure we are choosing the license that makes financial sense,” Escalante wrote.
“We are also exploring some cost per borrow models to address demand quickly.”
Meeting in the middle
Wait times for e-content have gone up tremendously across the country, Rainwater said. Library budgets can’t always align with the whims of reader trends, and if budgets aren’t expanding, the hope is that book publishers seize the opportunity to increase access by making e-content more affordable for libraries.
“There’s only so much money that can be spent on e-content, so the wait times go up and up because we can only afford to buy so much of this material,” Rainwater said.
“The only way that you can solve this is either to get better usage terms, better contract terms, rethinking the way that we have our relationships with the big five publishers in particular, or if local governments want to spend more money on e-books — and to me it feels like the amount we are spending now is more than fair. There’s got to be a way that we can meet in the middle.”
It would be preferable, and a more responsible use of taxpayer funds, for e-content to be licensed by number of checkouts instead of by time, Rainwater said. Otherwise, libraries are using precious funds for items they aren’t getting full use of. He also suggests libraries having the option to pay a premium for older titles to keep them in perpetuity in order to both build and sustain their collections.
It’s a misconception that libraries and book publishers are in competition with one another, Rainwater said. Libraries can be a first-stop for readers looking for books to add to their personal library or experimenting with a new author or genre before purchasing. Plus, they really have the same goal.
“Collectively, we in the library field as well as the publishers want to see more people reading,” Rainwater said.
“Libraries as a location are a place where people come in and read and often buy books. It’s not as though the people coming to libraries only utilize libraries for reading. That is where the preponderance of people that do read go. We have author talks all the time, and then people go out and buy those books.
“So,” Rainwater said, “There’s a misnomer within the publishing industry that somehow there’s competition rather than all of this is truly a complementary business environment where everybody wants to make sure people have the access to reading.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Business groups sue to block NJ law fining big employers for workers on Medicaid
description: Business groups want a judge to void a new state statute that they say forces employers to ask workers their health status in violation of federal privacy laws.
text:
Business groups want a judge to void a new state statute that they say forces employers to ask workers their health status in violation of federal privacy laws. (Getty Images)Four business industry groups have sued New Jersey in a bid to overturn a new law that requires companies with at least 50 employees covered by Medicaid to pay the state annual fees to offset the state’s cost for that publicly funded health insurance coverage.
The statute, which Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed in June, orders big employers to pay up to $725 yearly for each of their workers, and each of those workers’ dependents, who are on Medicaid. Sherrill earlier this year characterized the fees as “fines” meant to drive large employers to insure their own workers, rather than leaving the state shouldering that cost.
But in a federal complaint filed Thursday, the groups call that pressure “an unlawful intrusion” on the federal framework governing the establishment, administration, and regulation of employer-sponsored health benefit plans. They say the state law conflicts with, and so is preempted by, the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, the 1974 federal law that sets minimum standards for private-sector retirement and healthcare plans.
The Restaurant Law Center, National Retail Federation, American Hotel & Lodging Association, and International Franchise Association also argue that they cannot verify the accuracy of or dispute the fees the state charges without asking employees about their healthcare status or whether they incurred any medical costs, queries that would violate federal privacy laws.
New Jersey Treasurer Aaron Binder at the Statehouse on March 9, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
State Treasurer Aaron Binder and Kevin Jarvis, the state’s acting labor commissioner, are named as defendants. Spokespeople for Binder and the Attorney General’s Office did not respond to a request for comment, and Thomas Wright, a labor department spokesman, said he cannot comment on legal matters.
The business groups are seeking an injunction to block enforcement of the law. They also want a judge to nullify the state law as unconstitutional and declare it preempted by federal law.
Sherrill built the fees into her first annual state budget, and lawmakers narrowly approved the Democratic-sponsored measure with votes in both chambers split along party lines, despite warnings from one Democratic legislative budget officer that the plan had “legal implications.”
The groups noted those legislative reservations in their lawsuit.
“The economic effects of the Act — both direct and indirect — impermissibly force a private sector employer to adopt a certain scheme of substantive healthcare coverage,” attorney William J. Delany wrote for the plaintiffs.
“For employers that operate both in New Jersey and other states, the Act would require them, to avoid the fee assessment, to provide health care coverage different from healthcare coverage provided to employees in other states, leading to a patchwork of state-by-state regulation, rather than application of national standards and administration,” Delany added.
