name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas insurance department assists with $29M in consumer recoveries, a 147% increase
description: Kansas Department of Insurance's report for 2025 reveals an increase in money recovered for consumers based on complaints against insurance companies.
text:
Vicki Schmidt, the state's commissioner of insurance, says the Kansas Department of Insurance's investigation of more than 3,000 complaints led to a substantial increase in the amount of money recovered from companies on behalf of consumers in 2025. In this image, Schmidt takes the oath of office Jan. 9, 2023, at the Capitol in Topeka. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas Department of Insurance assisted consumers with recovery of $29.2 million from insurance businesses in 2025 to more than double the amount the agency retrieved for policyholders during the previous year.
The office of Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt said the department worked with consumers and companies in 2024 to recover $11.8 million for Kansans. In the 2025 annual report released Thursday, the agency documented a 147% year-to-year increase in cash recoveries for consumers.
“Complaints and inquiries equip the Department to hold insurance companies accountable and better serve Kansans,” said Schmidt, who chose not to seek reelection this year to a third term as commissioner. “I am proud to advocate on behalf of our consumers to ensure they receive the services and protections outlined in their policies.”
Schmidt said the department relied on consumer complaints to identify insurance companies or agents that warranted investigation for violations of state insurance laws or regulations.
The department’s latest annual “complaint index” was compiled by tracking the top 20 premium-writing companies operating in Kansas and taking into account companies with 10 or more closed complaints for a specific type of insurance during calendar year 2025.
The agency’s report says more than 3,000 complaints were submitted in relation to auto, accident and health, home, life, annuity and long-term care insurance last year. One-third of those requests were tied to vehicle insurance, the report said, while one-fourth related to homeowner or insurance policies.
Overall, the department said, 69% of insurance complaints submitted to the state agency were related to claims handling.
When a consumer submits a written complaint to the department, an insurance company was required by state law to respond to the department’s inquiry within 15 business days. The insurance department retains a record of each complaint filed by a consumer for up to three years.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Why are political insiders so afraid of giving voters more choices?
description: This November, Massachusetts voters can decide whether our elections are working for them, or whether they are mostly working for the people already in power.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS POLITICIANS LOVE talking about democracy. They love reminding voters how sacred the process is, how important participation is, and how deeply they value every voice.  
Then a reform comes along that might give voters more competition and more meaningful choices, and suddenly everyone in the political class starts clutching their pearls. It’s so typical. 
In November, Massachusetts voters will be asked whether they want to adopt an important reform to our election system by approving Question 3, which would institute all-party primaries in state elections and races for congressional offices. Under the proposal, all candidates for an office would appear on one primary ballot, regardless of party, and the top two vote-getters would advance to the general election. 
Maybe you love that idea. Maybe you do not. There are fair arguments to have about how it would work, what it would change, and whether Massachusetts should move away from traditional party primaries. The most important point is simple: voters should get to decide. Whether they would be able to do so was in question until June, when the Supreme Judicial Court rejected an effort by two Democratic Party insiders to have the measure thrown off the ballot.  
The opposition from insiders has been very telling. Both major parties have reasons to feel uncomfortable about this proposal, and honestly, that may be the best argument for taking it seriously. Party insiders like systems they understand, control, and benefit from. They like predictable primaries, protected incumbents, and races where the real decision is made before most voters are even paying attention. 
The problem is that the current system is not working for many voters. Massachusetts has some of the least competitive elections in the country. Roughly three in five legislative races this cycle have only one candidate on the ballot. In a state that loves lecturing everyone else about democracy, too many voters show up to find what amounts to a very expensive coronation. 
That is not healthy, and it is certainly not surprising that the people who benefit from it would prefer to leave it exactly as it is. When elected officials do not have to compete, they do not have to listen. They do not have to defend their records. They do not have to explain why housing is unaffordable, why families are leaving, why taxes keep climbing or why Beacon Hill seems allergic to basic accountability. They can simply survive another cycle, smile for the picture, and carry on. 
All-party primaries would not magically fix every problem in Massachusetts politics. No ballot question can do that. But the proposal puts forward a question worth asking: What would happen if more voters were brought into the process earlier and more candidates had to actually earn support? 
As the former Massachusetts Republican Party chair, I understand the concerns about weakening party identity or changing the traditional path to the general election. Parties matter. Clear political differences matter. Voters should know what candidates believe and what they stand for. But parties should serve voters, not the other way around. 
Too often, our current system seems designed around the comfort of insiders instead of the needs of the public. Massachusetts has a huge number of unenrolled voters, frustrated taxpayers, young families, small business owners, and residents who feel politically homeless. They do not fit neatly into the boxes political professionals keep trying to preserve, which is probably why the professionals get annoyed by them. 
If an incumbent is doing a great job, wonderful. That person should have no trouble making the case to voters. If a challenger has better ideas, voters should get to hear them. If two Democrats, two Republicans, or two candidates with no party label earn the most votes in an all-party primary, voters can make the final call in November. That is not chaos. That is competition. There is a difference, even if Beacon Hill sometimes acts confused. 
The funniest part of this debate is watching insiders pretend their concern is really about protecting voters. Voters are perfectly capable of hearing arguments, comparing candidates, and deciding what kind of system they want. The real fear is not that voters will be confused. The real fear is that voters might finally have more choices. 
This November, Massachusetts voters can decide whether our elections are working for them, or whether they are mostly working for the people already in power. 
No wonder the insiders are worried. 
Jennifer Nassour is the co-founder of the Pocketbook Project, host of the Political Contessa podcast, and former chair of the Massachusetts Republican Party. She serves as the co-finance Chair of the Mike Minogue for Governor campaign.

 Catching Our Eye

• $40 trillion in debt. The New York Times reports, “U.S. Debt Hits $40 Trillion as America’s Borrowing Binge Continues.”
America’s gross national debt topped $40 trillion for the first time on Wednesday, an ominous milestone for an economy that sits on a shaky fiscal foundation after decades of borrowing to pay for the rising costs of the military, social safety net programs and President Trump’s tax cuts.
This year alone, the United States is on track to borrow more than $2 trillion to help pay for its obligations, including spending on the war in Iran and the sweeping tax cuts that Republicans enacted in 2025. Soaring interest payments to investors who have purchased America’s debt now make up about half of that red ink, pushing the United States into a deeper financial hole.
• Trump’s “clean, beautiful coal.” Louisville Public Media reports, “Black lung rates in Appalachia are high as the 1970s, with thousands of miners sick.”
NIOSH researchers found that working veteran underground coal miners in central Appalachia are suffering from the incurable and fatal lung disease at the highest rates in nearly 50 years.
Ohio has only around 15 active coal mines today, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. But, at its peak in the early 1900s, there were hundreds, employing tens of thousands of Ohioans underground.
Miners working in Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia who’ve had at least 25 years underground have the worst rate of coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease. One in three — 32.5% — tested positive in X-rays conducted by NIOSH during the last five years.
• The forever target for corporate and industrial exploitation: Appalachia. The Athens County Independent’s Amanda Pirani reports, “Appalachian Ohio a target for data centers.”
Athens County is just the latest community in Southeast Ohio to be shaken up by data center proposals.
Some public officials and residents hope the centers will bring long-awaited economic development — or at least substantial tax revenue. However, researchers at the Georgia Institute of Technology found that data centers can have positive economic impact — but mostly in metropolitan areas. Rural counties see “negligible gains,” they wrote.
• Disability rights. NPR reports, “They grew up with disability rights. Now, they’re fighting to keep them.”
(A) lawsuit brought by several Republican-led states, Texas v. Kennedy, is working its way through the courts. The plaintiffs argue that the federal government cannot require states to provide disability services in the community rather than in institutions. Then, in June, the Department of Justice (DOJ), which enforces the integration mandate, issued a legal opinion taking a similar position — essentially aligning itself with the plaintiffs in the case. “Congress has not imposed an integration mandate on states,” the memo reads. It goes on to say the Olmstead decision “held only that a state cannot institutionalize such patients without justification. … What counts as adequate justification remains an open question.” In July, the DOJ also clarified that it would no longer enforce Olmstead in the same way it had in the past.
• School attendance. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s Grace Tucker reports, “Why parents might get more calls about student attendance this year.”
Changes in Ohio state law require schools to respond sooner when students are absent. It also removes the condition of medically excused absences, which means doctor appointments can now count toward a student’s chronic absenteeism. The legal definition of truancy, which is based on unexcused absences, has not changed.

name: Nevada Current
title: After 2 Lombardo vetoes, lawmakers plan to again send him a bill capping senior rent increases
description: State lawmakers plan to reintroduce legislation that would limit rent increases for seniors after two previous bills were vetoed by Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo.  Measures to prevent cryptocurrency scams, allocate money to food banks for senior anti-hunger programs, and require more support for deaf and hard of hearing individuals were also included as propo[...]
text:
In his 2025 veto message, Gov. Joe Lombardo said capping rents for seniors could create “ripple effects that disrupt the rental market as a whole.” (Photo: Richard Bednarski/Nevada Current)State lawmakers plan to reintroduce legislation that would limit rent increases for seniors after two previous bills were vetoed by Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. 
Measures to prevent cryptocurrency scams, allocate money to food banks for senior anti-hunger programs, and require more support for deaf and hard of hearing individuals were also included as proposed bill draft requests at Monday’s interim Committee on Senior Citizens, Veterans, and Adults with Special Needs. 
The high cost of living, exacerbated by the lack of affordable housing in Nevada, has made it difficult for seniors living on fixed incomes to afford rent, putting them at risk of eviction and potentially experiencing homelessness. 
A number of older adults are seeing rent hikes they can no longer afford with their Social Security Income or retirement benefits, said Donna Clontz, a retired attorney and volunteer with AARP Nevada.
“They’re forced to choose between paying their rent and having medicine or having food,” she said. “We all see the information online and on television about the fact that about one out of five or one out of six of our kids are going hungry. The same number is true for our seniors. It is really a terrible situation for all of us.” 
The bill draft request approved Monday revives previously failed legislative efforts to offer some rent stabilization for seniors by capping rent from increasing more than 10% for a five year period.
Though the proposal was supported by members AARP and other seniors speaking during public comment, they warned lawmakers even if the cap is approved it could still put people at risk of unaffordable rents. 
Some seniors are “already paying $1,500 a month in rent or $2,000 a month in rent,” Marcy Cooper Smith told lawmakers Monday. “If you’re letting us get a 10% increase on that amount, that’s still a pretty good increase we’re getting hit with.” 
Democratic Assemblywoman Sandra Jauregui first introduced legislation in 2023 seeking to place a one-year 10% rent increase cap rent for people older than 62 or who rely on disability insurance benefits. 
The legislation, which also required landlords to refund fees if they don’t screen a tenant who applied for the unit, was supported by the Nevada Association of Realtors at the time.
Lombardo vetoed the legislation. 
When Jauregui introduced the bill with identical language in 2025, it no longer had the support of the Nevada Association of Realtors. Jauregui later strengthened the legislation by amending the 10% cap down to 5%, saying the association “did not negotiate in good faith.”
Lombardo, once again, vetoed the bill. 
He wrote in his 2025 veto message the legislation could create “ripple effects that disrupt the rental market as a whole.” 
“By prohibiting landlords from increasing rent by more than 5% for certain tenants, the bill may inadvertently encourage preemptive rent hikes before the cap takes effect, making housing less attainable in the short term,” Lombardo wrote. “In the long run, potentially as soon as this biennium, the cap could discourage investment in rental properties, especially as owners struggle with rising costs while being unable to adjust rents to match.” 
At the committee meeting this week, state lawmakers also approved a bill draft to address the rise of cryptocurrency scams by banning the installation, placement, and operation of crypto kiosks and cashier-facilitated cryptocurrency exchange transactions. 
Often located in grocery stores and convenience stores – where ATMs are also typically found –  the kiosks allow people to convert cash into Bitcoin or another cryptocurrency.
The kiosks have become vehicles for scammers, who extort or con victims to deposit cash into a crypto kiosk and transfer it to the scammer’s digital wallet, never to be seen again by the victim, state lawmakers were told in March.
Clontz told lawmakers Monday this has led to people being defrauded out of thousands of dollars, with most of those victims being seniors.
Nevada has 447 bitcoin kiosks, 336 of which are in Southern Nevada, according to a public listing by Bitcoin Depot.
The committee also approved a request to allocate $330,000 to support and expand senior and veteran anti-hunger programs administered by the Three Square Food Bank and the Food Bank of Northern Nevada.
State lawmakers also asked legislative counsel to draft  a bill requiring the administrator of the Division of Human Resources Management to employ a veterans coordinator to oversee a new veteran hiring program and peer mentor program.
Another subject of a bill draft request would require the Nevada Health Authority to maintain a list of assisted living and senior living committees specializing in services for deaf or hard of hearing and require medical intake forms to include an option for individuals to indicate their preferred language to include American Sign Language.

name: Missouri Independent
title: ‘Got to play the game’: Missouri doctors group jumps into state politics with $1.5M PAC investment
description: Missouri’s oldest business association is the state’s newest big political donor. On Aug. 14, the Missouri State Medical Association split $1.5 million between two newly created political action committees, Asclepius PAC, named for the hero god of medicine in Greek mythology, and Patients First PAC. The association, which represents doctors and doctors in tr[...]
text:
(Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)Missouri’s oldest business association is the state’s newest big political donor.
On Aug. 14, the Missouri State Medical Association split $1.5 million between two newly created political action committees, Asclepius PAC, named for the hero god of medicine in Greek mythology, and Patients First PAC.
The association, which represents doctors and doctors in training, already has a committee, MO Medical PAC, for pass-through contributions from members. But until this year, the association had used its own funds to contribute only $19,625 to political committees since 2001, Missouri Ethics Commission records show, and has made no donations since 2014.
The money will be contributed to candidates in this year’s legislative elections, said Jeff Howell, executive vice president of the association. The association supports legislation to put limits on prior authorization for medical services and ending the use of managed care for the state’s Medicaid recipients.
“We’re interested in ensuring that Missourians have access to the highest quality healthcare and to reinvest in that through those two PACs,” Howell said.
The donations immediately put the two PACs among the ranks of the best-funded political action committees representing lobbying interests. Only two donors, Michael Rayner, part of the family that owns the agribusiness firm Cargill, and retired investor Rex Sinquefield have contributed more to non-ballot issue committees.
And only four PACs have contributed or spent more than $1.5 million to influence this year’s elections.
The donations got the attention of other big contributors, who wonder how the money will be used.
“Anytime anybody drops that kind of money into a couple PACs, the light bulb kind of goes off, and you’re kind of trying to figure it out,” said Andy Arnold, a long-time lobbyist who donates client funds to candidates from an entity called Paladin PAC.
Paladin PAC has contributed $579,700 to candidate committees and other PACs since the start of 2025 as Arnold pursues legalization of video lottery terminals. All of the money came from J&J Ventures, an Illinois game vendor.  
The medical association already drew notice in the political world when it gave $100,000 to the PAC supporting Dr. Ellen Nichols in her unsuccessful campaign against incumbent state Sen. Jill Carter in the 32nd District Republican primary.
The donation was unusual for the association, Arnold said, but didn’t necessarily signal a change in legislative races statewide.
“She’s a physician. She was running against somebody that wasn’t a physician, and they apparently had some beef with Sen. Carter,” Arnold said. “I don’t know what the beef was, but apparently they did because you don’t just drop $100,000 into a campaign against an incumbent just to do it.”
In this year’s legislative session, the association supported Republican state Rep. Melanie Stinnett’s bill limiting the use of prior authorization for common medical treatments and making other changes intended to make prior authorizations more transparent.
The bill passed the House and stalled in the state Senate. Stinnett is a candidate for state Senate in the 30th District.
The association wants to end or limit the use of managed care in Medicaid, Howell said.
Missouri has paid private insurers to manage parts of the program since the 1990s and expanded their role in 2015 to cover all recipients except people with disabilities and those 65 and over.
“We’d prefer to have it be fee-for-service the way it used to be,” Howell said. “There’s a reason they passed that in the middle of the night.”
A September report by Physicians for a National Health Program, which advocates for a single-payer system, estimated Missouri could save up to $259 million a year in general revenue if the state managed Medicaid directly. Managed care companies refute those findings, arguing their services are necessary to ensure there are financial incentives for care that makes enrollees healthier.
Ed Weisbart, Missouri chair of Physicians for a National Health Program, said the decision to use association funds for politics is long overdue.
“I’ve always thought they were not doing enough,” Weisbart said. “The challenge has been finding the common ground that I thought they should work on that they wanted to work on.”
In 2013, Democratic Gov. Jay Nixon wanted the Republican-controlled General Assembly to expand eligibility for Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act provisions that capped Missouri’s share of the program at 10% of the cost.
The effort failed, and Missouri did not expand eligibility until a 2020 ballot measure mandating coverage. 
Weisbart was on the association’s legislative committee.
“The committee voted to support that initiative, but leadership above the committee didn’t seem particularly interested in prioritizing that as something that they were going to really fight for,” Weisbart said.
The association’s MO Medical PAC, used to accumulate modest donations from physicians, has raised $113,364 since the start of 2025 and made $123,275 in contributions.
The Missouri Health Plan Association PAC, which backs keeping Medicaid recipients in managed care programs, has raised $180,000 and contributed $204,700.
The decision to create the two new PACs is part of being a lobbying interest in Jefferson City, Howell said.
“If other people are going to play the game, you’ve got to play the game,” he said.
The medical association was founded in 1850 and predates the Missouri Chamber of Commerce and Industry by more than 70 years. 
“People have acted a little bit surprised by this,” Howell said. “They really shouldn’t be. We’ve been around forever.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Experts skewer new Trump administration analysis claiming 24,000 noncitizens voted in 2020
description: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. President Donald Trump this week unveiled another effort by his administration to raise questions about the outcome of the 2020 election he lost: an unusual U.S. Census Bureau analysis concluding with “high confidence” th[...]
text:
President Donald Trump is touting a new Census Bureau report that claims that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. (Official White House Photo by Andrea Hanks)This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.
President Donald Trump this week unveiled another effort by his administration to raise questions about the outcome of the 2020 election he lost: an unusual U.S. Census Bureau analysis concluding with “high confidence” that 24,000 noncitizens illegally voted in the 2020 election.
Trump touted the finding on social media and wrote that it supports his long-running false claims that he actually won the 2020 election.
But experts said there are substantial questions about the Census Bureau study’s methodology and validity. And even if 24,000 noncitizens had voted in 2020, it wouldn’t have been enough to change the election’s outcome.
The seven-page Census Bureau report said researchers examined more than 128 million voters in the 2020 presidential election and determined with “high confidence” that more than 24,000 of them were noncitizens. If so, that number would be less than 0.019% of the sample.
Trump said census researchers are still analyzing another 32 million voters and predicted that the number of illegal noncitizen votes would “explode” after that was done.
The Census Bureau did not respond to a request for comment. But experts said some aspects of the bureau’s release raise fundamental questions.
Most Census Bureau reports identify the authors of the report and detail the reliability of the data they are using. This analysis did neither.
“A properly done Census report would have had that information and the fact that it is missing is glaring and makes me think that they are hiding something,” said Beth Jarosz, a senior fellow at Georgetown University’s Massive Data Institute who has worked as a contractor on Census Bureau reports.
Terri Ann Lowenthal, who served as staff director for the U.S. House of Representatives subcommittee overseeing the Census Bureau from 1987 to 1994, said the report’s minimal methodological information raised questions about the accuracy of the results.
Lowenthal said the report was “beneath the Census Bureau’s stellar reputation.” The failure to include the names of any career staff members, she said, suggested that the work may have been done by someone with a political agenda “and may not reflect the sound, reputable analysis for which the Census Bureau is known.”
 Trump administration searches for noncitizen voters

Trump has focused the efforts of his second administration on rooting out voter fraud, especially any instance of illegal voting by noncitizens, which audits, investigations, and studies have found happens only rarely. But the federal government doesn’t possess a comprehensive database of citizens, and efforts to match different data sets have so far yielded inaccurate results.
The administration pushed states to run millions of records of registered voters through a revamped federal data tool to check if they were citizens. But election officials found the system, which cross-referenced federal records from various federal agencies, in some cases erroneously flagged citizens. In June, a federal judge blocked the use of the overhauled tool, finding it threatened privacy and voting rights.
In a televised primetime speech on July 16, Trump said his administration had found more than 250,000 noncitizen voters on the voter rolls of just four states: New Jersey, California, Pennsylvania, and Nevada. Officials in all four states pushed back on Trump’s claims and said they didn’t understand how the administration arrived at those numbers. The Trump administration has yet to provide any detail on its methodology in that case either.
The president has lobbied for federal legislation to require people registering to vote to prove their citizenship, and he repeated that call when releasing the Census Bureau findings Tuesday, describing it as his highest legislative priority. But the effort has stalled in the U.S. Senate. He has also released two sweeping executive orders on elections, but their major provisions have been so far blocked by federal courts.
 Questions surround Trump administration’s data analysis

The voting data used in the analysis was provided by Data-Clear, a business in Virginia that secured an $885,000 Census Bureau contract from former President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024. Carolyn Carlson, Data-Clear’s president and founder, said she provided nationwide voting data to the bureau that year as part of a project to try and prevent an undercount of minority voters in the 2030 census.
Carlson said she was surprised to see the data she provided used in the new review of noncitizen voters.
The report says the Census Bureau matched the Data-Clear voter files with federal immigration records to determine if people were citizens and eligible to vote. The report offers only general descriptions of how and when it was able to match verifiable information.
Justin Levitt, an election law specialist at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who worked in the Biden White House on voting rights issues, said a typical analysis would include caveats around the possible margin of error, and the 24,000 figure for noncitizen voters could be within it. However, the Census Bureau report doesn’t specify one.
“In most statistical exercises, it’s not unthinkable that there might be 0.019% false positives – and if that were the case here, that would turn the total conclusions to zero,” he said.
Should the analysis hold up to scrutiny, the underlying numbers showed that they would not involve enough voters to change the result of the 2020 election. The report said it found 500 noncitizens illegally cast ballots in Wisconsin, which Trump lost to Biden by more than 20,000 votes. The survey said it identified 1,100 noncitizens who cast ballots in Arizona, which Trump lost by more than 10,000 votes. And the report cannot say whether those voters supported Trump or Biden.
In response to questions about whether the release supported the president’s assertion, the White House responded with a link to a social media post by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

name: VTDigger
title: After a nearly six year saga, Burlington’s new high school opens its doors
description:
The new school year marks the end of a difficult chapter for the district, but the specter of potential PCB contamination still looms for many Vermont schools.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  After a nearly six year saga, Burlington’s new high school opens its doors.
text:
The atrium the new Burlington High School building is seen on Wednesday, August 19, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Batula Kassim sat in front of a wall of floor-to-ceiling windows in her school’s new library, the sunlight a welcome contrast to the refurbished Macy’s department store where she spent her freshman year. 
Kassim, an incoming sophomore at Burlington High School, is one of a cohort of students who spent part or all of their high school years attending classes at the renovated store in downtown Burlington. 
Kassim described the environment at the Macy’s building as “claustrophobic.”
“It was just like, not enough space,” she said. “There was not much you could do in that building.”
The nearly six year saga began when buildings on the school’s former campus in Burlington’s New North End were found to have elevated levels of polychlorinated biphenyls, more commonly known as PCBs. PCBs were used in building materials before the U.S. banned them in 1979, and exposure to them is associated with an array of health risks, including cancer. 
Although the district had planned for high schoolers to return part-time to in-person classes in fall 2020 after a spring of remote learning due to Covid protocols, the PCB contamination prompted the district to return to online classes in September of that year. The school relocated to a speedily renovated former Macy’s building in downtown Burlington in early 2021. 
The district eventually chose to demolish the former campus and build a new school, citing the extensive remediation that would have been needed to make the old buildings safe for students and staff. 

The new Burlington High School building is seen on Wednesday, August 19, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Now Burlington’s new high school building, built on the site of the former campus, is ready to welcome students. 
The project to demolish the old campus and build the new school on the same site cost about $206 million, according to Burlington School District Superintendent Tom Flanagan. That cost was largely footed by Burlington taxpayers, who overwhelmingly approved a $165 million bond to support the project in 2022. The project was also supported by $16 million in state funding and a federal stormwater grant, Flanagan said. The district did not respond prior to publication to a question about the amount of the federal grant, although documents on the district’s website indicated the project received about $1 million in federal funding for the stormwater portion of the project. 
The district has offered tours of the new high school building throughout the summer for students, families, alumni and interested community members. A week before the start of the school year, Kassim joined one, eager to see the new building. 
“I’m really loving it, but I know I’m gonna get lost for the first few weeks of school,” Kassim said as she walked through the new school, joking about its size compared to the Macy’s building. 
“I feel like I can breathe,” she added. 
Students on the tour seemed ready to leave behind the numerous quirks of life in the Macy’s, which included science classrooms without running water, a lack of sound separation between classrooms and a walk to the YMCA for gym class. 
But the biggest throughline for students was the light. While the former Macy’s lacked windows, the new building is full of natural light and windows that overlook the school’s athletic fields and the neighboring woods. 
Flanagan, the superintendent, said he was especially excited about the physical accessibility that is woven into the school’s new design. That includes wheelchair-accessible bathrooms, showers and a balcony that looks down onto the school’s new gymnasium. 
Hannah Harris, president of the incoming senior class, was excited about the gym for another reason. 

People tour the gymnasium at the new Burlington High School building on Wednesday, August 19, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

“Being the class president, I run, like, pep rallies and stuff like that, and so we actually have a gym for every person in the school to come together,” she said. “We didn’t have that at Macy’s.”
Harris said the few pep rallies at the Macy’s building had been held on the roof of the nearby parking garage. 
“The music wasn’t connecting. It was really, really hard to get everyone up there and together,” she said. “So I think I’m really most excited for that.”
PCB worries persist  
While the Macy’s chapter is finally closed, the specter of possible PCB contamination still hangs over schools across the state. 
In 2021, the state Legislature mandated PCB testing for the more than 300 Vermont schools built or renovated before 1980, but the program has suffered from a lack of adequate funding. 
As of January 2026, 171 of the schools covered by the mandate hadn’t tested for PCBs. This session, after initially considering ending the testing mandate, the legislature extended the deadline for schools to complete mandated testing from 2027 to 2035.   
The state of Vermont is pursuing a state lawsuit against against Monsanto, which is now owned by pharmaceutical giant Bayer, over the company’s role in manufacturing and selling materials that contained PCBs. A group of nearly 100 Vermont school districts is pursuing a separate federal case against Monsanto. The company has faced lawsuits across the country related to its role in manufacturing PCBs. 
And as the Burlington School District celebrates the start of a new era in a new building, it’s also looking towards its own day in court. The district has an ongoing federal lawsuit against Monsanto, which is expected to go to trial in early 2027. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  After a nearly six year saga, Burlington’s new high school opens its doors.

name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Trump’s court workarounds push limits but are within legal bounds, experts say
text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has not slowed his pursuit of central policy goals and personal pursuits, even after major setbacks at the U.S. Supreme Court and other federal courts.The high court in its 2026 term delivered blows to Trump’s core campaign promises to upend a constitutional provision governing who becomes a U.S. citizen at birth and to swiftly address the growing national debt with “trillions of dollars” raised by taxing imports. The justices also ruled the president cannot fire, without cause, Fed Board Gov. Lisa Cook and deny her a chance to plead her case. And a lower court blocked Trump from installing his name on the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.But even after the Supreme Court ruled against him, Trump is forging ahead and using what some legal observers describe as “creative lawyering” to find alternative routes to push his agenda, even as public support fades.He ordered new blanket tariffs in late July on at least 60 trading partners. He signed a new round of birthright citizenship orders Aug. 6. Reports also revealed that Cook received a letter Aug. 5 from administration officials that Trump is again “considering” firing her.The moves test the power dynamic between the executive and judicial branches, but are not illegal or even unconventional in modern times, experts said.“They look at it and they say, ‘We want to advance a particular policy agenda. Here's the whole array of legal arguments that we might be able to use that give us authority,’’’ said Scott Anderson, senior fellow at the centrist Brookings Institution and senior counsel and editor of the publication Lawfare.Trump is not alone in this pursuit. After all, President Joe Biden found another route to student loan debt relief after a loss at the Supreme Court. A federal appeals court effectively axed the Biden-era relief program in March.“It does happen, and (administrations) will sometimes run the risk of legal reversal, but it's a rarer move,” Anderson said. “For this administration, it's become the standard move.”‘Spirit of the law’While Anderson said Trump’s responses to the rulings are “not surprising” given the legal strategy of his second term, one could argue the “legal brinksmanship … often clearly runs contrary to some of the spirit of the law, and it capitalizes on a lot of institutional inefficiencies.” Thomas Berry, a legal scholar with the libertarian Cato Institute, said while Trump has often used rhetoric to “delegitimize the court,” his recent actions are not out of legal bounds.“What he's doing is distinct from outright disobedience or ignoring a Supreme Court's decision, and it's important to stress that that line has not been crossed,” said Berry, who directs the institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies.A White House spokesperson said the administration has “always followed court orders.”“The Supreme Court’s ruling on the Cook case required notice and an opportunity for a hearing in considering whether the President should take certain adverse employment actions. The President’s notice sent to Fed. Governor Cook offers exactly that within the precise structure enunciated by the Court,” said Lauren Bis in a brief written response from the White House.A Department of Justice spokesperson, who did not provide a name, wrote in a statement, “Investigative and prosecutorial decisions are made based on the law and the facts. To date, DOJ has prevailed in 24 emergency applications before the Supreme Court, winning over 80 percent, an unprecedented win rate that speaks for itself, and has also won dozens of merits cases at the Court.”The spokesperson highlighted the department’s Supreme Court win in June that allows the administration to follow through with plans to deport between about 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians who were living in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status.

 







Members of the media set up outside the U.S. Supreme Court ahead of Trump's arrival on April 1, 2026. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Trump v. Barbara to determine if Trump's executive order ending birthright citizenship is constitutional. According to historians and the Court, it was the first time a sitting president has attended oral arguments at the nation's highest court. (Photo by Al Drago/Getty Images)

Birthright citizenshipOn the final day of its 2026 term, the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s sweeping attempt to deny citizenship to children born to parents who either do not have legal status or hold temporary legal visas. Chief Justice John Roberts led the 6-3 opinion on June 30, writing that children born in the U.S. to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present “are ‘subject to the jurisdiction’ of the United States and are citizens at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause.”Today’s exceptions for those who are not subject to U.S. jurisdiction include foreign diplomats and their families, members of invading armies and in most cases foreign public ships passing in nearby waters.On Aug. 6, Trump signed two executive orders again aimed at curtailing birthright citizenship. The first targets children born to the staff working for foreign diplomats; to children born in American Samoa, where Congress has yet to pass a citizenship law; and to the children born to parents who belong to what the U.S. defines as a “Foreign Terrorist Organization.”  “So what Trump is trying to do with these executive orders is he's trying to say, ‘OK fine, those are the categories you've given us. We're going to try to push those to the maximal extent possible,’” Berry said.“And he interprets them broadly,” Berry continued. “Do people have diplomatic immunity or not? That's kind of a factual question. Literally the ambassador and the ambassador's spouse, they get diplomatic immunity. But does everyone from the foreign country working in the embassy similarly get immunity from U.S. law? That wasn't my impression.”Trump is also seeking to limit birthright citizenship by taking what Berry described as a “maximalist view” of what an invading army is.“It's not obvious that that analogy extends to people who are part of designated terrorist groups because they're not literally rampaging and pillaging,” he said. “This is more people who are living here but have been, you know, labeled as part of a group that's at odds with the United States.”  Anderson said the administration “clearly is intending to just take advantage of every hint and every limitation the Supreme Court decision left open.”The American Civil Liberties Union on Aug. 12 began the process of asking the federal judiciary to reaffirm the Supreme Court ruling. TariffsTrump’s trade policy provides another example of the administration finding a new legal reasoning after the Supreme Court struck down the initial basis for a major administration goal.In the midst of refunding roughly $166 billion to businesses that paid taxes on imports under Trump’s emergency tariffs, the president has hopscotched across multiple trade statutes to continually impose at least 10% duties on most global goods since his Supreme Court loss in February.In a 6-3 opinion, the high court struck down Trump’s unprecedented claim of tariff authority under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act. Congress retained tariff authority in most circumstances, Roberts wrote for the majority, and Trump could not use the statute to impose duties after declaring emergencies on trade imbalances and illegal drug smuggling.Trump lost the case to a handful of small business owners and Democratic state officials. Tariffs are taxes paid by the importers, meaning American businesses were shouldering the additional costs.Trump immediately turned to another statute, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the president to unilaterally set up to 10% in tariffs for 150 days. The order set off another round of legal challenges, including from Democratic-led states, in the U.S. Court of International Trade.Less than a month after the Supreme Court loss, the U.S. Office of the Trade Representative also opened broad trade investigations under Section 301 of the 1974 law into the practices of nearly all U.S. trading partners.As the clock ran out on Trump’s 10% blanket tariff under Section 122 on July 24, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced his office had found forced labor practices by roughly 60 of America’s trading partners, including Canada, the European Union, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, Taiwan and the United Kingdom, among dozens more. The findings triggered a 10% to 12.5% duty on most goods from those countries.Days earlier, Trump announced he would use a Depression-era provision that had never been enforced — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — to slap a 50% duty on most Canadian imports. The U.S., for now, has delayed the start of the high tariffs as talks with Canada continue, according to reports.Trump’s strategy on pushing tariffs is “not really surprising at all,” Anderson said, adding “it’s not even inappropriate.”“The Supreme Court never said, ‘You can't do tariffs.’ In fact, it said basically you can. It just said ‘You can't do it this way.’ And that automatically points to these other ways, which everyone said is probably a more sound way to do this if the president really wants to do this,” Anderson said.“It doesn't mean it's good policy,” he added. “It doesn't mean it's a good idea, but there's at least a very colorable case the president can do this all legally. ”

 







Trump holds a chart while speaking during an event in the Rose Garden at the White House on April 2, 2025. Touting the event as “Liberation Day,” Trump announced sweeping tariffs on imported goods. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

2025 deportation flightsTrump’s “aggressive” legal strategy has set him apart from other presidents, and, despite specific recent examples that haven’t crossed a legal line, the administration likely violated court orders in relation to immigration, according to observers.“I think there are some cases that push the envelope, might be unlawful, particularly around, like, some of those early deportations,” Anderson said. “But the majority of the time, the executive branch has been responding and complying with court orders. It's capitalizing on the fact that those orders are often very narrow.”Berry also highlighted the March 2025 deportation flights that took off with hundreds of immigrants on board despite a court order as a potential example of cases “where these agencies have outright violated court orders.”Overall, the courts have been a check on the administration’s view of expansive power, both experts said.“It is worth taking a moment to realize, like, just how vastly smaller the scope of this (most recent) birthright executive order is after the Supreme Court,” Berry said. “The decision did cut off the vast majority of options the administration has. I mean, you think about the scope of millions of people that the original order would have affected, and compare that to this. It's just night and day.”Electorate another checkVoters are also a check on power, observers say.With crucial midterm elections approaching, Trump’s net approval rating is -26, meaning the percentage of voters who approve of him is 26 points below those who disapprove, according to The Economist/YouGov poll figures published Aug. 18. A Reuters/Ipsos found Trump’s approval rating at a record low of 33%, according to data published Aug. 17.A recent Fox New poll last month showed most voters disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy. And 55% told Reuters/Ipsos just days before the Supreme Court ruling that they disapproved of Trump’s attempt to end birthright citizenship.Trump surrounded himself in his second term with people who “openly denigrated” a lot of norms of the executive office and are “acting accordingly” to what they saw their voter base wanted, Anderson said.“I think they probably overreacted to this idea that simply by winning the last election, that voters have a high tolerance for this,” Anderson said. “And Republicans in Congress and potentially in 2028 are going to pay a price for that.”Anderson added if voters and lawmakers don’t like the loopholes Trump’s legal strategy is employing, then maybe it’s time for Congress to close them.“If we don't think our laws align with what we think is right ethically and good policy, then maybe they do need to be adjusted,” he said. "Maybe if we want a robust separation of powers, we need to take actions that will empower the courts and Congress to push back on executive aggrandizement more effectively, as opposed to the trajectory over the most of the 20th century, which was implicitly, sometimes expressly, more or less empowering the executive branch on the assumption that the executive branch was going to self-constrain itself.” 

 







A  tarp covers the facade of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., on June 15, 2026, after a federal judge ruled Trump's name must be removed from the center. (Photo by Sam Gauntt/States Newsroom)

‘Everything people don’t like’As for the Kennedy Center: Despite a judge’s order that led to the yanking of Trump’s name from the facade of the revered performing arts venue in mid-June, Trump’s hand-picked board voted Aug. 13 to again affix his name to the building. This time, instead of above John F. Kennedy’s name, the board voted to add an inscription underneath to read “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump,” according to court records.A federal judge had found that Trump’s name, which had already been added, could not officially remain there without authorization from Congress.“It's sort of everything people don't like about lawyers at its extreme. … This is kind of again looking for a loophole —  they're going to argue ‘We are not naming the center. We are adding this appendage,’” Berry said. “So long as it's just like naming the renovation, you know, kind of like a sponsorship deal at the end of the name of a stadium or something like that, that's acceptable because it's not renaming the center,” he continued. “So we're likely to have litigation about that too, and it's going to be a pretty lawyerly and probably annoying debate.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Feds look to the Great Salt Lake in push to produce critical minerals
description: The Trump administration wants to ramp up production of critical minerals without relying on other countries, and it’s looking to Utah for help.
text:
Lilac Solutions' lithium extraction pilot program near the Great Salt Lake is pictured in August 2025. (Photo courtesy of Lilac Solutions)The Trump administration wants to ramp up production of critical minerals without relying on other countries, and it’s looking to Utah for help. 



This article is published through the Great Salt Lake Collaborative, a solutions journalism initiative that partners news, education and media organizations to help inform people about the plight of the Great Salt Lake — and what can be done to make a difference before it is too late.


A company extracting lithium from the Great Salt Lake was awarded a $100 million grant from the U.S. Department of Energy Thursday, with the money dedicated for construction of a new large-scale operation on the north arm of the lake. In all, the department is distributing $500 million between seven projects across the country. 
Lilac Solutions, a California-based company, says most every drop of water it pulls from the lake goes right back in through a process using manufactured “beads” similar to grains of rice that pull lithium from brackish water as it flows through a container. They’re made in Nevada, with the rest of the process taking place at the company’s site on the lake, he said. 
It’s a much different process than typical methods relying on expansive evaporative ponds or, increasingly, on mining hard rock that ends up in China for processing, said the company’s CEO Raef Sully. 
“So it’s really about breaking that supply chain stranglehold that the Chinese have on it,” Sully told Utah News Dispatch.
Federal administrators with the U.S. Department of Energy and the Environmental Protection Agency touched down in Utah this week, in part to speak in closed meetings with heads of mining companies, along with state lawmakers and other elected officials. 
When it comes to critical minerals, Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly told reporters at the state Capitol Thursday that “the overall plan and strategy is deceptively simple, which is to try to onshore as much of the critical minerals extraction, processing, and commercial availability as possible in the United States.” 
The Beehive State factors into the push for two reasons. 
One has to do with its natural riches. Danly said 80% of listed critical minerals — deemed to serve essential functions in technology, with a high risk of supply chain disruption — are found in the state. The other reason is that state leaders are enthusiastic about developing a workforce and technical pilot programs, he said.
Utah aims to host critical minerals lab, hoping for federal recognition — and funding 

“I think Utah is likely to be one of the leaders in critical mineral efforts simply because of the natural resources and the willingness of the state to partner with the federal government,” Danly said during the news conference.  
After running a smaller-scale pilot program, the lithium project at the Great Salt Lake is awaiting state approvals in a permitting process that Sully said has been rigorous.
Conservationists are weighing in, with Friends of the Great Salt Lake saying they’re not opposed to the project but want to see careful monitoring for chemicals used to treat the water before sending it back to the lake. 
The company has “validated their technology,” said Rob Dubuc, general counsel for Friends of the Great Salt Lake. “Whether it can work at scale, well, there’s only one way to find that out, right? Which is to build a plant.”
Lilac Solutions plans to conduct sampling on a daily basis for internal use and weekly for the state, and didn’t detect those compounds in testing during its pilot program, said project director Steve Morrey. 
A rendering shows the vision for a first phase of a large-scale lithium extraction operation. (Image courtesy of Lilac Solutions)
The company has laid out a plan to produce 5,000 metric tons of lithium carbonate each year by 2028, then ramp up to 20,000 tonnes per year in a second phase. It’s not just used in electric car batteries, Sully said, but for storage for wind and solar power and to keep data centers humming. To help meet the demand, the water the operation pulls from the lake and sends back won’t be the only source it uses. 
“What I like to tell people is, if you had an irrigated farm there, you would be using about the same amount of fresh water as we do for our industrial process,” Sully said. 
The Great Salt Lake is sliding back toward a historic low water level after prolonged drought and diversion of water, primarily for farming, but also for cities and industrial use. Asked during Thursday’s news conference about Utahns’ concerns for the lake’s health, EPA Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi noted the federal government has contributed to programs getting more water to the lake and monitoring the hazardous dust kicking up from its dry lake bed. 
“So it’s an ongoing discussion, and the federal government is standing with the state to address these issues directly,” Fotouhi said.
