name: Washington State Standard
title: Watchdog data shows higher WA child welfare deaths than previously reported
description: Deaths and serious injuries of children involved with Washington’s child welfare system last year were even higher than record levels the state previously reported, according to new data. In 2025, 35 children died and 49 more nearly died either from abuse, neglect and other maltreatment, or amid these concerns, after having some connection to the […]
text:
In 2025, 35 children died and 49 more nearly died either from abuse, neglect and other maltreatment, or amid these concerns, according to new data. (Photo courtesy of the state Department of Children, Youth and Families.)Deaths and serious injuries of children involved with Washington’s child welfare system last year were even higher than record levels the state previously reported, according to new data.
In 2025, 35 children died and 49 more nearly died either from abuse, neglect and other maltreatment, or amid these concerns, after having some connection to the child welfare system in the past year. This is according to a report from the state’s Office of the Family and Children’s Ombuds presented to an oversight board Thursday. 
A few cases remain pending, so could add to the 2025 total. 
Accidental drug ingestion by children fueled last year’s surge in deaths and injuries. Most incidents took place when children were in their parents’ care, and the majority of children who died were reportedly under one year old. Through the first half of this year, critical injuries have dropped significantly, as drug overdoses have declined statewide.
The Department of Children, Youth and Families, which runs the state’s child welfare system, reported 23 fatalities and 34 near fatalities last year. The ombuds office examines different cases than the department, accounting for the discrepancy between the two datasets.
State Rep. Tom Dent, R-Moses Lake, who sits on the Department of Children, Youth and Families oversight board, said it’s time for action. 
“How do we put this data to use and make it happen?” he said. “We need to move forward and start finding some things. Take a risk. Let’s do something because I struggle with these deaths.”
The ombuds’ total of 84 incidents — counting both deaths and injuries — outpaced 82 in 2024. It is still under the watchdog’s 2023 figures. 
(Graphic courtesy of the Office of the Family and Children’s Ombuds)
When including cases not explicitly connected to maltreatment, 167 children died or nearly died in 2025, far more than previous years, according to the ombuds. This includes deaths from medical issues without clear links to abuse or neglect, if the family had involvement with child welfare.
Of the 35 fatalities, a quarter were determined to be homicide, while another 23% were accidental, with many others with unknown manners of death, according to the ombuds. Two others died in the hospital due to complications from prenatal drug exposure and one died while with foster parents.
Three died after being reunified with their families following a previous removal, according to the ombuds report. And three more were from families who had other children taken away.
The ombuds includes cases where the Department of Children, Youth and Families wasn’t directly involved, like referrals that didn’t lead to state staff opening a Child Protective Services response. 
“Maybe someone says one of my students reported that their house is always dirty,” said Yordanos Gebreamlak, the director of the ombuds office. “It’s not meeting that definition of a CPS investigation needing to be opened, but that information nonetheless was received.”
These referrals made up 17% of the maltreatment deaths and 14% of the near fatalities. Others had open Child Protective Services cases or ones that were closed in the year before the incident, according to the ombuds office.
The Department of Children, Youth and Families and ombuds office do not review cases if the family had no child welfare history in the past year.
The watchdog office also identifies cases as related to maltreatment if there had been abuse or neglect concerns, not just if this was the direct cause, which is a requirement for the state agency’s review, according to a department spokesperson.
Gebreamlak recommended the department install a specialized roving unit that can travel around the state when certain regions are beset with limited child welfare staff. Jenny Heddin, the agency’s chief programming officer, said officials “had been having that conversation in-house” about a similar team. 
Funding for this staff could be tough as the state continues to face budget struggles.
The ombuds also encouraged the department to establish an accountability process to evaluate its own reviews of these incidents to assess progress on strategies to avoid them in the future.
Coming into 2026, there was some bipartisan momentum to revamp state law to stem the rise of deaths and injuries, as a policy passed in recent years had made it harder to remove kids from their parents. But no proposals became law this year. The budget instead included some new money for caseworkers, public health nurses and programs to help. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The current budget also funded a new workgroup focused on addressing injuries and deaths through increased drug treatment options. 
“It’ll take all of us to come up with the solutions and support of what kids and families across our state need,” said Sen. Claire Wilson, D-Federal Way, and co-chair of the agency oversight board.
In the first six months of 2026, 10 children have died and eight more suffered critical injuries, half of what was reported in the same period in 2025, according to agency data. The ombuds office hasn’t published 2026 numbers.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Restricting legal immigration won’t fix America’s immigration system
description: America’s immigration system is dysfunctional and, in the words of one federal judge, second only to the tax code in its complexity. For decades, presidential administrations and members of bipartisan congresses have failed to reform our outdated immigration system, despite clear, workable reforms. The result is disrupted family and community stability, cons[...]
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer watches a crowd of protesters at Delaney Hall, a detention center, in Newark, New Jersey, on May 25, 2026. Employing new tactics, ICE arrested more people in July than in any previous month of the Trump administration. (Photo by Ben Ackman/New Jersey Monitor)America’s immigration system is dysfunctional and, in the words of one federal judge, second only to the tax code in its complexity. For decades, presidential administrations and members of bipartisan congresses have failed to reform our outdated immigration system, despite clear, workable reforms. The result is disrupted family and community stability, constrained economic growth, and diminished public trust in the government’s ability to administer immigration law fairly and effectively.
It doesn’t have to be this way.
But current White House policies reinforce these challenges, restricting lawful channels and weakening the institutions that sustain them while fixating on enforcement and removal. And the evidence shows that the plan will backfire, increasing the undocumented population and rendering enforcement less effective.
The most effective immigration systems pair interior enforcement and border security with sufficient legal pathways. Frameworks that rely on a “deterrence-only” approach attempt to suppress migration while ignoring the country’s economic and humanitarian needs and values. This funnels people into unsafe, unvetted, and informal entry and increases the number of alleged immigration violations the state must investigate, adjudicate and pay for.
Legal pathways, representing about three-quarters of long-term immigration to the United States, were already severely constrained before the current presidential term. But the country admits far fewer permanent immigrants per capita than many peer nations. Canada, for example, grants permanent residence at roughly three times the U.S. rate. Available pathways are hobbled by insufficient administrative capacity, restrictive numerical limits, and an extraordinarily convoluted legal code.
Family-based immigration accounts for 63% of permanent legal immigration to the United States and is by far the most common legal route. Applicants still wait decades for their cases to move forward. For siblings of U.S. citizens originating from Mexico, the government is now reviewing green card applications going back to 2001; a 25-year wait.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Employment-based immigration is also expensive, slow and unpredictable. Securing permanent residence through employment takes an average of nearly three and a half years and imposes substantial costs on both workers and the private sector, weakening the country’s global competitiveness. A system that cannot adjudicate cases on a reasonable timeline cannot function as either a credible deterrent or a viable pathway. Instead, it produces a significant population in prolonged limbo.
Current federal policy has deepened these longstanding failures by further restricting lawful immigration for those seeking to come to the United States “the right way.” After accounting for the decline in immigration that began under the Biden administration, this White House has actually done more to reduce legal immigration than unauthorized immigration.
Among the most sweeping of these restrictions are the indefinite travel ban imposed on 39 countries and a visa freeze for 75 countries. Additionally, companies must now pay a $100,000 fee for foreign talent, pricing out universities, start-ups, and other important economic contributors. The administration has also worked to shut down legal humanitarian immigration, imperiling some of the world’s most vulnerable populations.
Refugees and asylees, who account for only 16% of U.S. immigration, were also restricted. On day one, refugee admissions, among the most deeply vetted immigrant populations, were suspended for all but white South African populations. A new system of fees prevents people with legitimate asylum claims from seeking protection in the U.S. Additionally, the administration tried to terminate a lifeline for about one million individuals in the United States known as Temporary Protected Status. These include Syrian TPS holders, of which nearly 30% reside in Michigan.
Together with other fundamental changes, such as  forced deportation to third countries (including Venezuelans that were sent to a torture facility in El Salvador), the current administration appears to be pursuing a policy of deterrence for both unauthorized and legal immigrants.
The record of enforcement-only deterrence policies is costly and inconsistent. Enforcement-only strategies have repeatedly failed to eliminate demand for migration at the national level. They may redirect migration toward different routes, encourage repeated entry attempts, or force temporary and seasonal migration into permanent unauthorized settlement.
Most Americans support legal pathways for immigration and the majority support allowing undocumented immigrants to obtain citizenship if they meet a set of requirements. Federal policy now is both extreme and self-defeating. Dismantling lawful channels while leaving the forces that drive migration in place may increase unauthorized immigration, add pressure to immigration courts and federal agencies, separate families, and constrain economic growth.
An effective system should make accessible, reliable legal pathways the foundation of immigration policy rather than treating them as a limited exception to an enforcement-driven approach.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota has taken steps to address post-partum mental health, but more needs to be done
description: Lindsay Clancy is on trial in Massachusetts where she has been charged with killing her three children. Her defense is that she was experiencing psychosis with command hallucinations. This tragedy has put the spotlight on maternal mental health. People are sharing their opinions – and their own personal stories. Whether you agree with her defense […]
text:
An article in the Journal of the American Medical Association found a nearly 65% increase of mothers reporting “fair to poor mental health.” (Photo by Getty Images)Lindsay Clancy is on trial in Massachusetts where she has been charged with killing her three children. Her defense is that she was experiencing psychosis with command hallucinations. This tragedy has put the spotlight on maternal mental health. People are sharing their opinions – and their own personal stories. Whether you agree with her defense or not, most agree that caregivers missed warning signs  and her care was suboptimal. It has led to an outcry to pay attention to new parents’ mental health and to put more resources into education and treatment. 
Minnesota had our own experience with a tragedy that led to change. 
In 2003, Mine Ener struggled with her mental health following the birth of her baby and returned to St. Paul to be close to family. Unbeknownst to the family, Mine developed psychotic thinking that led her to kill her 6-month-old daughter, Raya, who was born with Down syndrome and several health conditions. Ener died by suicide a few weeks later in the Ramsey County jail. The Ener family was saddened and shocked; they knew little about postpartum depression, anxiety and even psychosis that can accompany it, broadly known as perinatal mood and anxiety disorders, or PMAD.
Depression, anxiety and psychosis are serious mental health conditions that affect nearly 20% of people before, during and after pregnancy. It’s more than just the “baby blues.” Mothers report feeling isolated, severely depressed, overcome with intrusive thoughts, panic attacks, insomnia and a state of numbness. Those experiencing psychosis will have hallucinations, delusional thoughts and paranoia. Many are ashamed to share what they are experiencing since the expectation is that having a new baby is a joyous time. Left untreated, it can lead to poor outcomes for both the birthing parent and the child. 
While high-profile cases involving infanticide are extremely rare, mental health and substance use disorders are the leading cause of pregnancy-associated deaths in Minnesota;  nationally 20% of maternal deaths are due to suicide.
The more the Ener family learned about this issue, the more they wanted to do something. They took their grief and vowed to create change.
With the help of social workers, psychiatrists, friends, NAMI Minnesota and mothers who had experienced PMAD, they successfully passed a law in 2005 requiring education on PMAD. The Minnesota Department of Health — working with families and health and mental health care facilities and providers — were tasked with developing materials and information on postpartum depression, including treatment resources. Physicians, midwives and other health care professionals providing prenatal care to women were required to make this information available to women and their families. Hospitals and other health care facilities were to provide departing new mothers and fathers and other family members with the information.
An annual conference (“Beyond the Baby Blues”) developed out of these efforts and recently held its 20th year educating thousands of mental health and birthing professionals and students on perinatal screenings, assessments, treatments, supports and much more. The Minnesota Chapter of Postpartum Support International created an impressive list of resources along with contact information of providers trained on this issue.
A lot has been done in the past 20  years to raise awareness, improve screening rates, and increase access to appropriate treatment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
So where are we today?
Nationwide, the mental health of women pre-, during and post-pregnancy has worsened. An article in the Journal of the American Medical Association found a nearly 65% increase of mothers reporting “fair to poor mental health.” Dr. Uruj Kamal Haider shared in a recent column in Time that she is seeing an increase in psychosis among postpartum women.
While we need to support awareness campaigns and conduct screenings during — not just after — pregnancy, we also need to make sure we have effective programs to treat mothers.
For the past few months, I have volunteered at the Redleaf Center for Family Healing housed at Hennepin Healthcare. This clinic offers a 20-hour a week mother-baby partial hospitalization program for parents during pregnancy and parenting of children ages birth-5 years, who are experiencing symptoms of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder or other emotional distress. Parents are encouraged to bring their babies. Treatment includes therapy, support for mother-baby bonding, parent education,  mindfulness, medication  management, and individual appointments with a lactation consultant or infant feeding and growth specialist. It’s the type of intensive program that should be available to any parent who needs it. 
Trapped and alone: Fear of ICE is deepening postpartum isolation for immigrant mothers

Once a week I sit in on one of the daily group therapy sessions. At various times during the session, I am asked to hold or play with a  baby. It’s incredibly satisfying to rock babies or get down on the floor to play with them and to give the parent a needed break. During this time, I also hear their struggles and coping strategies. While the incredibly competent therapist is there to help them, what I have also seen is the importance of peer support. Other moms comment on what someone has shared, offering acknowledgement, advice and support. They learn they are not alone. I witness how much they love their babies and it’s gratifying to watch them heal and graduate from the program.
Like so many parts of our mental health system, the payment rate is not sufficient to cover the costs of providing all the components of this robust program and other mother-baby programs in the state. They operate on a tenuous basis, especially those that serve a high percentage of people on Medicaid.
Investing in these types of programs is an investment in our future — for healthy babies and parents.  Minnesota received barely a passing grade from the Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health. They recommend fully funding these important programs, tracking screening and quality, creating inpatient programs, forming a task force, funding a perinatal psychiatry consultation program for obstetricians, and funding group prenatal care, among other things. 
Early identification is critically important, so I urge you to take time to learn about maternal mental health and reach in to support new parents who are struggling — bring food, clean their house, give them time to sleep, share resources. Let them know they are not alone. Legislators should pass bills that address the shortcomings in our own state. 
If you are struggling with your mental health call or text 988, the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262) for free, confidential support.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Fannie Lou Hamer Digital Driving Tour relaunches
description: In this Sept. 17, 1965, file photo, Fannie Lou Hamer of Ruleville speaks to Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party supporters outside the Capitol in Washington after the House of Representatives rejected a challenger to the 1964 election of five Mississippi representatives.
text:
Students, researchers and tourists have a new tool to learn more about the Mississippi-sharecropper-turned-civil-rights-activist Fannie Lou Hamer with the relaunch of her digital driving tour. 
The refreshed tour builds on the award-winning educational project Fannie Lou Hamer’s America, which includes the nationally broadcast documentary, a K–12 curriculum and digital resources dedicated to preserving and amplifying Hamer’s voice. 
The driving tour, originally developed as part of the “Find Your Voice” curriculum, features locations connected to Hamer’s life and activism, including sites in Ruleville, Sunflower County and Winona that help tell the story of her leadership in the civil rights movement. The M.W. Stringer Lodge in Jackson where Hamer and several others founded the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party in April 1964 was added to the upgraded tour. The tour now also has short videos with archival audio footage of Hamer singing or talking about each location, current footage of the site, and archival news articles and photos.  
Funded by the Mississippi Humanities Council and the W.K. Kellogg Foundation, the digital tour  with immersive views is designed to make Hamer’s story more accessible for classrooms, cultural heritage travelers and anyone seeking a deeper understanding of Mississippi’s role in the Civil Rights Movement. Visitors can explore historic locations, learn the significance of each site and connect Hamer’s grassroots organizing to broader themes of voting rights, civic participation, education, food justice and community empowerment.
Fannie Lou Hamer testifies before the Credentials Committee at the 1964 Democratic National Convention.  Credit: Courtesy: Library of Congress (Warren K. Leffler, photographer)
“Mrs. Hamer’s story personifies the Mississippi Freedom Movement – how local people inspired and partnered with young activists to change the state and the country,” Stuart Rockoff, executive director of the Mississippi Humanities Council, said in a news release. “This driving tour will help people from across Mississippi and the world understand the vital role Mrs. Hamer played in the movement and her continuing relevance to the issues of justice we still face today.”
The original driving tour, which included site descriptions, photos and a map of 10 relevant locations in Hamer’s life, launched online in August 2019. Fannie Lou Hamer historian and author Davis Houck and Pablo Correa designed the tour. Houck was a consultant on the film, and Correa was a videographer. 
Joy Davenport, the film’s editor and director, had the vision for the new driving tour that features the same 10 locations, such as William Chapel Church in Ruleville where Hamer attended her first mass meeting, the Sunflower County Courthouse in Indianola, where she tried to register to vote, and the Winona jail site where she and several others were beaten. 
“There was so much we couldn’t show in the film due to time and cost,” Monica Land, Hamer’s niece and producer of the film and the driving tour, said in the news release. “So, the motivation for doing this was to see another aspect of Aunt Fannie Lou’s life explored. And we’re asked all the time, ‘Where is Fannie Lou Hamer buried?’ ‘Is there a statue of her?’ ‘Is there a museum?’ By expanding the reach of the driving tour, we allow visitors to hear Aunt Fannie Lou herself describe what happened at that location. And for those who can’t visit in person, this tour makes them feel as if they were. It preserves those places as living classrooms.” 
Archival footage for the new driving tour was taken from the film with current locations shot by Jackson-based videographer and editor Tommy Kirkpatrick of CommonHouse Productions.  
The last video to be released, Atlantic City, is the only out of state location and is where Hamer gave her historic and emotional testimony before the Credentials Committee at the Democratic National Convention on Aug. 22, 1964. That video will post Friday to commemorate that event. Visit Atlantic City funded the video, and New Jersey-based videographer Pernell Pounce captured the footage. 
The driving tour is available on the film’s website, fannielouhamersamerica.com with maps and tourist information, and  YouTube channel.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri can bring clarity to a confusing vaccine landscape
description: A mother carries her 12-month-old into the pediatrician’s office for a routine visit. The doctor recommends the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine- the MMR vaccine- just as pediatricians have for decades. This time, she pauses. She heard the President say the MMR vaccine was “sort of like a nuclear weapon.” She heard the head of […]
text:
A health care worker places a bandage on a child after giving a vaccination shot (Scott Housley/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention).A mother carries her 12-month-old into the pediatrician’s office for a routine visit. The doctor recommends the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine- the MMR vaccine- just as pediatricians have for decades.
This time, she pauses.
She heard the President say the MMR vaccine was “sort of like a nuclear weapon.” She heard the head of HHS raise the possibility of a link between vaccines and autism. She loves her child, and is trying to make the best decision she can with the information she has been given.
How can we blame a parent for hesitating when the information landscape has become so confusing?
Her hesitation comes at a critical moment. As of August 13th, the United States has recorded 2,566 confirmed measles cases in 2026, already surpassing the 2,289 total from 2025 and the highest total in more than 35 years.
Measles was considered eliminated from the United States in 2000. As another school year begins, MMR coverage among American kindergarteners has fallen to 92.4%. Exemptions from one or more vaccines rose by ~17% from 3.6% to 4.2% in a single year – meaning ~280,000 kindergarteners are entering school without documented completion of their MMR series. The roughly 95% coverage needed to reliably prevent a measles outbreak is no longer being reached.
Fear travels quickly. Measles can travel with it.
Measles in not simply a childhood rash. It can cause severe pneumonia, hospitalizing one in five unvaccinated persons. Even after apparent recovery, the virus can leave an invisible scar on the immune system. Measles infection can erase 11-73% of children’s pre-existing antibody repertoire a phenomenon called “immune amnesia”- leaving children more vulnerable to infections their immune systems had previously learned to fight.
Years after an apparently complete recovery, a small number can develop subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, SSPE, a degenerate brain disease that is fatal.
Against those risks, we have something remarkably effective: two doses of the MMR vaccine provide ~97% protection against measles.
The question parents are hearing most loudly – does MMR cause autism? – has been asked repeatedly and studied on an enormous scale. Large population studies involving millions of children have found no increased risk of autism after MMR vaccination. Researchers have even looked specifically at children with an older sibling with autism, a group already at higher baseline risk. The result was the same: MMR vaccination was not associated with an increased risk of autism.
This is why the August 10th executive order matters.
The order states that the combined MMR vaccine should be replaced with separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella when available and “to the maximum extent feasible” childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits.
There is no published scientific evidence that splitting MMR into three vaccines makes children safer. But it could turn a two-dose series into six injections; each additional visit creating another chance for children to remain incompletely protected.
This is not an abstract inconvenience. About 60% of rural counties do not have a pediatrician. For a parent paid by the hour, getting a child vaccinated may already mean a long drive, lost wages and scare time off. US data show that combination vaccines result in fewer total needles and a higher likelihood of completing the full vaccine series.
Separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines are not currently licensed or manufactured in the US, and have not been since 2009. Re-establishing manufacturing and attaining regulatory approval would take years and substantial investment, Merck has estimated the process could take roughly a decade.
History should make us cautious about fragmenting vaccine programs. After Japan discontinued MMR in 1993, it later experienced major measles resurgences. Its eventual response included a national catch-up campaign using a combined measles-rubella vaccine and aggressive efforts to restore high coverage.
We do not need to repeat every experiment in public health to learn from it.
None of this means vaccines should be immune from scrutiny. Parents deserve answers to hard questions. Safety signals should be investigated and recommendations should change when better evidence emerges. Our vaccine safety system was built to do exactly that. One example is the rotavirus vaccine: an earlier version was withdrawn after post licensure monitoring detected an increased risk of intussusception.
Earlier this year, the federal childhood vaccine schedule was revised from vaccines routinely recommended against 17 infections to 11 without the traditional evidence -review process. Since ACIP was created in 1964, changes to the federal vaccine schedule have traditionally followed a rigorous process of evidence review, risk benefit analysis and revision when safety monitoring reveals new evidence.
A federal judge subsequently blocked implementation of those changes while litigation proceeds. The August 10 order goes further, urging states to reconsider school vaccination requirements and directing the Attorney General to support certain legal challenges involving exemptions.
The order itself does not rewrite Missouri law. School vaccination requirements remain principally a state responsibility.
This gives Missouri lawmakers both an opportunity and a responsibility.
Missouri legislators should ensure that any change in childhood vaccination policy comes with clear accessible and evidence- guidance for parents. Families should be told what each vaccine prevents, its known risks and benefits, what the evidence does and does not show, and whether a federal announcement actually changes
Missouri law or medical recommendations.
Missouri should also consider safeguards already used elsewhere: requiring parents seeking nonmedical exemptions to receive evidence-based information about vaccination; making school-level vaccination and exemption rates readily available to families; and ensuring that state recommendations are grounded in a transparent scientific review process.
This is not a choice between parental rights and public health. A choice is only truly informed when the information behind it is reliable.
Missouri cannot control every message a parent hears from Washington, a television commentator or an algorithm on a phone. But Missouri can control what happens next.
When that mother sits across from her child’s pediatrician, wondering whom to believe, our state can make sure she has clear evidence rather than more noise – and that a preventable disease does not become the price of preventable confusion.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: High schoolers’ free overseas trips highlight noncompliance with NJ watchdog reports
description: A South Jersey high school was slow to heed a watchdog's warning to stop paying for students' pricey trips. Now, a state lawmaker is angry.
text:
A South Jersey high school was slow to heed a watchdog's warning to stop paying for students' pricey trips. Now, a state lawmaker is angry. (Getty Images)Students at Salem High School with an interest in global affairs have long gotten a pricey perk: all-expenses-paid trips to faraway places that have included Scotland, Portugal, and the Czech Republic.
State auditor David K. Kaschak flagged the unique benefit in 2024, advising Salem City’s school district to require students in its “international baccalaureate” program to pay their own way for the annual excursions that averaged $3,900 per pupil. Last month, he repeated that recommendation, noting in a new compliance report that the district continued to cover the full cost of the trips from its general fund — and had ignored more than a dozen other belt-tightening recommendations.
Thursday, Salem City School District Superintendent Carol L. Kelley told the New Jersey Monitor that future trips will not be funded by taxpayers and that the district “understands the State Auditor’s concern” and will pay for the trips through “grants, partnerships, fundraising, and other outside resources.”
But a state legislator who sits on the Senate’s budget committee said the district’s compliance failures are troubling and deserve legislative attention.
After Kaschak first revealed his findings in 2024, Sen. Declan O’Scanlon (R-Monmouth), the GOP budget officer in the Senate, wrote to the state attorney general and other state officials to demand a criminal investigation into Salem City schools. He also called on his colleagues in Trenton to expand state funding to ensure more school districts get audited.
Sen. Declan O’Scanlon (Photo by Hal Brown/New Jersey Monitor)
He reupped those demands this week, saying full, timely compliance with the auditor’s recommendations is a reasonable expectation of any auditee, particularly when taxpayers’ money is at risk of waste or abuse.
“It’s outrageous,” O’Scanlon said. “It is time to revisit. We need more money for the audits, and more audits, and more teeth.”
Salem City school officials have “an obligation to be accountable for their decisions and to the taxpayers who are funding their jobs,” he added.
Kaschak examined Salem City schools because he’s tasked with auditing state departments to ensure efficiency and accountability in government operations and the proper spending of public funds.
For schools, his office is authorized to audit any district that reports a budget deficit, as well as the 31 low-wealth districts that get at least 80% of their funding from the state.
Salem City School District fit both categories, reporting a $621,000 deficit in 2019 that initially triggered Kaschak’s review. The district got $25.7 million in K-12 state funding this year for its 1,100 students, about 72% of whom qualify for free or reduced lunch.
The free travel was just one of multiple deficiencies Kaschak reported in 2024 after scrutinizing Salem schools’ finances between 2018 and 2023.
He identified problems with procurement, employee reimbursements and leave, healthcare eligibility determinations, nonresident students, outside groups’ use of school facilities, and athletic fund purchases, among other things.
The more eye-popping spending included $115,650 paid to colleges and universities for tuition, room, and board for eight former Salem City students; $103,075 paid to students as an incentive to attend an exam-preparation course; $68,921 on travel for the football team; and $45,315 for athletic championship jackets and rings.
To send the international baccalaureate students overseas, the district spent an average of $75,000 per trip on five trips Kaschak scrutinized — and about $35,000 for booked airfare and accommodations that no one used. He also found that one adult chaperone went for every three students even though the hosting organization provided chaperones, most of the Salem chaperones did not stay with the students during the trips, several chaperones’ spouses also got free trips, and some trips and spending never got school board approval as required.
At the same time, he found the program had a graduation rate of just 12%, lagging far behind the 84% average of similar programs elsewhere.
Altogether, he tallied over $1 million in spending he found objectionable. He also determined the district collected at least $1 million in overpayments of state aid in 2022, 2023, and 2024, due to errors in pupil counts.
He issued 58 recommendations for Salem City administrators to avoid future deficits and better safeguard district funds.
In a compliance check completed in March and released last month, Kaschak found that the district had not complied with 13 of his recommendations, partially complied with another 23, and fully complied with 20. Two recommendations were deemed “not applicable” in July’s report.
Kelley defended her district Thursday, saying those figures represent a 76.8% implementation rate.
Many of the problematic practices Kaschak and his team identified predate the district’s current leaders, she added. Kelley took over the top job at Salem City School District in January 2025, 14 months after she resigned from a tumultuous two-year tenure at Princeton Public Schools.
“The current administration remains focused on resolving outstanding findings,” Kelley said. “The district recognizes its responsibility to maintain strong internal controls, comply with applicable laws and regulations, and ensure that public resources are used appropriately, efficiently, and transparently.”
The district’s international baccalaureate program is part of a global effort to promote intercultural understanding, with about 6,200 schools in 160 countries participating, according to the Switzerland-based nonprofit that leads it.
Salem administrators acknowledged to Kaschak in 2024 that they knew of no other districts that covered the trips’ entire price tag. But they insisted it was “worth the cost” because the district is economically disadvantaged and many attendees had never previously ventured out of the area and couldn’t afford to travel.
But Thursday, Kelley reversed course, telling the New Jersey Monitor that future trips will be funded from a $100,000 grant from the Congregation of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Peace. That’s a Catholic order based in Englewood Cliffs to which Sister Carol Adams, a longtime Salem City school board member and the current board vice president, belongs.
The district, though, did pay for trips for international baccalaureate students this year. School board members approved spending nearly $10,000 total on trips to Prague in April for two students and one chaperone and to Wildwood in June for 10 students and three chaperones, meeting minutes show.
Kaschak declined to comment on Salem City schools’ compliance with his recommendations, saying he prefers to let his reports speak for themselves.
As for O’Scanlon’s call for more state funding for audits, Kaschak said that’s an issue for policymakers to decide.
But he agreed the public money flowing out of Trenton warrants closer scrutiny.
“We couldn’t possibly do everything that the statute empowers us to do. We have to work within our existing resources,” he said, adding, “If that issue is raised again, I’d be willing to discuss that with any legislator.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Temporary Assistance for Needy Families at 30: Centering dignity for New Jersey families
authors: Special to the New Jersey Monitor
description: The Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program is an important lifeline, but its rigid structure has not kept up with today’s economic pressures.
text:
The Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program is an important lifeline, but its rigid structure has not kept up with today’s economic pressures. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)By Tonanziht Aguas & Andrea Hetling
September is approaching and so is a new school year. Whether a child is starting kindergarten or their last year of high school, the first day of school is a milestone to celebrate. Parents look forward to the small milestones that mark their child’s growing independence: a birthday celebration, the start of a new school year, a chance to feel part of something.
Yet moments that should feel joyful often reveal how fragile family budgets can be. When money is stretched to cover rent, groceries, and necessities, even other expenses — a gift, a backpack, a pair of shoes — can force parents into impossible trade‑offs. Decline the birthday invitation? Skip items their child needs for class? Sacrifice something else the family relies on?
These everyday decisions capture a reality that is all too familiar: when money is limited, even modest costs can become barriers to a family’s wellbeing. Forgoing school or sports supplies for their kids or saying no to that birthday party invitation is unavoidable when basic needs are unmet, but education and social connections are also essential for child development.
For families balancing bills and uncertainty, direct cash is often the difference between stability and setback. When emergencies arise, such as a missed shift or a medical bill, flexible cash support helps parents protect their family’s footing. Rather than treating cash aid as secondary to other supports, we should see it as the foundation that allows families to rebuild and move forward.
Direct cash is one of the most effective ways to reduce hardship, yet New Jersey’s safety net remains largely a patchwork of in-kind and voucher supports. The only program that consistently provides direct cash assistance to families with low-incomes and young children is the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program, or TANF. TANF is an important lifeline, but its rigid structure has not kept up with today’s economic pressures.
In 2023, just 11 out of every 100 New Jersey families living in poverty received TANF. Challenges such as excessive paperwork and complicated rules often turn away families who qualify. Caseloads have fallen since the program began, and that decline held even as need rose. National research on the COVID-19 pandemic shows TANF failed to respond to rising hardship the way other safety net programs did.
TANF remains a cornerstone of that safety net all the same. When strengthened, it can provide the flexible, reliable cash assistance families need to weather crises, support their children’s growth, and build lasting economic security.
This gap between TANF’s promise and its current reach makes its upcoming anniversary especially significant. On August 22, TANF turns 30 as New Jersey’s only program offering direct cash assistance to families with the lowest incomes under the Work First New Jersey program. That milestone invites reflection and a much-needed shift in narrative. Centering dignity means recognizing direct cash assistance not as a last resort, but as the stabilizing foundation that helps families meet life’s everyday challenges with agency and respect.
Unfortunately, current debates about the program center more on fraud than on helping families. Spending public funds responsibly is a legitimate goal. But the federal government’s near-total focus on fraud, paired with new demands for data sharing, has piled burdens onto states. Those burdens trickle down to families, who face more red tape both when they apply and when they try to keep their benefits. Each additional document, verification requirement, or data check can delay assistance, increase stress, and reinforce the message that applicants are viewed with suspicion.
When public opinion is impacted and the media and public dialogue similarly focus on rooting out fraud, stigma surrounding cash assistance rises. This discourages eligible families from applying and reinforces harmful stereotypes about poverty instead of addressing its root causes.
Research shows that fraud is rare, and most improper payments stem from confusing rules or paperwork issues. When we talk about direct cash assistance, the focus should not be on suspicion, but on recipients’ capacity to make the best choices for their families. When parents have access to flexible support, they use it to meet essential needs and build stability. TANF’s future depends on shifting from narratives of doubt to a vision rooted in opportunity.
TANF’s shortcomings reveal what’s possible and what’s holding progress back. Federal inaction and new administrative demands have made it harder for states to focus on families instead of compliance. Yet even within that environment, New Jersey has room to lead. Raising benefit levels, updating eligibility rules so families have enough time to build stability, and aligning program requirements with the realities of low‑wage work and caregiving are just some of the ways the state can show what a dignity‑centered safety net looks like.
As TANF turns 30, it is time to replace misguided conversations about fraud with dialogue rooted in dignity. That shift demands a person‑centered process, and one that allows frontline staff to serve as partners rather than gatekeepers. Cash reaffirms our belief in families and changes everyday lives in ways that are easy to overlook: covering the small, regular expense that keeps a household steady, paying for the school supplies that help a child start the year with confidence, or making sure a parent does not have to choose between a utility bill and giving their child a chance to grow.
Tonanziht Aguas is a policy analyst at New Jersey Policy Perspective, covering safety net issues and economic security policy.
Andrea Hetling is a professor at the Bloustein School of Planning and Public Policy and the associate director of the Heldrich Center of Workforce Development at Rutgers University – New Brunswick.

name: WyoFile
title: Trump administration plan could bring new roads to pristine woods covering 4% of Wyoming
description:
The effort to overturn 25-year-old Roadless Rule protections “anticipates” potential motorized networks across Wyoming national forest areas as large as the Shoshone National Forest.
The post Trump administration plan could bring new roads to pristine woods covering 4% of Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Trump administration unveiled a plan Wednesday to build more roads in pristine national forests, releasing figures that show near-term construction of new motorized networks would be possible across almost 4% of Wyoming, an area the size of the entire Shoshone National Forest.
The plan – which rescinds the 2001 National Forest Roadless Rule – would affect 3.2 million acres of national forest roadless areas in the Equality State. That roadless acreage is valued as wildlife habitat and widely used for non-motorized recreation like hunting, fishing, riding, skiing and backpacking.
It’s also the target of the timber industry and advocates of motorized recreation interests that could benefit from overturning the 2001 conservation measure. The Department of Agriculture states that the proposal will pit motorists and industry against others who use federal public lands in national forests.
The construction of new roads “would result in tradeoffs with opportunities for quiet, remote and self-reliant recreation and may increase user conflicts,” the federal notice states, “and result in lost economic benefits.”
Expansion of road networks “is uncertain and anticipated to be limited due to land management plans, budget, and resources,” the plan states.
“They continue to prove that they are hell-bent on breaking our public land heritage with insane giveaways to the few.” Land Tawney
Conservationists condemned the initiative. Trump’s administration is “hell-bent on breaking our public land heritage,” Land Tawney, co-chair of American Hunters & Anglers said in a statement. The rescission is “a giveaway to the timber industry,” said Kate Groetzinger of the Center for Western Priorities.
The plan will harm “elk country, trout streams, hunting grounds, and backcountry places that define this state,” Julia Stuble, Wyoming state director for The Wilderness Society, said in a statement.
The roadless issue already has become a political hot potato with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Byrd blasting Republican opponent U.S. Rep Harriet Hageman over her support for more roads.
He called her an “out-of-touch politician” who is “playing fast and loose with the facts.”
Hageman isn’t representing Wyoming, he stated earlier this year, but is “auditioning for corporate campaign donors.”
‘Environmental catastrophe’
Hageman has been critical of the Roadless Rule. 
“The United States Forest Service Office created an environmental catastrophe when it issued the Roadless Rule in the final days of the Clinton administration,” Hageman said in June. She made her comments at a hearing about forest fires and the upcoming wildfire season where she quizzed Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz.
“It’s definitely increased catastrophic wildfire risk,” Schultz said of the rule. “It inhibits our ability to actively manage the land to protect communities. It limits public access to enjoy their national forest.”
Earlier this year, Hageman introduced a bill to overturn the Roadless Rule. The bill, separate from the administrative rescission, would prevent the rule from ever being adopted again.
Hageman’s bill also would require the construction of new roads across untrammeled forest lands. The Roadless Rule violates the Forest Service’s 1897 Organic Act, the Wilderness Act and National Environmental Policy Act, her office stated.
Hageman’s bill will lead to “improved forest health, reduced wildfire risks, reduced insect infestations, and the creation of jobs in sectors like logging, construction, and maintenance,” her office stated.
Designated roadless areas, like these timber stands on the Shoshone National Forest near South Pass, would be eliminated under a 2001 Roadless Rule rescission proposed by U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile/EcoFlight)
Byrd criticized Schultz’s comments as “agency capture,” or the takeover of a department by the industry it is supposed to regulate.
“It is deeply disappointing to see the leadership of the Forest Service capitulate to political pressure,” he said. Fully 99% of comments submitted last year on repealing the Roadless Rule opposed overturning it, he said.
“A democratic government is supposed to listen, not find legislative loopholes to ram a corporate subsidy through Congress,” he stated.
Roads and wildfires 
Both sides fiercely debate the relationship of roads to wildfires. “Forest Service Associate Chief Chris French conceded under questioning that it is a ‘longstanding fact’ that most wildfire ignitions are human-caused and directly tied to where roads are built,” Byrd said.
The Democrat accused Hageman of spreading falsehoods. “She has no problem standing up there and flat out being dishonest and lying,” he said in an interview this week.
Neither Hageman’s campaign nor her Washington office responded to WyoFile’s request for comment on Byrd’s charge.
Republican U.S. House nominee Chuck Gray has also advocated for doing away with the Roadless Rule. He characterized the rule as damaging, not conserving, and called it “a Clinton-driven, left-driven attempt to hurt our public lands.”
Gray said the rule inflated the cost of lumber and housing. “It needs to be rescinded so that we can log, we can reach our full potential, and we can recreate,” he said in a campaign debate.
Local decisions
Elimination of the Roadless Rule would return decision-making on roads to the local level, the Trump administration said. It cited “increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface,” as some of the reasons to roll back roadless protections.
“Any near-term permanent road additions would be anticipated to occur on lands where current land management plans allow them … totaling about 18.2 million acres, or 45.5 percent of the potentially affected environment,” the Federal Register posting states. “Temporary roads, if proposed, are more likely to occur on lands within 0.5 miles of existing roads—totaling about 11.3 million acres, or 28.3 percent of the potentially affected environment.”
The brown areas show roadless national forest areas in Wyoming. (Wyoming Outdoor Council)
Factoring in those percentages, the affected area where new roads are possible in Wyoming amounts to 2.36 million of Wyoming’s 3.2 million roadless acres. That’s 3,690 square miles or 3.77% of the state, an area larger than Delaware.
Reversing the 2001 Roadless Rule could cost the country’s recreation economy $6.1 million annually, according to the Federal Register filing. It would generate $5.2 million to $11.4 million in federal revenues and $4.6 million to $10.6 million for the timber industry, according to the announcement.
Any economic boon would be tempered by “road costs, maintenance funding gaps, and the $6.9 billion deferred maintenance backlog for roads and bridges,” the federal summary of the plan states.
The 25-year-old national forest Roadless Rule seeks to address “a national asset that should be conserved and managed consistently,” conservation group Defenders of Wildlife said. The existing rule generally prohibits road construction in inventoried areas larger than 5,000 acres but provides exceptions for public safety, floods, fires and pollution emergencies.
The public has until Sept. 21 to comment on the plan to eliminate the Roadless Rule. Hundreds of pages of government documents supporting the rescission include a 333-page draft environmental impact statement.
After spending a day analyzing the documents, the Center for Western Priorities called the plan an effort to spin logging subsidies into a wildfire mitigation strategy.
“The government’s own study shows repealing the Roadless Rule could actually increase wildfire risk as well as have shocking negative impacts on Western communities,” the group’s Communications Director Kate Groetzinger said in a statement. The documents show agency’s own scientists believe rescission will “harm hundreds of species already at risk of extinction, decrease the quality of drinking water in Western communities, cost rural communities millions of tourism dollars, and grow the Forest Service’s already-massive road maintenance backlog,” she said.
WyoFile’s analysis
Here’s how WyoFile analyzed the plan by the U.S. Forest Service to rescind the Roadless Rule.
Across the nation, there are 58.5 million acres of inventoried roadless areas – areas larger than 5,000 acres where roadbuilding has been largely prohibited for 25 years.
In Wyoming’s national forests, roadbuilding has been prohibited across 3.2 million acres, some 5,000 square miles or about 5.1% of Wyoming’s total land area of 97,813 square miles.
The plan to rescind the Roadless Rule states that the Forest Service “anticipates” proposed new near-term permanent or temporary roads would occur on 73.8% of existing roadless areas. If applied to Wyoming, that would pertain to 2.36 million acres of inventoried national forest roadless areas. Terrain, cost and other factors could limit locally where roads could go. 
The affected 2.36 million acres where new roads would be possible amounts to 3,690 square miles or 3.8% of the Equality State. That’s an area almost as large as the 2.4 million acre Shoshone National Forest which stretches from the Montana border to South Pass.
Sources: Federal Register (proposal), Wikipedia (state size); Shoshone National Forest.

title: Idaho Secretary of State’s Office updates voter look-up tool after public reports website glitch
description: A number of Idaho residents expressed alarm on social media last week when they attempted to verify their voter registration, only to find there was no record of it. The glitch in the website has since been fixed, according to the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office.  A member of a political Facebook group for Idaho […]
text:
Poll workers help voters register to vote for the primary election on May 21, 2024, at Thunder Ridge High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)A number of Idaho residents expressed alarm on social media last week when they attempted to verify their voter registration, only to find there was no record of it. The glitch in the website has since been fixed, according to the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office. 
A member of a political Facebook group for Idaho women said on Aug. 10 that she couldn’t find her registration online. Several comments echoed her concerns after they went to check. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Same, I have been registered to vote since 1988. I have never missed an election. I’ve lived in the same home since 1992. All of the sudden they can’t find me?1?!” One woman commented, attaching a screenshot of a message from VoteIdaho.Gov saying there were no results for her search. 
A spokesperson for the Secretary of State’s Office said the searches affected people accessing the website on their cellphones. 
“In some cases, an extra space or the use of a middle name that was not included when the voter originally registered prevented the system from finding the voter’s record,” spokesperson Joe Parris said. “We have updated the tool to account for these issues. The issues did not affect anyone’s voter registration.” 
Some voters may notice that more information is required to look up their voter registration, including a driver’s license number or the option of providing the last four digits of their Social Security number, than before. 
Parris said those search fields were added in a recent vendor update to add “another layer of security to access voter lookup information.” 
(Screenshot from VoteIdaho.Gov)
 How to register to vote in Idaho, check registration and stay on voter rolls 

Idaho residents may look up their voter information, including precinct number, party affiliation, district and voting history online here. 

The deadline to register to vote online is 11 days before an election. That is Oct. 23 for this year’s November general election. Eligible residents may also register at their polling location on Election Day or during early voting with a valid photo identification and proof of residence. A list of valid documents for voter registration can be found at voteidaho.gov/voter-registration/.
Registration must be updated if the voter moved, changed their name, or hasn’t voted in the past four years. Updating a registration uses the same process as registering for the first time and can be done online or by printing and filling out a PDF voter registration form and mailing it to the county clerk. 
To change party affiliation or become unaffiliated, voters must submit a signed form to their county clerk. 
Idaho election offices purge inactive voters every two years. In 2025, county election officials removed more than 144,000 individuals from voter rolls after performing required voter registration maintenance, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. Officials remove those who move out of state, have not voted in four years or who aren’t eligible.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: In Alabama lieutenant governor’s race, big plans and little ability to carry them out
description: Alabama candidates for lieutenant governor have ambitious plans for the office. Medicaid expansion. Job creation. A host of public safety and development programs. At a press conference Wednesday, Rep. Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery, his party’s nominee for the office, announced a host of policy priorities ranging from a voter-approved lottery to expanding Med[...]
text:
Voters will choose between Republican John Wahl and Rep. Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery, for lieutenant governor on Nov. 3, 2026. Both men have a host of policy plans for the office with no little power. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama candidates for lieutenant governor have ambitious plans for the office.
Medicaid expansion. Job creation. A host of public safety and development programs.
At a press conference Wednesday, Rep. Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery, his party’s nominee for the office, announced a host of policy priorities ranging from a voter-approved lottery to expanding Medicaid; expanding the state’s First Class Pre-K program to a data center moratorium and safe storage for firearms to term limits in Alabama. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“These are serious times that require serious leaders who want to solve problems rather than divide and distract. The people of Alabama deserve transparency from their elected officials,” Ensler said. 
Many of his priorities mirror bills that he filed during his time in the House of Representatives, but he will not be able to file a bill should he win in November. 
Ensler’s Republican opponent – former Alabama Republican Party chair John Wahl – also has many policy priorities, but they are more broad. He said in a phone interview Wednesday that he wants to increase job and educational opportunities, reduce crime and address affordability. 
“(Government) was created to help make sure that people enjoyed their liberties – the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. That’s going to always be my first priority,” he said. 
The problem is that the lieutenant governor has very little power to do any of that.
Limited power, and shrinking
The Alabama Senate chamber in the Alabama Statehouse on April 8, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
The lieutenant governor becomes governor should the occupant of that office die, resign or be removed. The office once had powers comparable to that of the Alabama House speaker, with powers to control legislation and assign senators to committees. 
But the office was stripped of its power in 1999 after a lengthy standoff between then-Lt. Gov. Steve Windom, a Republican, and the Democratic-controlled Senate, which transferred most of Windom’s powers to the Senate President Pro Tem.  
The role had its powers further decreased by the Senate this spring. Senate Resolution 108, sponsored by Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, allows Senate President Pro Tem to preside over the Senate if the lieutenant governor has not taken his or her seat five minutes after a meeting time. 
The resolution also removes the lieutenant governor from a committee that assigns committee chairs, removes their power to appoint members to conference committees, gives the Pro Tem the power to recommit bills to committees and gives the Pro Tem and to direct the lieutenant governor to call up legislation carried over to the call of the chair.
Republicans have held the office since 2010.
Wahl said that the influential power of the lieutenant governor and a party chair are similar, so he is equipped and excited for the actual power of the elected office.
“If you look at my record and what I was able to accomplish as party chair, the sky is the limit when we’re looking at the lieutenant governor’s office,” he said. “There are so many things in government that the lieutenant governor can do to make people better. I look forward to using every part of that for the people of Alabama.”
The bully pulpit
Lt. Gov. Will Ainsworth raising his gavels the Senate adjourned sine die, ending the 2026 regular session of the Alabama Legislature, on April 9, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
During meetings of the Legislature, the lieutenant governor presides over the Alabama Senate. They do not vote, file bills or debate legislation, but they do have the power to recognize senators on the floor and call lawmakers into session. 
Republicans hold a supermajority in both chambers of the legislature. If Ensler wins in November, he said he would work across the aisle like he did in the House to get legislation passed. 
“I can’t introduce the bills myself, but I will work with the colleagues. I have the relationships already, and that trust,” Ensler said. 
Ensler sponsored a bill banning Glock switches, a modification to firearms that turn semiautomatic weapons to automatic ones. It did not pass under his sole sponsorship, but it did pass in 2025 when Sen. Will Barfoot, R-Pike Road, sponsored the bill after Gov. Kay Ivey named it as a top priority following a 2024 mass shooting in Birmingham.
Ensler also worked with Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger, R-Cullman, to pass Beau’s Law, an animal welfare law that he sponsored for multiple sessions. The bill passed this spring with opposition from major interest groups.  
“People said the same thing about Beau’s law, dealing with welfare for dogs, and said there’s no way,” he said. “They said, ‘You’re not going to get it through. Every politician that’s tried to do it. It’s gotten killed, and that politician has gotten attacked.’ I worked with Senator Gudger, and we did it.”
Wahl and Ensler agree on at least one campaign promise: eliminate the grocery tax. 
“Our tax code here in Alabama is backwards in so many ways. We still tax groceries, which means we tax people for feeding their kids,” Ensler said. “The grocery tax is regressive, and we should eliminate it.”
Wahl said that cutting the grocery tax was a priority for him as ALGOP chair – a position with no legislative power on paper. He said he wants it “phased out completely as soon as possible.”
“The people of this state are the best in the country, and they’re hardworking, and they deserve a government that looks out for them and that makes sure we return a little bit of money back to their wallets,” he said.
The legislature has reduced the grocery tax from 4% to 2% over the last three years. Lawmakers this spring passed a two month suspension of the state tax in May and June. Democrats and Republicans have advocated for a full elimination, but leadership has expressed concern of the impacts to the Education Trust Fund (ETF) budget.
Ensler on Wednesday challenged Wahl to a debate, which Wahl agreed to with enthusiasm in an interview. 
“I love to debate and to talk about the issues that are facing the people of Alabama. For me, it doesn’t matter whether you’re a Republican, whether you’re a Democrat, or whether you’re Independent,” he said. “I am always excited to be on the debate stage and make that argument and talk about what I believe in, why I believe it.”

title: Banning of THCA potentially blows $110 million hole in Tennessee’s budget
description: Tennessee Republican lawmakers banned popular cannabinoid-derived hemp products starting in July, and after one month of sales tax collections, projections are on pace for a  $110 million loss. The state’s new hemp laws ban smokable products and, in particular THCA, which several industry groups estimated made up 75% of Tennessee’s cannabinoid market. When l[...]
text:
Tennessee lawmakers banned smokable hemp products like these starting in July, creating a budget loss. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Republican lawmakers banned popular cannabinoid-derived hemp products starting in July, and after one month of sales tax collections, projections are on pace for a  $110 million loss.
The state’s new hemp laws ban smokable products and, in particular THCA, which several industry groups estimated made up 75% of Tennessee’s cannabinoid market.
When lit on fire, THCA essentially turns into THC, the psychoactive ingredient in marijuana that is illegal in Tennessee. THCA, because it comes from hemp, technically has a THC content below the state’s previous legal threshold.
State Rep. Aftyn Behn, a Nashville Democrat, said the revenue shortfall was not surprising and that the ban “torched a $250 million industry.”
“Leadership can tout the revenue surplus all they want, but their decisions left Tennesseans who rely on hemp for chronic pain out on the side of our busted roads and stuck the rest of us with the tax burden,” Behn said.
Hemp taxes in limbo as industry braces for massive sales drop-off in July

Behn and state Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, renewed their push to legalize marijuana through their “pot for potholes” measure earlier this year. The legislation would allow people 21 and older to use marijuana legally and create a regulatory framework for growing, testing and selling products.
Under the Behn-Campbell bill, cannabis businesses would be required to obtain state licenses, and a 15% tax would be charged on sales, with the revenue going toward the nearly $60 billion backlog of highway and bridge projects.
The current hemp taxes go into the state’s general fund and aren’t dedicated to any specific purpose.
For the state’s 2025-26 budget, officials already reduced hemp tax collection projections by $55 million. That budget ended in June, with tax collections $55.8 million below projections.
For the 2026-27 budget, Tennessee’s Department of Finance and Administration and the governor’s office estimated hemp sales tax collections at around $130 million. In July, the first month of the new ban, the revenue projections were $9.4 million and actual collections were around $425,000. Over the course of a year, that over 90% drop would create at least a $110 million deficit.
Budget officials will have some room to maneuver after the state announced a $1.2 billion surplus after closing the 2025-26 budget.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho needs a 10-year plan to restore its decimated tax revenue as soon as possible
description: Please consider: For the last 40 years Idaho has been 49th or 50th in the nation in the funding of education. To coin a phrase, we have been the “Mississippi of the Northwest.” Over the last 61 years, we have pirated away the sales tax base by 89 special interest exemptions, so now the total […]
text:
Idaho's income tax base has changed from being a progressive tax to a single tax bracket, with a reduction in its rate, thereby reducing the tax base by more than $4 billion, writes guest columnist Robert Huntley. (Photo illustration by Getty Images)Please consider: For the last 40 years Idaho has been 49th or 50th in the nation in the funding of education. To coin a phrase, we have been the “Mississippi of the Northwest.”
New report finds tax cuts benefit highest-income Idaho households most

Over the last 61 years, we have pirated away the sales tax base by 89 special interest exemptions, so now the total exemptions cost approximately $600,000 more than the sales tax brings in.
When the sales tax was enacted, Idaho’s economy was approximately 60% production oriented. That is agriculture, mining, and manufacturing and 40% services. That ratio flipped to 60% services and 40% production approximately 35 years ago, and yet the sales tax has never been amended to reflect that change in revenue sources.
In the last five years, our income tax base has changed from being a progressive tax to a single tax bracket, with a reduction in its rate, thereby reducing the tax base by more than $4 billion.
A new report from the Idaho Center for Fiscal Policy found that income tax cuts passed by the Idaho Legislature have reduced state revenue by a combined $4 billion. (Graphic courtesy of the Idaho Center for Fiscal Policy)
It is a fantasy to think that the economy will grow us out of this problem without major restoration of the tax base. The chances that anything we can be proud of can happen without tax base restructure are slim and none, and Slim is out of town.
The people of Idaho need to find a leader who will put together a team of five persons, who in turn will put together a task force of 25 people from the Legislature, the business community, the public schools, and citizens at large, who will:

First: Present legislation at the opening of the 2027 session for some interim progress forward, such as an alternative minimum tax to begin to address the problem; and
Secondly: Develop and present, as soon as possible, a comprehensive 10-year plan to address not only revenue for operating budgets, but also for facilities repair and upgrading and constructing new buildings.

We will be “derelict in our duty” to the people of Idaho if we do nothing more than the usual thing of reacting to what the Legislature did or did not do — we must provide leadership.
