name: Colorado Newsline
title: As litigation looms and drought takes its toll, state officials defiant over Colorado River’s future
description: Routt County rancher Philip Rossi knew as early as January of this year — as the Flat Tops range above the Yampa River basin sat largely bare of snow — that 2026 would be a difficult water year. “You can just feel it,” said Rossi, whose family has run cattle in the upper Yampa River […]
text:
Water levels in the Wolford Mountain Reservoir in Grand County, which dams a tributary of the Colorado River, have dropped by more than 30 feet during extreme drought conditions in 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Routt County rancher Philip Rossi knew as early as January of this year — as the Flat Tops range above the Yampa River basin sat largely bare of snow — that 2026 would be a difficult water year.
“You can just feel it,” said Rossi, whose family has run cattle in the upper Yampa River valley for more than a century. “This is no good. We’re just not getting any moisture.”
Water managers at the Upper Yampa Water Conservancy District say that agricultural irrigators across the district received only about half of their normal water allocation from storage infrastructure like the Yamcolo and Stillwater reservoirs this year. For Rossi, it was even less, forcing him to pick the best quarter of his cropland to irrigate and let the rest go dry.
“Being in this area all my life, this has been the worst that I’ve seen,” Rossi said. “We’ve had our (bad) years — 2012, 2002, 1977. This is the worst that it’s been for me.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Some ranchers in the Yampa basin had to cull a third of their herds before the spring calving season, said Todd Hagenbuch, Colorado State University’s extension agent for Routt County. This summer, many are trucking water to overstressed pastures to keep their cattle alive.
Agricultural producers are coping with similar challenges in river valleys all across Colorado’s Western Slope, where cumulative streamflows — a measure of the total amount of water that has flowed past a given point on a river since the previous October — range from near-record to record lows. In nearly a century of record-keeping, total water volumes have never been lower on the Colorado River at Cameo, just upstream of Palisade and Grand Junction, than they have been this year.
The effects of this extreme drought, part of a long-term warming and drying trend fueled by human-caused climate change, will be felt long after the dismal 2026 water year ends, even if hoped-for projections of a wetter-than-average winter come true. Hard choices will need to be made as feed remains scarce, and fuel, fertilizer and other input costs for farmers and ranchers continue to soar.
“Decisions being made with cattle herds in Grand County will be similar to the ones being made in Routt County, in Gunnison County, in Saguache County,” Mike Ritschard, a Middle Park rancher and Colorado River District board member, told a state water conference Thursday. “How do we hold it together for the next year and the year after? Do we cut cattle numbers to the feed we have? Do we buy feed and haul it to the cows so they can stay on the ranch? How much is the cost of hay or alfalfa, the cost of trucking?”
Other drought impacts can be felt across Colorado’s economy, especially in mountain resort towns where dry streams and rivers limit fishing and rafting and many reservoirs are closed to boating. But it’s the agricultural sector where chronic drought conditions pose the most immediate and existential threats.
Roughly 90% of the water used in Colorado goes towards irrigating farms and ranches, the overwhelming majority of it to grow alfalfa, grass pasture and other crops used to feed livestock. And as long-running discussions about the future of water in the West enter a tense, high-stakes new phase, Colorado agriculture hangs in the balance.
Hay bales lie in pastures near Stagecoach Reservoir in Routt County this week. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Just as experts and decision-makers from across the water policy landscape gathered in Steamboat Springs this week for the annual summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress, grim news arrived from about 600 river miles downstream: Water levels in Lake Powell, on the Colorado River along the Arizona-Utah border, had officially fallen to a record low, the Bureau of Reclamation announced. Further downstream, Lake Mead, which together with Lake Powell forms the backbone of a Colorado River Basin system that serves an area home to 40 million people, hit its own record low a week earlier.
Years of negotiations between Colorado and six other Colorado River Basin states have failed to produce a new long-term agreement on water allocations, and a set of federal operating guidelines for Lakes Powell and Mead that had been in place since 2007 will expire at the end of this year.
Under a new plan announced by the Bureau of Reclamation last month, Colorado would continue to be spared from federally-mandated cuts to water use, while the Lower Basin states of Arizona, Nevada and California could face sharp curtailments. The new guidelines, which must be finalized by October, appear increasingly likely to prompt a historic lawsuit by Arizona over allegations that Colorado and other Upper Basin states aren’t sending enough water downstream.



Quotation







Being in this area all my life, this has been the worst that I’ve seen.


– Philip Rossi, Routt County rancher


Addressing the Water Congress, Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, the Democratic nominee for governor and the heavy favorite in November’s general election, sounded some of his campaign’s most well-worn themes as he emphasized the role of “collaboration and innovation” in meeting drought challenges, and promised “a system of water management that involves real listening and grassroots governance.” But he and other elected officials from both sides of the aisle also drew a sharp line against efforts by other states that could harm Colorado water users.
“My job as attorney general — and I will take this responsibility as governor as well — is to defend our rights and interests,” Weiser said. “We’re not going to walk away from our hard-earned rights.”
U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, a Windsor Republican, put things even more bluntly.
“I have a lot of dear friends in Congress. One of them, hopefully, will be the next governor of Arizona, Andy Biggs — and I tell him all the time, ‘We’re getting our water back,'” Boebert said. “Y’all better get real good at that xeriscaping for your lawns and everything you’re building out there. Your cacti might do just fine. But we’re taking it back.”
U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, a Windsor Republican, spoke at the summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress on Wednesday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
 Threats of litigation
The seeds of the West’s current water-management crisis were planted in the 1920s, when the seven states making up the Colorado River Compact agreed to divide the basin’s water based on a faulty estimate of typical annual flows. The agreement allocates a total of 16.5 million acre-feet of water each year to its member states and Mexico, but 20th-century flows in fact averaged closer to 14 million acre-feet, and the onset of the region’s climate-fueled megadrought has depressed them even further, to an average of less than 10 million acre-feet.
After years of stalled negotiations between the states, the urgency of looming federal intervention and this summer’s extreme drought conditions doesn’t appear to have brought them any closer to a deal. On the contrary, it’s led to an increasingly bitter and public war of words between the Upper and Lower basins, with Colorado at the head of the former and Arizona leading the latter.
Vast scale of wildfire threats to Colorado watersheds far exceeds funding

As Colorado officials tell it, the Lower Basin states failed to recognize the threat posed by the post-2000 megadrought until it was too late, and spent years recklessly depleting Lakes Powell and Mead after it was clear conservation was necessary. The Upper Basin states have long used less than their full combined allocation of 7.5 million acre-feet. As the Colorado River’s headwaters state, Colorado has never been able to rely on upstream storage to meet its water needs; it’s the first to feel the impacts of dry years, its defenders say, and has modeled conservation efforts that the Lower Basin has been slow to adopt.
“The fact of the matter is that the Lower Basin didn’t take cuts until 2022,” Becky Mitchell, who leads the state’s Colorado River negotiations as its commissioner to the Upper Colorado River Commission, said during a Water Congress panel Thursday. “We’ve been in a record drought for nearly 20 years, and cuts were not taken from the releases from those reservoirs until 2022.”
“If we don’t make fundamental changes before we continue to look upstream for more, there’s not going to be an ATM to pull from, and that’s what I’m looking for in the next agreement,” she added.
“We cannot provide certainty to our Lower Basin neighbors that we, as Upper Basin water users, have never had ourselves,” said Amy Moyer, chief of strategy for the Colorado River District. “And this year demonstrates better than any other the lack of certainty for water users in Colorado.”
Some water experts, however — including former Colorado River District general manager Eric Kuhn — have disputed the Upper Basin states’ claim that they already routinely use less water in dry years. And some conservation advocates are beginning to see cuts to water use in Colorado as an expedient way to keep a threatened river system alive: “Every drop of Rocky Mountain water that California is legally entitled to supports thousands of miles of riparian habitat as it flows downhill to its destination,” wrote author Zak Podmore earlier this year.
The Colorado River flows through Palisade on June 9, 2023. (William Woody for Colorado Newsline)
The Lower Basin states, meanwhile, consider Colorado’s refusal to accept any mandatory cuts — a position reiterated by Mitchell and Moyer on Thursday — to be a dealbreaker. The Arizona Department of Water Resources has retained a top law firm as it prepares for a possible legal challenge against the Bureau of Reclamation’s post-2026 operating guidelines, and reiterated its legal threats in a letter to the Interior Department, which oversees the agency, last week.
“By refusing even to articulate its understanding of (Colorado River Compact) requirements, the Department gives Arizona neither transparency about how the River will be managed nor any basis on which to plan for its water future,” wrote ADWR director Thomas Buschatzke. “As a result, Arizona reserves the right to seek the resolution of its Compact rights in an appropriate judicial forum.”
Weiser, at the Water Congress, called federal intervention a “suboptimal situation.”
“We’re going to work to make sure we’re protecting all of our communities, and make sure that all basins can make reasoned and sustainable decisions,” he said. “I’m not going to be afraid to make the right deal. I’m also not going to be afraid to challenge the wrong deal.”
Later, Mitchell’s voice wavered with emotion as she responded to critics who say that what Colorado has offered at the negotiating table is “not enough.”
“I ask you to think about your children’s futures, and what you’re willing to give on their behalf,” Mitchell said. “When you say more, I want you to pick out who you want that to come from — and if it’s not yourself, then that’s not where the solution lies.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Tenn Republican Caucus chair irritated by extremism
description: After 16 years in the Tennessee Legislature, Rep. Jeremy Faison has had enough of political polarization. The Cosby Republican, who entered the General Assembly as more of a libertarian than a party ideologue, is heading home to the mountains of Cocke County, not necessarily because of fatigue, though it is a long drive, but feeling […]
text:
Republican House Caucus Leader Jeremy Faison is retiring from the Tennessee General Assembly after 16 years in office. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)After 16 years in the Tennessee Legislature, Rep. Jeremy Faison has had enough of political polarization.
The Cosby Republican, who entered the General Assembly as more of a libertarian than a party ideologue, is heading home to the mountains of Cocke County, not necessarily because of fatigue, though it is a long drive, but feeling caught up in the tug-of-war between the far left and far right.
For the last few years, Faison says, he’s been mulling the need for people outside of politics to raise their voices, “reminding us that America’s not where this ‘Democrat Socialist’ agenda is, and America’s not really where … when you have a big part of your party who wants to give a woman a felony that got an abortion, that’s not where America is at. America’s not where we think dudes ought to compete against girls.”

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
He acknowledges these are “extreme examples.” Tennessee doesn’t have any Democratic Socialists in the legislature. But he says those issues are becoming “litmus tests” in primaries in extremely partisan districts. Considering his job as House Republican Caucus chairman for the last few years was, and remains, to help GOP candidates win elections, this is a bit of a confession. 
“That’s not where America’s at, bro,” Faison says repeatedly.
Faison tries to take a common-sense approach. He once made a push to legalize medical marijuana but hasn’t broached the idea lately. 
He hasn’t steered completely clear of cultural issues, passing a bill this year requiring reports to the state on transgender procedures. Faison also passed the bill last year that ended the Tennessee Human Rights Commission and put it under control of the Attorney General’s Office, which hired less staff and took up far fewer cases. The move has raised questions about whether the state is doing enough to stamp out discrimination, but Faison said this week he’s OK with smaller staff.
On the odder side, he passed the measure this year that allows people to keep raccoons as pets.
Yet as House Republicans went full tilt this year — and last — for the White House’s aggressive immigration agenda, Faison wasn’t exactly a fan. He cites legislation that would have allowed school districts to charge tuition to immigrant children without citizenship status as a sticking point. 
The measure passed the Senate in 2025 but couldn’t find traction in the House as Majority Leader William Lamberth ran into concerns about losing $1.1 billion in federal funding if lawmakers violated the constitutional requirement to educate all children, including immigrant kids without full legal documentation. 
The faces of Faison








House Republican Caucus Chair Jeremy Faison, photographed in the Tennessee Capitol in 2021. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









As the 114th General Assembly drew to a close, Rep. Jeremy Faison rested his eyes during debate. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









House Republican Caucus leadership, from left: House Majority Leader William Lamberth, Caucus Chair Jeremy Faison, Assistant Majority Leader Ron Gant, and Speaker of the House Cameron Sexton photographed in 2022. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









Near the end of the 2024 legislative session, Faison made a nonverbal plea for a colleague to renew his motion on a bill, (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)






“Leader Lamberth is one of my best friends. Love him dearly,” Faison said. “He and Chairman (Bo) Watson filed that bill two years ago, and I saw a good group of people in my caucus agree with that, and in society. When I opposed it, I got burnt up at home opposing that. It definitely is somewhat popular in the GOP circle.”
He understands the cry coming from the right but says he has a “major issue” with it. Numerous lawmakers didn’t want to treat kids as pawns in the fight over immigration enforcement. 
“They knew it then, I had a major issue with it, and I was going to do everything I could to stop the bill,” he says. 
The House wound up turning it into a headcount bill this year, but Watson, a Chattanooga Republican, didn’t bring his version back to the Senate for approval.
“Once we turn our attention to things such as that just to excite our base … well, I can’t tell why they do that. But I think the left and the right are both doing this. That’s not where America’s at,” he says.
Faison, who owns a pest control company, definitely holds conservative credentials. He doesn’t favor the idea of socialism in which people claim to deserve to be fed and housed, preferring to point out that people deserve what they earn.
When he finally leaves politics, or at least the state legislature later this year, he wants to be able to push back and be a little more open, something that’s hard to do in a House Republican Caucus leadership post.
“Society’s downstream of government and politics. People think it’s vice-versa. It’s not,” he says.
Faison contends that’s why voting percentages are so low. People don’t like either candidate, so they stay home, saying, “this is ridiculous.” 
He wants to build up, not tear down. How he does that remains to be seen. But in the Tennessee Legislature, that’s hard to do, and Faison isn’t the only one saying farewell because of the fighting.
A big disappointment
Lame-duck Gov. Bill Lee pooh-poohed the idea of calling a special session this year to rehash Tennessee’s property appraisal laws to give a break to Broadway bar owners who’ve seen their taxes skyrocket in Nashville’s tourism district.
Asked this week if he would bring lawmakers back to Nashville, Lee said, instead, he spoke to Metro Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell about the impact of reappraisals and taxes on honky tonks and urged him to act.
Stockard on the Stump: Special session talk on tax appraisals rears its head

“It’s really important that we listen to business owners and we’re doing that and we’re hearing that,” Lee told reporters. “It’s also important to remember that the city makes collections for those business owners. So, I have talked to the mayor and I have encouraged him because the right direction to go there is for the city to provide temporary relief until a more permanent solution’s ready.”
The legislature passed legislation this year creating a state-controlled board to oversee $30 million in excess revenue and tap into $300 million in surplus funds held by the Nashville Convention Center Authority. It also allows the board to divert some of that money to Lower Broad businesses to pay property taxes. A bigger portion is expected to pay for part of Nashville’s 2030 Super Bowl bid.
Look for the legislature to take up something on property appraisals in 2027. But rewriting state laws to pick winners and losers among property owners is likely to run into constitutional problems. Such a move also puts the Republican-controlled legislature in danger of violating the values of capitalism they once held sacred.
A done deal
A saving grace for some Middle Tennessee motorists is one step closer to reality — if you live long enough — after a state transportation committee picked a consortium of transportation-related companies to build and operate toll lanes in southeast Nashville and down I-24.
DriveTN, which is made up of companies from Spain, France and Australia, offered to build lanes along I-40 and I-440 and down to Murfreesboro for $9.2 billion, nearly twice as much as the Department of Transportation estimated. The group promised to limit impact on local businesses and homeowners.
But clearly, the reason they’re getting the work is that they promised to give the state nearly $25 billion over the next 50 years. Two other bidding groups agreed to concede more than $7 billion and one bidder wanted the state to give it $250 million to start the job.
There’s no explaining why the offers are so divergent, except maybe that one group is ready to take a bigger risk. 
Tennessee taps road-building group for $9B toll lanes project

But this was a negotiated deal, not a hard bid. Thus, the nice packet of information stating why DriveTN is the preferred contractor, which was put together before the Transportation Modernization Committee cast any votes. State officials say more negotiations are forthcoming.
Somehow, the DriveTN group is planning to make a profit from tolls while spending $9.2 billion over about eight years and giving up almost $25 billion over half a century. The only way they can make money, though, is by charging motorists to use it. And they won’t collect a penny for several years, raising the question of whether anyone in the investment arm will be around to cash in. 
The state’s info packet assumes a minimum trip cost of $1 for the length of the roughly 30-mile corridor down I-24 toward Murfreesboro. That might be the case in the dark of night, not during rush hour. 
Toll rates in Virginia range from $2 on RMTA Powhite Parkway to $8.23 in peak periods on Midtown Tunnel from Norfolk to Portsmouth, according to TollGuru. Rates are dynamic on I-66, which is operated by the group that would run Tennessee’s toll lanes.
No doubt, motorists will have to make a “choice” about spending extra money to use these lanes, on top of the price of gas, which appears to depend on the next war. Investors are gambling that they’ll pay just about any price to get home a few minutes quicker.








U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn said she intends to appoint her Senate replacement. (Photo: John Partipilo/ Tennessee Lookout)









"We take governors one at a time," said Gov. Bill Lee on Wednesday when asked if he would attempt to fill a U.S. Senate vacancy created should U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn become governor. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)






One governor at a time, please
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican primary winner for this November’s election, says she’s going to pick her successor. And Lee doesn’t seem to be willing to get in her way.
Asked this week if he would try to circumvent Blackburn and pick her replacement, Lee said, “I think we will take governors one at a time, and I don’t give advice to the next governor.” He declined to comment further.
You’ll have to make your own interpretation. But one has to wonder if the inauguration took place Aug. 6.
The bigger point, though, is this: Either one of them at once is more than enough.
“Too much, too many people, too much” *
* “New York New York”, Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five 
Lookout photographer John Partipilo contributed to this week’s endeavour.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Some lawmakers frustrated by Morrisey’s hidden details of federal TANF spending
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey has tied continued delays with the school clothing allowance program to a looming shortfall in the federal funding that pays for the program. School has started around West Virginia while that program continues to be held up.
text:
House Health Chair Evan Worrell, R-Cabell, has requested more detailed information on how Gov. Patrick Morrisey is spending federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families funding. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Gov. Patrick Morrisey has tied continued delays with the school clothing allowance program to a looming shortfall in the federal funding that pays for the program. School has started around West Virginia while that program continues to be held up.
As lawmakers —both Republican and Democratic — have demanded answers from the administration for its handling of the back-to-school program, some elected officials are also frustrated by a lack of information about how the governor is spending federal funds. 
They want to know in detail how the state is using Temporary Assistance for Needy Families dollars, a federal block grant program that gives states broad flexibility with how they spend it.
Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“I want to make sure that a federal block grant that’s coming in for TANF is being utilized at its maximum potential to assist needy families in West Virginia,” said House Health Chair Evan Worrell, R-Cabell.
House Finance Committee member Del. John Williams, D-Monongalia, is in the dark about how the governor is spending the TANF funds. He stressed that it’s important to know this temporary assistance program will be available when needed.
“This isn’t just a bunch of freeloaders who buy beer and cigarettes, as has been illustrated with past comments,” Williams said. “These are people who found themselves in a really bad spot, and we need to make sure that this program, which they depend upon, is being administered the best way to get the best benefit to needy West Virginians.”
“There’s a lack of being forthright on the administration’s part,” he added.
Del. John Williams, D-Monongalia (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Back in May, Morrisey unexpectedly announced a projected multi-million structural deficit in TANF dollars, which the state uses to pay for its child care subsidy program, foster care and other programs helping low-income children and families. The announcement came after lawmakers finished the legislative session and the state budget was completed. 
West Virginia has around $98 million to use in TANF funding, but $137 million in expenses funded by those federal dollars, leaving a gap that Morrisey is trying to reduce. 
The state has less than 13 months — $41 million — in TANF carryover funds at this point, according to Morrisey.
West Virginia Watch asked Morrisey’s office for documentation about the TANF deficit and a breakdown of spending; that was not provided to our newsroom by deadline.
A spokesperson for Morrisey did not return a request for comment for this story.
The lack of clarity around spending comes after Morrisey wanted to use TANF dollars to pay for an outside education group linked to his political donations. The governor’s office said in May that the specific project was “still in the proposal (and) planning stage” during the TANF spending review.
Worrell, who sits on the House Finance Committee, has led the charge in the House on trying to gather information about how the governor is spending TANF dollars.
Morrisey’s office shared some TANF spending information with Worrell earlier this summer.
“Some questions were answered, some are still left,” Worrell said. “I received a response on Aug. 4th that said they were working on getting me the information. Today’s Aug. 19. I still don’t have anything.”
As part of his request, Worrell wants specific information on how the state is spending TANF dollars on its child care assistance program. Morrisey previously signaled that the TANF deficit could impact that program used by thousands of working West Virginia parents. 
“I think there’s a variety of ways to maybe reduce the spend in TANF to get it back under the federal block grant. But the department and the governor’s office has to be willing to share that information with us,” Worrell said.
The state also puts in around $25.8 million in funding toward TANF in what’s called a “maintenance of effort.” Worrell said lawmakers are owed a line-by-line breakdown of where that state money is spent. 



Quotation







The way this has been handled, and some would say mishandled, has had real consequences. It's time to set maybe the politics aside, come together for West Virginia's kids. 


– Jim McKay, state director of Prevent Child Abuse West Virginia


Jim McKay, state director of Prevent Child Abuse West Virginia, said the lack of clarity around the state’s TANF spending has led to instability for organizations working directly with children in need of help. There are ongoing concerns about state support for Family Support Centers, which were only granted TANF funding through this fall. 
“Everything is just up in the air unnecessarily when there is a state plan,” McKay said. “There’s a budget that’s been approved at the level requested by the administration each of the past two years, and yet contracts have been delayed every step of the way. There’s been more questions than answers.”
Lawmakers may consider using state dollars to keep programs open
TANF spending has increased under Morrissey, according to previous information from the governor’s office. Lawmakers recently learned that the state is using nearly $8 million in TANF dollars to pay for a broken online database system that is supposed to run Medicaid, foster care and more. 
Senate Finance Chair Jason Barrett, R-Berkeley. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
In the Senate, Finance Chair Jason Barrett, R-Berkeley, felt he had enough clarity on how the governor spent TANF funds. It “appears to be pretty cut and dry where the dollars are going,” he told West Virginia Watch.
“They’re going to spend just short of $137 million. Of that, the clothing voucher is $11.4 million, which is the same dollar amount as last year, is not an amount that was originally budgeted for fiscal year ‘27, but it is the same amount that was spent in fiscal year ‘26,” Barrett said. “I think I’m satisfied with the information they gave.”
While the governor’s office has full authority over how the state spends TANF, the Legislature could be tasked with deciding if they’ll invest state dollars to keep programs.
“That’s a decision that the entire Legislature will have to make,” Barrett said. “ … I’d be interested to hear what Senate members think, specifically Senate members on the Finance Committee … about where their priorities are, if using state dollars to supplement TANF is something they want to do.
Sen. Mike Oliverio, R-Monongalia. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Senate Finance Committee member Sen. Mike Oliverio, R-Monongalia, is hoping for more transparency on this issue from the governor’s office.
“I hope the governor’s office will be more forthcoming with some of the questions that were asked during the interim (meetings) that will help us craft policy solutions to help those citizens in need,” Oliverio said.
McKay stressed that TANF is a “critically important” program in West Virginia. 
“Its number one core purpose is to support families so that their children can remain home with their family. We know there’s a huge child welfare crisis, and the number of kids who are being placed into foster care is a huge challenge for our state,” McKay said. 
“The way this has been handled, and some would say mishandled, has had real consequences. It’s time to set maybe the politics aside, come together for West Virginia’s kids,” he said.

title: Alabama Public Library Service staff, board at odds over new compliance employee
description: Alabama Public Library Service staff Thursday advised members of the APLS board to not fill a position created to assist libraries with compliance with controversial administrative code changes over the last two years. Pennie Broussard, who works in the human resources department for APLS, told the Board she advised rescinding the posting without filling it.[...]
text:
A collection of books on display in Fairhope Public Library in Fairhope, Alabama on March 2, 2026. Members of the The Alabama Public Library Service (APLS) Board Thursday expressed concerns that parents will complain about library books in children's section after APLS staff recommended the board not fill a position designed to help local libraries comply with administrative code changes. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)Alabama Public Library Service staff Thursday advised members of the APLS board to not fill a position created to assist libraries with compliance with controversial administrative code changes over the last two years.
Pennie Broussard, who works in the human resources department for APLS, told the Board she advised rescinding the posting without filling it.

“We really have no need for this position,” she said. “The agency really has no need for this position. We have got an assistant director, and some of the duties that were mentioned for this position to do are Katie’s (Bailey) duties that she is graded on for her appraisal.”
Board Chair John Wahl, the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, and board member Amy Minton disagreed with the recommendation. Both said they believed the position was necessary after hearing from libraries about the resources required to make changes aligned with the code.
“I think putting someone in this role that could really work with local libraries, and make sure we go above and beyond, to make sure they do have someone they can lean on and a resource they can use, I think that is good for local libraries,” Wahl said in an interview after the meeting.
Read Freely Alabama, an organization opposed to restricting access to library books, also said that the position is unnecessary.
“Board member Amy Minton admitted that she intends for the ‘sole job’ of the assistant director to be to identify individual books libraries would be forced to censor or lose their state funding,” the organization said in a statement. “This creates a state censorship officer, and expands inappropriate state control over local libraries.”
Kelyn Ralya, the director of APLS, delayed a final decision because of the concerns from Minton and Wahl.
Staff said during the meeting that APLS cannot go into every library to review books shelved in the youth sections of libraries in the state. The only way to determine whether books have been appropriately shelved is to have the public inform the Board.
Staff members of the Fairhope Public Library traveled multiple times to Montgomery to address the APLS Board about their concerns related to the books. Wahl took it upon himself to read the books for about a month and found that Fairhope was not in compliance with the administrative code by keeping them in the teen’s section.
“So then, is the answer to these parents, who have gone to their local library, the answer is they come back to us?” Minton told the staff.
Ralya said that several libraries will likely not comply with the updated administrative code imposed by the APLS Board.
“They may be willing to leave state aid on the table,” Ralya said. The Fairhope Public Library refused to move books that Wahl claimed were not permitted in the youth section of the library.
APLS announced in March that it planned to advertise for the position.
“This position was an at-will position,” Minton said after the meeting. “It is not a merit position. It is literally in place to help these libraries, so no one loses their funding. We don’t want them to lose their funding.”
According to the job description, one of the responsibilities is to “serve as a point of contact in an advisory role for public libraries regarding policy and administrative code compliance.”
The person hired will also monitor legislation that lawmakers are considering that will affect APLS and respond accordingly, as well as develop relationships with board members, staff and policymakers to advance the goals of the agency that is responsible for distributing state aid to local libraries.
“That hard part is moving the books and identifying the books,” Minton said. Without assistance from APLS, Minton said, libraries may not move the materials but continue to receive state aid.
State libraries became a flashpoint of fighting between conservatives who claimed Alabama’s libraries had inappropriate material shelved in youth sections and critics who said the activists were attacking content with LGBTQ+ themes or characters. In 2024, the board required libraries to develop policies to limit access for minors to books considered sexually explicit, obscene and or “otherwise inappropriate” or risk losing their state aid.
In 2025, APLS changed the administrative code to bar books that dealt with “gender ideology,” a term the board did not define.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Talking about how we talk about things
description: Somehow we are supposed to have efficiency in government while not having efficiency in how we talk to each other about government. No wonder we get more of the same but louder, faster, harder.
text:
The West Virginia Legislature Capitol dome in Charleston, West Virginia. (Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)Somehow we are supposed to have efficiency in government while not having efficiency in how we talk to each other about government. No wonder we get more of the same but louder, faster, harder. 
In ancient Rome there was a job titled nomenclator, taken from the Roman way of naming things, who was an assistant or slave explaining who folks were and what they were doing. In a formal setting they announced important persons entering the room by title and such. Those important persons would also have a nomenclator attending them to subtly jog their memory as to names and details of whoever the next person to greet was, if need be. Modern important personages still have this in their assistants, entourages, crews, teams, so on and so forth. 
As for the term itself, by the time nomenclator worked its way through Latin then French and eventually English in the 17th century the meaning had shifted from the more literal “calling out a list” to a cataloging of common terms. By the end of The Enlightenment, our modern nomenclature term was set as a standardized naming and classification system for everything from science to art to technology. 
Scientists and professionals of the expanding and globalizing world figured out pretty quickly that standardized terms are essential for talking across languages, cultures, classes, professional fields of expertise, and educational levels. Without standard terms and universal classification and the understanding thereof, basic communication breaks down quickly and the opportunity for new ideas to cross human nature barriers never has a chance. 
Nomenclature matters.
Politics and the socio-cultural issues surrounding politics have a nomenclature problem, and the modern mix of changing news media and content creation information ecosystem that is both the headwaters and tributary to the media cycle is making it worse, not better. 
There is the general purpose, generalization nomenclature that makes for easy hot takes but poor discussion on substance against the always popular they, them, those over there. Magically useful singular,  plural and downright magical words worm through the discourse to apply to others but not yourself with specific unspecificity. 
One level up on the nomenclature is the nomenclature of groupings. “The rich” and “the poor” and “the middle class,” which all three have sliding meanings and means testing that means exactly what the wielder of the term means it to mean while not meaning what any inbound criticism means it to mean because why don’t you understand the plain meaning?
Then there is the thicket of omnidirectional terms and color coded meanings. “The left” is opposite “the right” and may or may not fit into Team Blue or Team Red. In America, Blue is usually the Democratic Party and the political left while the GOP is Red and political right. Except when you are railing against socialism and its cousin communism, both repping the color red, but those terms Team Red in America ascribe to Team Blue. Unless you are talking about the French fascists or Spanish Falange fascists who use blue, but are on the far right. 
See how confusing this is when nomenclature isn’t universally understood? 
Thankfully, by 1921 Frank and Lillian Gilbreths’ groundbreaking work on combining understanding of human nature and industrial labor invented the modern flow chart to help us keep things straight. While they were mostly working with and for major corporations, their work was particularly of interest to an exiled Russian feller named Lenin. Old Vlad took the scientific movement of time-motion studies the Gilbreths were part of and took “efficiency” in stark and horrifying new directions once he attained power. The Gilbreths meaning of “efficiency” led to what we now understand as ergonomics and work-life understanding; Lenin’s meaning of “efficiency” led to millions of dead and millions more suffering.  
Nomenclature matters. 
Complicated matters of policy and governance suffer from political word games when universal understanding is needed. Unproven companies from outside areas get tax breaks and government incentives for this proposed new business or that latest gizmo factory that will employ X amount of workers for Y amount of revenue to the economy, a big splashy headline. But too often those gotta-have-it-for-the-future promises wind up underdelivering if ever opening at all. This is termed “investment”. Meanwhile, declining areas lose services, lose schools, struggle with infrastructure, and other things that cost money but those needs are met with the term “fiscal responsibility”. 
It is a neat trick we do with political terminology. 
Mostly, folks from office holders to the media commentariat, to citizens on their social media accounts fall into the same habit of using nomenclature to take the nasty edges off the problems people have no easy answers for. There is no single fix for rural areas that either have to be heavily subsidized or will continue to decline. There is no easy fix for disproportionate growth in regions that have ready access to growing metro areas while other places are demographically bleed to death with an aging population, shocking declines in young people, and poor workforce participation for the ones who are left. 
There are tough choices to be made, with no easy words to dull the cutting edge. Not enough money to go around and political consideration as to who gets what are not new problems. Nor are issues like poverty, healthcare, infrastructure, education, economic growth, and the forbidden topic of managed decline. All of those issues incubate an ecosystem of terminologies that are easy to spout off in conversation or thumb into a phone but also makes rhetorical cul-de-sacs that keep folks from actually addressing the issues in a productive way towards a solution. Understand that school, that road, that water system, that hospital is something involving people and the first step to tyranny and suffering is always making people a line item instead of living, breathing, reactive individuals.Vastly imperfect individuals, who will require compromise and negotiation with unless they are just to be oppressed and told to shut up and deal with it. Which too often happens. Maybe some modern day Gilbreths will arise and make flowcharts to explain how social media and news media have created this chimera information monster which is everything everyone wants but nothing anyone doesn’t want it to be all at the same time.
Maybe just start with a simple term like “efficiency,” which, in a vacuum, governments at the local, state, and federal level could certainly use if applied correctly. The question is: will it be a Gilbreth model of “efficiency” or a Lenin model of “efficiency”?
Same word, vastly different outcomes for the people involved, while the nomenclature itself doesn’t care. No matter how much louder, faster, or harder it gets.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: A data center developer says it is committing to Beshear’s data center requirements
description: An investor-owned developer looking to build a hyperscale data center at an idled Hancock County aluminum smelter says it’s committing to the governor’s requirements to pay its share of taxes, follow environmental laws and “build a meaningful relationship” with the community.  That’s according to an “energy plan” that TeraWulf filed before the state utility[...]
text:
Century Aluminum is selling its idled Hawesville smelter in Western Kentucky to a data center company after choosing Oklahoma as the site for a new smelter, the first built in the U.S. since 1980.  (Century Aluminum photo)An investor-owned developer looking to build a hyperscale data center at an idled Hancock County aluminum smelter says it’s committing to the governor’s requirements to pay its share of taxes, follow environmental laws and “build a meaningful relationship” with the community. 
That’s according to an “energy plan” that TeraWulf filed before the state utility regulator Kentucky Public Service Commission on Aug. 14. Developer TeraWulf said the plan is a part of complying with an executive order issued by Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear. 
The governor said his executive order would implement an array of protections against the potential impacts of data centers, though some experts have questioned how much legal “teeth” his order has without the backing of specific state laws addressing data centers. 
Still, TeraWulf wrote in its Aug. 14 filing it was committing to the governor’s demands laid out in the order. 
“TeraWulf is committed to invest billions of dollars in Kentucky to construct a state-of-the-art data center which will provide significant economic benefits to Hancock County and its school system,” the company wrote in its plan. “TeraWulf takes Governor Beshear’s executive order, the commission approval process, its commitment to the local community, and its commitment to the commonwealth very seriously.”
TeraWulf wants to build a 482-megawatt hyperscale data center at the site of the former Century Aluminum smelter that halted operations in 2022, a project that has the backing of artificial intelligence company Anthropic. It also wants to build another hyperscale data center at an Eastern Kentucky industrial park, telling investors recently it wants to expand the size of it.
The Kentucky Public Service Commission is considering whether to approve a special electricity contract for the Hancock County project with electric utility Big Rivers Electric Corporation. Hancock County residents have voiced strong concerns to the commission about, among other issues, the potential local environmental impacts of the data center. 
Beshear’s executive order seeks to implement a number of protections against the impacts of data centers by requiring them to commit to “paying their full and fair share of state and local taxes” and to engage in fully transparent and public discussions with a community where the developer wants to locate. 
Additionally, the order requires data center developers to submit an energy plan to the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet, the state’s environmental regulator, explaining how the developer would source its electricity and protect residential ratepayers from being burdened with costs. TeraWulf wrote it had also submitted a copy of its energy plan to the cabinet. 
Addressing the commitments in the executive order, TeraWulf wrote it would get its electricity from the MISO regional energy grid through a “carefully structured” contract with the Big Rivers Electric Corporation. The company also wrote that its operations would generate tens of millions of local tax revenue. 
In an Aug. 7 comment filed to the Public Service Commission, an attorney for an enviornmental legal group raised several concerns he had about uncertainties with the proposed special contract for TeraWulf, though he didn’t weigh in on whether the commission should approve the contract.
Kentucky Resources Council Attorney Byron Gary, who also filed his comment on behalf of the advocacy nonprofit Kentuckians for the Commonwealth, wrote that neither TeraWulf nor the Big Rivers Electric Corporation had conducted an “independent” economic analysis of the proposed project. He also asked the commission to examine the allocation of costs of regional electricity transmission upgrades — and whether other ratepayers would pay for it — spurred by the project.
Included with TeraWulf’s plan is an Aug. 13 letter from Hancock County Judge-Executive Johnny Roberts, where he writes to the Energy and Environment Cabinet and the commission that the company has demonstrated “transparency, open communication, and genuine community engagement.” 
“While every large infrastructure project deserves careful evaluation, I believe Tera Wulf has demonstrated the character, transparency, and commitment that is required by the executive order, and that Kentucky should encourage the same for other data center projects,” Roberts wrote in the provided letter. “They have earned my confidence through their actions, and we are excited about the opportunity to welcome them into our community.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland launches court-ordered mental health care in Baltimore, some counties
description: Maryland health officials are rolling out a new and controversial program to help those with severe mental health challenges stay on top of their treatment --  by using a court order to mandate that those patients comply with their medical plans.
text:
Anne Arundel County is one of the first local jurisdictions that will allow circuit courts to mandate that someone suffering from severe mental health challenges adhere to a determined treatment plan. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Maryland health officials are rolling out a new and controversial program to help those with severe mental health challenges stay on top of their treatment —  by using a court order to mandate that those patients comply with their medical plans.
The Maryland Department of Health on Thursday announced the launch of the new Assisted Outpatient Treatment program that will grant mental health professionals, concerned family members or friends the ability to petition a circuit court for someone to receive mandated medical treatments for their mental health conditions.
Some conditions, such as bipolar disorder or schizophrenia, can interfere with the patient’s ability to recognize that they need medical care, depending on how their conditions manifest.
Such situations can lead to repeated hospitalization or incarceration for an individual suffering from behavioral health challenges, while being heartbreaking for families who watch a loved one’s struggle with mental health.
“For many individuals living with severe mental illness, maintaining engagement and consistency in treatment can be a daily challenge,” Maryland Health Secretary Meena Seshamani said in a statement announcing the launch. “The Assisted Outpatient Treatment program is designed to bridge the gap between an individual’s struggle and effective, consistent care by creating a structured pathway to community-based treatment, stability and recovery.”
But it’s still a controversial proposal.
County leaders look for options as budgets get tighter

Disability rights advocates have raised concerns that assisted outpatient treatment orders step on a patient’s right to make their own medical decisions, referring to the program as “involuntary outpatient commitment.” Meanwhile, local officials are still working out logistics with state officials on how to implement the program.
“We’re going to work to make this program as successful as we can, because this is a serious program,” said Karrington Anderson, associate policy director with the Maryland Association of Counties. “We want to do this in the best way possible, making sure that everything is being considered from the ethical side to implementation and do it as effectively as possible.”
The program starts in Baltimore City, Anne Arundel county and counties on the Eastern Shore, with statewide implementation for all Maryland jurisdictions in July 2027.
Under the program, a medical professional or any person with a relationship with the patient can petition for an AOT plan using an online form. The “respondent” will have the option to voluntarily enter the plan, but there are few details on what happens next if the patient does not cooperate.
Back when the Maryland General Assembly debated the legislation in 2024, Maryland was one of just three states without assisted outpatient treatment programs. Disability rights advocates testified against the legislation, concerned by unanswered questions on how enforcement would work if the individual does not agree to the court-ordered treatment plan.
They worried that the law could lead to traumatizing interactions with state agents, leading to further distrust in court systems and hospital settings.
Meanwhile, the development of the program had some “surprises” over the last few years.
When the bill passed in 2024, local governments had two options. They could develop their own assisted outpatient treatment program or defer to the state health department to build the program.
Should people with severe mental health needs get court-ordered treatment? State Senate to decide

All 24 jurisdictions in the state deferred to the state health department for implementation, and none opted to develop a county-run program.
“A lot of that was because there were a lot of unanswered questions,” Anderson said. “The health officers and local behavioral health authorities didn’t feel like they had the information to move forward in a responsible way.
“There was a lot of back-and-forth in the interim,” she said. “We feel like we got to a good landing spot.”
But this year, she said county officials were “surprised” to see new budget language that will require local governments to reimburse the state for AOT services provided by the state starting in fiscal year 2028.
Language added to the Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act this past session said counties would be required to reimburse 25% of state funds used for AOT service in the jurisdiction. The BRFA language says that counties would be reimbursing the state 100% by 2031 for opting into the state-run version of the assisted outpatient treatment program.
It was an unexpected “cost shift” to counties that Kerrington said should have had more discussion.
“We understand the state is in a difficult financial situation,” she said. “We would have liked to see that have its own hearing, so there could have been conversation rather than that happening in the BRFA.”
“It’s difficult to figure out how much this costs,” Anderson said. “We still have a lot of questions, but we’re going to partner with the state where we can.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Going from good to great in Kentucky’s education reform story
description: In the 1990’s, Kentucky set the pace for the nation in improving education outcomes. We led with a national following not unlike the heyday of University of Kentucky Wildcat fever; we were the ones to watch! We climbed from the bottom of the national rankings to the middle. Now, led by Kentucky’s educators who helped […]
text:
Kentucky's education reform movement is continuing to grow, says Brigitte Blom. (Getty Images)
In the 1990’s, Kentucky set the pace for the nation in improving education outcomes. We led with a national following not unlike the heyday of University of Kentucky Wildcat fever; we were the ones to watch! We climbed from the bottom of the national rankings to the middle. Now, led by Kentucky’s educators who helped make that improvement happen – the players on the championship team court – Kentucky is positioned to take the next giant leap to the top tier of all states with new legislation enacted this past spring.
As the new school year begins, Kentucky’s public schools are growing from standards-based accountability, which led to the 1990’s improvement, to community-connected vibrant learning. Local innovation and community partnership are the levers of change and will ensure success of Kentucky’s move from foundational improvement in education to deeper learning that equips more students with the skills, knowledge and experiences they will need for future success and upward mobility.   
Three innovations are key to this next chapter in Kentucky’s education reform story, and they will surely succeed with robust community partnerships and local engagement.

Vibrant learning experiences will help ensure students do work that matters to them. This can mean reporting on local history, rebuilding computers, researching uses for the invasive kudzu vine, or anything else that offers a genuine, meaningful, relevant challenge for an individual learner. Vibrant learning builds student engagement and agency – helping each learner discover what they love, what they do well, what the world needs, and how their talents can support a good living. 
Writing across the curriculum will mean students can communicate effectively in science, history, art, mathematics, social studies and other subjects. Kentucky will no longer give statewide writing tests. Instead, local programs will call for relevant writing connected to what students are studying and designed to build skills they can use for a lifetime: evaluating information, organizing arguments, sharing insights effectively with others. These are durable skills Kentucky employers say they need most – built right inside academic content.
Local indicators of quality will allow each school district to design part of its own accountability measures. School districts in partnership with their community will define their local goals for students, including things like being effective problem solvers, inspired innovators, responsible collaborators, or having a service orientation. Through teaching and learning in each subject, still aligned to the Kentucky Academic Standards, teachers will move students toward the locally defined goals. Districts may create “dashboards” to transparently report student progress to the community, giving a more holistic snapshot of student success. 

Each of these innovations require community involvement if they are to result in the added improvement in student learning that will take Kentucky from good to great. And, together, these key enhancements to Kentucky’s education reform story can help a high school diploma signal real readiness for post-high school success and fuel our continued climb to the top tier of the nation in education outcomes.  
This work will need authentic teamwork by schools and communities working closely together. Community members should be invited to the design table to discuss local indicators that matter most to students, families, and businesses locally. Once the design phase with the community’s input is complete, community-connected vibrant learning will need the support of community members in many fields and across many kinds of lived experiences. Students will be seeking mentors, people they can interview, folks who can share tools or space or time with younger learners, internships and apprenticeships, community partners extending learning outside the classroom and a wide variety of other supports. 
Finally, local accountability will require checking on how close students are to meeting local goals and supporting continuous improvement of a system of partnership with students and families at the center. In many places, educators and community volunteers will review student “demonstrations of learning.” Everywhere, teams will need to check how well things are going for students who have often been overlooked or underserved, including those from less prosperous families, those with major learning differences, and those from varied cultural backgrounds. 
This is an exciting next phase of Kentucky’s story. One that calls us all to be part of the movement, part of the good to great story. By working together, we can build strong schools, foster powerful partnerships, and achieve real results for today’s students and for Kentucky’s future. It’s time to ask locally how you can be part of the effort – and commit to showing up in the arena as one of Kentucky’s #1 fans! 
At the Prichard Committee, we’ve shared explanations, examples and resources to support school-community partnerships at prichardcommittee.org/vibrant.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. health dept. improves nursing home inspection backlog, reforms sanction criteria for facilities
description: Stories of neglect in care or unsanitary living situations have plagued several of Virginia’s nursing home facilities in recent years and data backs up a lapse in oversight by state agencies.  With reform efforts underway, the Virginia Department of Health officials said they aim to adopt sanction criteria by the end of the year to […]
text:
(Getty Images)Stories of neglect in care or unsanitary living situations have plagued several of Virginia’s nursing home facilities in recent years and data backs up a lapse in oversight by state agencies. 
With reform efforts underway, the Virginia Department of Health officials said they aim to adopt sanction criteria by the end of the year to rein in bad actors and get troubled facilities back on track. 
As of July, 58% of Virginia’s nursing homes were overdue for inspections and 68 of Virginia’s 289 nursing homes were found to have serious deficiencies, according to ProPublica. Several of the state’s flagged facilities with numerous deficiencies also had high staffing turnover rates. 
The issue has been salient among various healthcare spaces, including VDH. 
In recent years, the state health department has grappled with staffing turnover — some of which stemmed from COVID-19-era retirements and burnout — along with management and financial issues that the agency has worked to overcome. 
But problems within VDH also meant problems within nursing homes have not always received swift remedies or reprimand. 
How the Virginia Department of Health is healing internal issues amid federal funding cuts

A series of WTVR investigations over the past year revealed deficiencies in nursing homes ranging from failure to report violence between residents, lack of attention to residents’ health conditions like incontinence, or misuse of medications. 
Office of Licensure and Certification Director April Dovel, who stepped into her role late last year, has spent the bulk of this year making adjustments to get nursing home oversight operating smoothly.  
To start, VDH has worked on hiring more inspectors and getting them trained for the job.
Industry representatives like the Virginia Health Care Association have supported state laws to boost oversight efforts and adjust once-stagnant licensing fees. 
“They agreed to an increase in licensing fees so that we can increase our staffing,” Dovel said. “They want us to come out and complete these surveys.”
Bulked up staffing doesn’t translate to the agency immediately dispatching inspectors around the state in droves, Dovel said.
The federally-required training has typically taken a year to complete but Dovel’s team has pared the training process down to six months by providing trainees on-the-job experience in team outings for re-certification processes. 
Seasoned staff handle investigations into filed complaints.
To date, she said, all new staff that have taken their certification tests within six months have passed. 
In addressing backlogged inspections, she said her team has triaged the situation by focusing investigators on facilities that racked up multiple allegations. 
More recently, VDH is fielding public comment on a proposed sanction mechanism Dovel said she hopes will be in effect by the end of the year.
Key provisions include that if a facility has had the same or similar violation on two consecutive inspections, the same violation three times within 18 months and repeated failures in correcting deficiencies, that entity could lose its license. 
Sanctions would fall into three levels. The first step would be restriction on new admissions. Level two would entail a prohibition on new admissions and reaching level three would revoke or suspend a facility’s license. 
If a nursing home is marked for closure, Dovel explained that her team regularly meets with officials in the Department of Medical Assistance Services and the Department of Aging and Rehabilitative Services to brainstorm how residents may be relocated to other nursing homes.
Public comment runs on the state’s regulatory town hall website until Sep. 9. People are already chiming in. 
“Thank you for tightening (regulations), decreasing backlogs and increasing inspectors,” wrote an anonymous commenter who said they lived in a rural area of the state. 
The person described nursing homes with broken heating or air conditioning, residents with unchanged bandages and the presence of pests and cleanliness issues in facilities. 
Rural areas leave families little choice of where to house their aging loved ones, the commenter wrote, adding that meaningful enforcement can help ensure facilities fix issues. 
“Please don’t give up, just push harder and keep asking for more help,” the person wrote. “Those are people living in these places, and they don’t deserve what they are getting.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: After eastern groundwater report detailed aquifer concerns, Va. lawmakers consider policy shifts
description: After the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality released a 117-page report indicating that available groundwater east of Interstate-95 is “declining (in) availability in the near future,” the agency pitched recommendations on how to tackle the issue to lawmakers Thursday in Richmond.  The report detailed the groundwater needs for the Eastern Groundwat[...]
text:
The International Paper mill at Franklin, Va., photographed in August 2019, is one of the largest users of groundwater in the Eastern Virginia Groundwater Management Area. (Photo by Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury)After the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality released a 117-page report indicating that available groundwater east of Interstate-95 is “declining (in) availability in the near future,” the agency pitched recommendations on how to tackle the issue to lawmakers Thursday in Richmond. 
The report detailed the groundwater needs for the Eastern Groundwater Management Area, and showed that the region would not be able to handle any new major water withdrawal permits for industry use without risking water availability.
It also outlined potential impacts from ground subsidence and saltwater intrusion into the aquifers in the management area.
The report triggered a bipartisan set of senators to request that Gov. Abigail Spanberger call a special session to address potential policy changes and solutions. Spanberger has not publicly responded to that request.
Virginia senators request special session to act on ’deeply alarming’ groundwater report

DEQ Director Mike Rolband told legislators Thursday that the state’s Groundwater Management Act of 1992 has had mixed results. While water withdrawals have significantly reduced, the issues laid out in the report are still present and could present major challenges if left unaddressed.
One potential solution is the SWIFT water injection project that is currently under construction. It  will conduct regular injections of highly treated wastewater back into the aquifer to help raise the water levels. 
The Hampton Roads-based project has already done a test run of injecting one billion gallons of water. One of the locations, set to start daily operations of about 10 million gallons a day off the James River, will begin in October. Another location is anticipated to begin injections in 2029.
It is an experimental project that has never been performed in Virginia before, and is one of the largest projects of its kind in the nation, according to DEQ representatives. Still, DEQ’s water availability concerns remain, especially since it will take time for the water injections to spread through the aquifer. 
“It would be a good idea to, you know, take the bull by the arms and try to solve those problems. So we don’t have to worry about the future,” Rolband said.
Lawmakers also considered whether the state and localities should invest in more treated water injection projects farther north in the groundwater management area, which would help send more water to areas in need. 
The agency proposed several policy recommendations that would have to be enacted by the General Assembly.
DEQ suggested the legislature allow the department more discretion in being able to deny water withdrawal permits. The agency is also seeking more autonomy to direct permit applications towards alternate water sources such as wastewater reuse or reducing leaks in existing infrastructure.
The department also asked for increased funding to hire more staff to study the groundwater issues and manage permit reviews. 
The biennial budget lawmakers passed and Spanberger signed in late June includes funding to allow the department to locate potential sites for a SWIFT-like project in Northern Virginia. 
DEQ representatives also suggested that the price of groundwater withdrawal fees could be increased to pay for more projects like the SWIFT injections.
The Chesapeake Bay Foundation weighed in at the meeting with a suggestion for lawmakers to scrutinize the existing Groundwater Management Act to find the weak points allowing a projected decline in water availability, even though the aquifer is stable for the time being.
“Because we have been here before. And so, I know we have sort of conflicting opinions on the efficacy, but we are once again projected to decline, despite having the Groundwater Act in place,” said Jay Ford with CBF.
Ford said the closure of a paper mill in Franklin that has since partially reopened at a reduced rate was part of the reason the aquifer was able to stabilize after years of decline.
Mission H2O, a group representing industrial, municipal and agricultural industries, stated in a presentation that the aquifer is stabilized and that the 1992 law has been successful in reducing permitted water withdrawals. 
They said SWIFT is revolutionary in terms of improving groundwater levels but acknowledged the need for further discussions on how to manage unpermitted withdrawals from the groundwater management area, which reportedly take up a third of the water use.
“The aquifer is better understood, continues to be monitored, and is stable,” said Andrea Wortzel, a representative of Mission H20 Virginia. “Existing protections and regulatory authority are working and will continue to work. SWIFT is a game changer that will further improve the situation.”
Despite the industry representatives’ testimony, Rolband and Ford agreed that policy shifts are necessary to make human consumption the top priority when maintaining groundwater in the eastern region of the commonwealth.
“The biggest concern, if you do nothing, is if SWIFT is not as good as we hope this is gonna be, we’re gonna have a problem,” Rolband said. “We think that things are relatively balanced right at this moment, but a slight damage trend. SWIFT could show us a slight upward trend. But we’re, you know, it’s just kicking the can down the road. It’s been a problem for over 30 years.” 



 Groundwater report prompts senator’s letter over proposed Amazon data center

DEQ’s report also outlined potential impacts from data centers on the growing decline of groundwater availability in the eastern region. On the day of the hearing, Sen. Richard Stuart, R-King George, wrote to Director Mike Rolband about a proposed Amazon data center that has applied to withdraw 6.4 million gallons of water a year from the Potomac aquifer for its cooling system.
Stuart expressed his “firm opposition” to the permit being granted, pointing to the report explicitly stating that the aquifer would not be able to handle new major water withdrawals. 
Meanwhile, DEQ has asked King George County to shift to surface water use from the Rappahannock River, which has experienced historic lows due to drought this year.
“The Commonwealth should not tell the people of King George County that the aquifer is too depleted for their drinking water while declaring it available for a data center campus. Issuing this permit would make a mockery of the Department’s own findings,” Stuart wrote in his Aug. 20 letter.
The senator urged DEQ to deny the permit based on the findings of its own report.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Judge rejects request to move redistricting lawsuit from Dorchester County
description: A Dorchester County judge rejected a request to move a lawsuit challenging the state's proposed new redistricting regulations to Anne Arundel County, meaning two challenges to the planned constitutional amendment will move on two tracks on a tight timeline.
text:
A Dorchester County Circuit Court Judge has denied a motion to move a challenge of a constitutional amendment on redistricting to Annapolis where another case is set for a hearing on Aug. 31. (Maryland Matters illustration)A Dorchester County judge rejected a request to move a lawsuit challenging the state’s proposed new redistricting regulations to Anne Arundel County, meaning two challenges to the planned constitutional amendment will move forward on two tracks on an extremely tight timeline.
The Dorchester lawsuit was the second by filed by Republicans aiming to block the proposed amendment, a week after the case in Anne Arundel County. An attorney representing the Maryland State Board of Elections had asked that the cases be consolidated in Annapolis, where the first case is set to heard by the end of the month.
Language for the Nov. 3 general election ballot has to be approved by Aug. 31.
At issue is House Bill 2100, a proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution passed earlier this month.
If approved by voters, the amendment to the Maryland Constitution would effectively nullify a 2022 decision by Judge Lynne Battaglia that struck down a 2021 congressional map. Battaglia’s decision cited language in the state constitution that requires districts be compact, contiguous and mindful of jurisdictional and geographic boundaries — language that had always been interpreted to apply only to legislative districts, not congressional districts.
Battaglia’s ruling was not precedent but created enough of a concern that it hamstrung efforts by House Democrats to pass a bill that redrew the state’s eight congressional districts. Democrats eager to respond to a wave of hyper-partisan mid-cycle redistricting in red and blue states wanted to put Rep. Andy Harris’s 1st District in the crosshairs.
Maryland Republicans predict legal challenge to constitutional amendment on redistricting

Harris, whose district stretched from the Atlantic Ocean to a portion of easter Baltimore County, is the only Republican in Maryland’s eight-member congressional delegation. Democrats were hoping a redrawn map would allow the party to run the table and control all of the congressional seats.
That effort was stymied earlier this year by Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City). The Senate leader cited the Battaglia decision as potential problem.
But Ferguson changed his mind in May as he faced a primary opponent who adopted congressional redistricting as a key campaign issue at the same time the U.S. Supreme Court effectively gutted the Civil Rights-era Voting Rights Act. It also came after Republican lawmakers in Indiana who blocked redistricting there were turned out by primary challengers backed by President Donald Trump, who has called on GOP-controlled states to redraw maps for party advantage in this fall’s elections.
The constitutional amendment that could head to voters in November would make it clear that the compact and contiguous language in the Battaglia decision only applies to state legislative districts.
The challenge in Dorchester, while similar to one filed in Annapolis on Aug. 6, focuses on how the proposed amendment would end protections in the state’s 250-year-old bill of rights and “strip away all criteria” that a court could use to determine the legality of a congressional map.
Opponents of the amendment say it would effectively leave Maryland residents with no legal avenues to challenge future redistricting maps in a state where the Democratic Party holds supermajorities in the House and Senate and 2-1 edge in voter registration over Republicans.
Plaintiffs in the Dorchester County case include four state lawmakers and a member of that county’s Republican Central Committee. One of the plaintiffs said they believed keeping the case in an Eastern Shore county was important.
“I think this was the only option for the Eastern Shore. I think everyone wanted to have the case heard in the area most affected. It’s an extra layer of assurance,” Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Lower Shore), a plaintiff in the case, said in an interview earlier this week.
Sen. Chris West (R-Baltimore County), another plaintiff in the case, said the case was filed in Dorchester because attorneys were “trying to find a judge they thought would give it [the case] a fair shake.”
As of Thursday afternoon, the Dorchester judge had not set a hearing schedule.
The Annapolis case was filed by members of the Maryland House Freedom Caucus, the Senate minority leader and minority whip, and the president of a conservative advocacy group, the Oversight Project. Motions and briefs in that case must be filed by Friday. The judge in the case has ordered an in-chambers conference on Aug. 25 and set aside a full day on Aug. 31 for a hearing.
